articles.title: North Korea defense minister dismissed — state media
articles.summary: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea’s defense minister has been dismissed as part of a reshuffle of the country’s military leadership, state media reported Sunday. The “structural…

blocks.text: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea’s defense minister has been dismissed as part of a reshuffle of the country’s military leadership, state media reported Sunday.
The “structural reorganization plans” were decided during a meeting on Saturday led by Kim Jong Un, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.
No Kwang-chol was not only dismissed as defense minister but also demoted in the ruling party leadership to first vice director of the Munitions Industry Department, KCNA said.
Kim Song Gi, director of the General Political Bureau of the Korean People’s Army, was named as the new defense minister.
Another senior official, Defense Advisor Pak Jong Chon, was given the position of vice chairman of the Central Military Commission and named to the ruling party’s Political Bureau.
Several other promotions were also announced.
In a separate report, KCNA said Kim had lauded scientists, researchers and officials at a ceremony on Saturday for their advances in defense technology, giving them top national honors.

The honorees greatly contributed to “resolving scientific and technological problems of epochal significance in developing new combat weapon systems,” KCNA said, without specifying the type of system.
In late June, Kim oversaw tests of a new extended-range multiple rocket launcher and artillery systems.
The leadership shuffle comes shortly after joint annual drills between South Korea and the United States wrapped up.
The drills, which are regularly denounced by Pyongyang as preparations for an invasion, were closely watched this year after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered them to be shortened.
Trump criticized the drills as provocative toward the North and bashed Seoul for not supporting his war against Iran.
The U.S. president also praised North Korean leader Kim, whom he met twice during his first term in office, as he eyes a new meeting, potentially this year.
Despite Trump’s overtures, North Korea has shown little sign of reciprocating, firing missiles and condemning the scaled-down drills.
Pyongyang has also slammed Washington’s approval of arms sales to South Korea and plans to fund programs documenting human rights abuses in the North. /das

articles.title: Officer killed, another wounded in South Carolina park shooting
articles.summary: A South Carolina police officer died and a second was injured in a “gunfight” Saturday in a park that followed a call about a domestic dispute, Columbia police Chief W.H. “Skip” Holbrook said. The…

blocks.text: A South Carolina police officer died and a second was injured in a “gunfight” Saturday in a park that followed a call about a domestic dispute, Columbia police Chief W.H. “Skip” Holbrook said.
The suspect, a 33-year-old man with a lengthy criminal record, also died, Holbrook said at a news conference in the capital city.
The deceased officer, 29-year-old Christopher DeLong, had been with the police department for two years and leaves behind a wife and two young children, Holbrook said.
“Our hearts are broken this evening,” he said, appearing to be choked up at times.
DeLong’s wife, in a social media post, praised her husband as the “best dad to our babies” and said she was “living a nightmare.”

After a Saturday night news conference, Holbrook and other law enforcement officials joined in a procession from the hospital. The second officer, David Dymock, was in stable condition, the chief said.
“I hope that our officers know that they’re not alone in this. We will lean on each other in this tragic time,” Holbrook said. “Let’s pray for this department.”
The shooting unfolded after a woman called police around 9:30 a.m. Saturday saying a man who she had a restraining order against was destroying property at her home.
DeLong quickly arrived on scene and learned the suspect had left the residence. The woman gave DeLong a description of the suspect and vehicle description, the chief said.
Around 10:30 a.m. DeLong left the home but just minutes later he initiated a call about a suspicious person after seeing a man near a vehicle that matched the woman’s description, Holbrook said.
Dymock arrived as backup and minutes later radioed that officers “were hit and a suspect was down,” the chief said.

The suspect was Adam Tyler Dowdy, a man with a history of arrests across at least four states who had faced charges including disorderly conduct, contempt of court, public intoxication, possession of a controlled substance and probation violations, the chief said.

Holbrook, who did not take questions at the news conference, said the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division would investigate the shooting. A spokesperson for that agency said in an email that the investigation was ongoing. /das

articles.title: Heavy rainfall alert up in 23 Luzon areas due to habagat
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Due to the southwest monsoon, or “habagat,” state meteorologists warned of heavy rainfall of up to 200 millimeters in 23 Luzon provinces on Sunday. In its 5 a.m. outlook, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Due to the southwest monsoon, or “habagat,” state meteorologists warned of heavy rainfall of up to 200 millimeters in 23 Luzon provinces on Sunday.

In its 5 a.m. outlook, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said an orange rainfall warning was in effect over Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac and Pampanga.
Under an orange rainfall warning, these areas are expected to experience 100 to 200 millimeters of rain in the next 24 hours.

Meanwhile, a yellow rainfall warning was hoisted over Metro Manila, Ilocos Norte, Abra, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro.
These areas are anticipated to receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rain within the day.
According to Pagasa, three weather systems are being observed inside the Philippine area of responsibility.
These are Tropical Depression Sauder, formerly Obet, which is not directly affecting the country; a low-pressure area east of extreme northern Luzon; and the monsoon.

“Right now, the southwest monsoon or habagat is still the main weather system affecting the country, particularly parts of Luzon. A large part of the western section of Luzon has been affected by the cloudiness brought by the southwest monsoon,” Pagasa weather specialist Obet Badrina reported. /das

articles.title: Nepal, China floods: Rescuers dig as missing toll nears 3,000
articles.summary: BIDUR, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China on Saturday battled to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan…

blocks.text: BIDUR, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China on Saturday battled to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing entire villages.
Figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 682 bodies recovered — and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India.
In a breakthrough late Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” Home Minister Sudan Gurung said in a statement.
More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
The US Geological Survey said a glacial collapse was behind the deadly torrent on Wednesday at the Nepal-Tibet border.
While the exact cause of the collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
“The sudden glacial collapse and flash flood is a devastating reminder of how fragile these mountain environments can be”, UN climate chief Simon Steill said in a statement.

“We also know a warming climate, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making tragedies like this one, and so many others around the world, much more likely, frequent and severe, with vulnerable communities often hardest hit,” he added.
‘Nothing left’
Survivors face an agonizing wait to learn the fate of missing relatives, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. “There is nothing left.”
At an army base serving as a key rescue hub in Bidur, relatives crowded around lists of rescued people pasted on a wall.

“I have come here looking for my son,” said Kalka Sharda, scanning the list in desperation. “He was a labourer at the hydropower plant, but I can’t find his name, and the authorities are not saying anything.”

In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority listed 933 hydropower workers among the missing, along with 517 foreigners, including trekkers and Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
The Isha Foundation, led by Indian guru Sadhguru, said in an Instagram post on Saturday that 80 members had been on a group trip in the area.
The group was at the hard-hit Chinese border port of Gyirong, which has been “completely washed away”, the post said.
“At this time, there seems to be no encouraging indications of survivors at the immigration office area.”
‘Enormous’ trauma

The United States will provide $3.6 million in humanitarian aid to Nepal, the State Department announced Saturday, including emergency food assistance. This came after Washington pledged $500,000 in the initial aftermath of the disaster.
Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the reconstruction bill could run into “billions of dollars”.
“The urgency is on rescue and saving lives as much as we can,” he said, appealing for specialised assistance, including heavy-lift drones and technology to help locate people who are trapped.
He also called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them, saying bodies that have been in water could decompose at a faster rate.
Fears of further flooding have compounded the search for the missing.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes, and one of these formations has become a risk of further floods.
The Chinese and Nepalese foreign ministers spoke Saturday and discussed sharing satellite and hydrological data, both sides said.

In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, rescue operations were temporarily paused at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of more flooding from a newly formed lake.
But state broadcaster CCTV said late Saturday that the lake was “discharging naturally” and had been “essentially drained”, citing China’s ministry of water resources.
A total of 2,141 rescuers were near the Gyirong site, the Xinhua state news agency reported, including the more than 500 in the worst-hit area.
Pilgrimage route
Nepal reported a death toll of 675 people on Saturday.
There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in the country.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, seven people died and 554 remain missing, Xinhua state news agency said on Saturday.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, officials said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Hope was fading for some still waiting desperately for news.
Kalka Sharda, in Bidur, was searching lists of rescued for his 18-year-old son Vinod Sharda, a hydropower plant labourer.
“I don’t think there is any hope left,” he said.
“Because, if he was alive, he would have found a way to get in touch.” /dl

articles.title: LPA likely to develop into cyclone Pilandok on Sunday – Pagasa
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The low-pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) has a “high chance” of developing into a tropical depression on Sunday, state meteorologists said.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The low-pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) has a “high chance” of developing into a tropical depression on Sunday, state meteorologists said.
According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), the LPA was last spotted 1,340 kilometers (km) east of extreme northern Luzon, as of 3 a.m.
“Based on our latest data, this low-pressure area is likely to become a tropical cyclone within the day and we will call it Pilandok,” Pagasa weather specialist Obet Badrina said.
Badrina then warned that as the LPA moves westward toward the landmass, it is likely to strengthen the southwest monsoon.
Apart from the LPA, Pagasa is monitoring two other weather systems inside the PAR.
Among them is the southwest monsoon, which has been affecting most of Luzon over the past few weeks.
Tropical Depression Saudel is also being observed within the PAR, but has no direct effect on the country, Pagasa noted.
Saudel, formerly Obet, was last spotted 1,105 kilometers west-northwest of extreme northern Luzon, moving southwestward at 25 km per hour (kph).
Pagasa said Saudel has maximum sustained winds of 45 kph and gusts of up to 75 kph. /das

articles.title: Uganda’s ‘youngest reigning’ king dies at 34
articles.summary: KAMPALA — A Ugandan king, who has been recognized as the world’s youngest reigning monarch after ascending to the throne at the age of three, has died aged 34, the Tooro Kingdom said in a…

blocks.text: KAMPALA — A Ugandan king, who has been recognized as the world’s youngest reigning monarch after ascending to the throne at the age of three, has died aged 34, the Tooro Kingdom said in a statement late Thursday.
Uganda is a republic led by longtime President Yoweri Museveni but officially recognizes traditional kingdoms, which serve mainly as cultural institutions with limited political power.

“It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty the Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at approximately 10:00 pm this evening,” the prime minister (Omuhikirwa) of Tooro Kingdom said in a statement.
King Oyo succeeded his father, who died of a heart attack in 1995, but was crowned after turning 18 years old.
Last year, Guinness World Records recognized him as the world’s youngest reigning monarch.
The king died while receiving treatment in the United States following weeks of speculation about his deteriorating health, local media reported.
Uganda’s Tooro region, in the west of the country, has a population of about 2.1 million people.
Africa has only three sovereign monarchies — Eswatini, Lesotho and Morocco — while several other countries recognise traditional kingdoms as cultural institutions without political power. /dl

articles.title: Community journalists face greater risks as press attacks mount
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — More than four years into the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) has documented about 260 cases of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — More than four years into the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) has documented about 260 cases of attacks against the press.
The rising number of incidents is alarming in itself. But beyond the figures is another troubling pattern: who bears the brunt of these attacks.
Based on NUJP data, more than 180 of the recorded cases involved media workers from local newspapers and radio stations, alternative media outlets and campus publications.

This indicates that a significant share of those targeted come from smaller and independent news organizations — outlets that often operate with limited resources, lower compensation and fewer protections for their workers.
For them, the risks can be far greater than the pay.

Working outside the country’s largest newsrooms can mean reporting from communities where journalists sometimes have fewer institutional safeguards and where local political and economic interests can exert considerable pressure.
Yet despite these vulnerabilities, they continue to cover stories that might otherwise receive little or no attention.

The data tell more than a story of attacks against the press. They reveal who is most exposed when press freedom is under threat: journalists working closest to the communities they serve, often with the fewest resources to protect them.
As the NUJP pointed out, “behind every number is a journalist, a newsroom, and a community whose access to truth is at risk.”
Fewer resources, greater risks

Jay Lavapiez, a radio broadcaster in Roxas City, Capiz, told the INQUIRER that working as a journalist outside Metro Manila means doing the same job with fewer resources, but sometimes with far greater risks.
“We report from the communities where we live — where the people we cover are our neighbors, and the officials we scrutinize are often people we personally know,” he said.
Last June, Lavapiez, 48, station manager of Baskog Radyo, survived an assassination attempt. His vehicle was blocked by two men on a motorcycle and hit by four bullets from a 9 mm pistol.
Earlier in April, the NUJP sounded the alarm over the filing of cases against Lavapiez and his wife, India.

Based on the spouses’ account cited by the NUJP in its statement, the harassment against them started last year, when they reported on a cemetery owned by a local official and other allegations of abuse and corruption.
“These reports were done in good faith, in service of the public,” the spouses said.
Since then, several cyberlibel cases have been filed against them and their staff in Manila, Muntinlupa and Capiz.

Lavapiez told the INQUIRER that when journalists question people in power, the risks are real — libel and cyberlibel complaints, online harassment, intimidation, threats, smear campaigns and even armed attacks.

“The hardest part is that provincial journalists don’t have the luxury of simply walking away,” he said. “This is our community. We go back to the same streets, we see the same people, and continue broadcasting the next morning.”
More of a public service
Lavapiez said salaries are modest for media workers in the provinces and “certainly not proportional to the risks we face.”

For instance, last April, community journalist RJ Ledesma was killed in Toboso, Negros Occidental, where he was conducting community work and reporting on renewable energy initiatives and their effects on agricultural communities.

He was among 19 people killed in a military operation that was condemned by a fact-finding mission for serious violations, including the alleged indiscriminate firing by the military despite reportedly having a clear view of the scene.
Lavapiez pointed out that “community journalism has never been primarily about money for us.”
“We do it because somebody has to ask the uncomfortable questions when public money is involved and ordinary citizens feel they have no voice,” he said.
Especially in the provinces, “our work is sometimes a test of courage,” Lavapiez said.

“Our work is community journalism,” he said, but “the irony is that the closer you are to the community, the more vulnerable you can become, because everyone knows where you work, where you live, and who you are.”
For Lavapiez, journalists do not expect special treatment.

“We simply ask for the same thing every journalist deserves — the freedom to do our work without being threatened, harassed, prosecuted into silence, or physically harmed for asking questions,” he said. /dm

articles.title: 4 migrants arrested in Ceuta for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers
articles.summary: MADRID — Four Moroccan migrants in Spain’s enclave of Ceuta were arrested Saturday for throwing stones at a patrol of Spanish soldiers, one of whom fell and injured himself while pursuing…

blocks.text: MADRID — Four Moroccan migrants in Spain’s enclave of Ceuta were arrested Saturday for throwing stones at a patrol of Spanish soldiers, one of whom fell and injured himself while pursuing the assailants, a police spokesman told AFP.

It was the second such incident to occur in recent days in the tiny territory located in North Africa, following the arrests on Thursday of 12 Moroccan migrants who threw stones at a Spanish military vehicle, injuring one of its four occupants.
Eleven of those 12 were deported to Morocco, according to local reports.

Ceuta remans a source of tension, politically and security-wise, for Spain since tens of thousands of migrants crossed over into it from Morocco on July 30 and 31, triggering alarm among Madrid’s EU partners.
Most of those migrants left in subsequent days, but thousands remain in Ceuta, wandering the streets and sleeping on beaches of the territory whose population is 80,000.
Ceuta residents protesting against the presence of the remaining migrants clashed with police on Thursday, prompting Spain’s government to appeal for calm.
Madrid is seeking ways to reduce the number of remaining migrants in Ceuta without breaching EU and international asylum and migration laws.

The EU’s commissioner for migration, Magnus Brunner, said on X on Saturday that Spain had asked for help from the European Union’s border control agency Frontex, the police cooperation agency Europol and the EU Agency for Asylum.
“We are already working on the request and will take a swift decision,” Brunner said, calling the situation in Ceuta “challenging”.
“The priority remains to ensure the swift return of all those who remain illegally in Ceuta,” he said. /dl

articles.title: Bayambang declares state of calamity over P31-M agricultural losses
articles.summary: CALASIAO, Pangasinan — The municipal council of Bayambang has placed the town under a state of calamity after Tropical Storms “Luis” and “Maymay” and the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat,…

blocks.text: CALASIAO, Pangasinan — The municipal council of Bayambang has placed the town under a state of calamity after Tropical Storms “Luis” and “Maymay” and the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat, caused more than P31 million in agricultural losses.
Municipal Resolution No. 371, Series of 2026, cited prolonged rains and flooding that affected hundreds of farmers and damaged crops and livestock across the predominantly agricultural municipality.
The Municipal Agriculture Office reported that 577 farmers were affected, with damage covering 615.79 hectares of agricultural land and estimated losses totaling P31,280,958.81.
Rice farmers accounted for most of those affected, with 550 farmers reporting losses across 586.53 hectares of rice fields. Damage to the sector was estimated at P17,849,243.81.
The high-value crop sector recorded the second-largest losses at P13,362,995, affecting 25 farmers and 28.26 hectares of farmland.
Corn production was also affected, with one farmer losing crops on one hectare of land, resulting in an estimated P43,720 in damage. Another farmer lost three goats valued at P25,000.

Bayambang is largely dependent on agriculture, with a significant portion of its population engaged in rice farming, high-value crop and corn production, livestock raising and other agriculture-related activities.

The Sangguniang Bayan said the damage went beyond the loss of standing crops, warning that the prolonged adverse weather had disrupted farmers’ livelihoods and affected their ability to purchase farm inputs, prepare their fields and replant.

Under the state of calamity declaration, the municipal government may intensify disaster response and recovery efforts and mobilize available resources for relief, rehabilitation and livelihood restoration.

The resolution directed the Municipal Agriculture Office to coordinate with the Department of Agriculture, Provincial Agriculture Office, Philippine Crop Insurance Corp. and other concerned agencies to secure assistance for affected farmers.
These may include seeds, planting materials, fertilizers, livestock support, crop insurance and other interventions.
Priority will be given to rehabilitating damaged agricultural areas, replacing lost farm inputs, supporting replanting and helping farmers resume production.

The state of calamity will remain in effect until conditions normalize and the Sangguniang Bayan determines, based on an updated damage assessment and the recommendation of the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, that it can be lifted. /das

articles.title: Russian strike on a Ukrainian warehouse kills 37 in the war's deadliest attack this year
articles.summary: MYLA, Ukraine (AP) — A Russian drone struck a warehouse west of Kyiv that Ukrainian officials say was storing shells, mines and other ammunition, sparking massive explosions and fires that swept…

blocks.text: MYLA, Ukraine (AP) — A Russian drone struck a warehouse west of Kyiv that Ukrainian officials say was storing shells, mines and other ammunition, sparking massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings and killing 37 people.

In this photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Service, firefighters put out a fire in a warehouse following a Russian drone attack near Kyiv, Ukraine, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP)

The Friday night attack on the warehouse in Myla, a village in the Bucha district, was the war's deadliest attack this year and came on the second of three days of nearly round-the-clock Russian strikes that have severely disrupted life in and around the Ukrainian capital.

Attacks on the capital and, to a lesser extent, the rest of Ukraine have been nearly constant since Thursday. Kyiv officials say Russia builds up missile stocks and launches major attacks every few days, hoping to exhaust Ukrainian defenses through the sheer weight of numbers.

The warehouse strike sparked fires that raced through homes and damaged at least 50 residential buildings, said Tymur Tkachenko, who heads the local regional military administration. He was later cited by local media as saying 34 of the people killed were residents of a care home for elderly and disabled people. More than 370 people were evacuated.
The blasts rocked Myla, causing people to frantically seek cover.
"At about 8 p.m., the drone hit a warehouse somewhere and then the detonation began," Oleksandr Vodolaz, a village resident, told The Associated Press. "No one knew that weapons were stored there."
Another local, Zhanna Kravchuk, said she had so many questions about what happened.
"Why are weapons like this ... in warehouses and not on the front lines where they would help?" she said.

As crews raced to get people to safety and extinguish blazes, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as a "terrible situation" and said it appeared to be the result of "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people."
He noted that Ukrainian law forbids the storage of ammunition close to people's homes and said criminal proceedings had been opened.
"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions," the president said.
Kyiv investigates warehouse targeted in attack
In a social media post Saturday, Zelenskyy shed more light on the situation.
"The first strike was on an ammunition storage site that definitely shouldn't have been there – a Defense Forces storage facility. Shells, mines, other ammunition, and drones detonated."

Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi didn't specify what was in the warehouse, but he referenced a July attack on the Kyiv suburb of Vyshneve that struck an ammunition depot, killing 22 people and triggering detonations and fires that tore through nearby homes.

"Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson," Koretskyi said. "In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again."
The 37 killed surpassed the 31 who died in a July 2 strike on Kyiv, which had been the war's deadliest attack of 2026.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it hit a warehouse in Myla that was storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It also said it attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, and a logistics center and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine's Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region.
Russian jet-powered drones pose a problem for Kyiv

Russian strikes damaged homes and apartment blocks in the southern Kherson region on Saturday, killing two people and wounding 27 more, including a child, Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the region administration, said in a statement.

Prokudin said earlier in the week that Russia had intensified its attacks on critical infrastructure in the region, which is about 70% under Russian control. He also urged tens of thousands of residents to move to safer regions because of the possibility of prolonged power and heating outages this winter.

Although officials haven't said whether they were used in the warehouse attack, Russia has significantly increased its use of jet-powered drones, and their numbers will keep growing as Moscow sees their effectiveness, Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine's presidential office, told reporters Friday.

"Means of attack always outpace means of defense. We will certainly need to adapt. It will take time," Palisa said. He said interceptor drones currently available to Ukraine, which could theoretically intercept jet-powered drones, have not yet demonstrated the expected effectiveness, though Ukraine is working on solutions.
Ukraine vows to increase long-range strikes

Meanwhile, Ukraine has stepped up its long-range attacks on Russian military industries and energy facilities in recent months. The attacks, which use domestically made drones, are meant to cut into a source of Moscow's war funding and make Russians feel the consequences.
In his evening statement to the nation Friday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv hoped to increase its long-range strikes to reach 1000 drone launches every day.

"Right now, we average over 300 of our long-range sanctions," Zelenskyy said, his preferred term for Kyiv's long-range attacks that have also lately targeted Russian large-scale online retailers. "There must be more. We have a very specific goal, and we will achieve it."
Moscow's forces destroyed 313 Ukrainian drones overnight, Russia's Defense Ministry said Saturday.
Ukrainian drone attacks wounded 11 people in Russia's Rostov region, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said. Writing on social media, he said that nine people were hospitalized, including four children.

articles.title: Over 400 areas flooded in four regions due to Habagat --OCD
articles.summary: More than 400 areas in four regions were flooded due to the rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat), the Office of the Civil Defense said on Sunday.

blocks.text: Published August 30, 2026 9:17am
More than 400 areas in four regions were flooded due to the rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat), the Office of the Civil Defense (OCD) said on Sunday.
The flooding occurred in Ilocos Region, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and the National Capital Region (NCR).

"Ngayong araw po, as of this morning, 429 pa po ang flooded areas sa apat na regions: Region 1, NCR, Region 3, Calabarzon," said OCD Deputy Administrator for Operation Bernardo Rafaelito Alejandro IV in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(Today, as of this morning, there are still 429 flooded areas across four regions: Region 1, NCR, Region 3, and Calabarzon.)
The OCD said that clearing operations on affected roads are also ongoing.

"So mayroon na tayong 3,158 damaged houses, at halos 100 road sections and 13 bridges na tuloy-tuloy na impassable hanggang kaninang umaga. Kini-clear natin ito. Ang problema talaga nating matindi ay 'yung bridge sa Tarlac, kasi dalawa na 'yung apektado dito, na talagang naputol at kailangan gumamit ng alternative routes," Alejandro added.

(So we now have 3,158 damaged houses, and almost 100 road sections and 13 bridges that remained impassable as of this morning; we are currently clearing these. Our severe problem is the bridge in Tarlac, because two are now affected there, which were completely cut off, requiring the use of alternative routes.)
The continuous heavy rains on Saturday triggered flooding not just in the capital region, but also in other parts of Luzon.
But the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) said that flooding has subsided in parts of the capital region as of Sunday morning.
Meanwhile, landslides have also been reported in Zambales and in a portion of the Subic-Clark-Tarlac Expressway (SCTEX).

"Nu'ng medyo gumanda last week ng dalawang araw, nagki-clearing agad 'yung DPWH at LGUs. Nu'ng nag-resurgence nitong monsoon, mayroon tayong bagong reports. Kahapon sa Subic, sa Zambales; even sa SCTEX, may landslide sa daan," said Alejandro.

(When the weather improved slightly for two days last week, the DPWH and LGUs immediately conducted clearing operations. But when the monsoon resurged, we received new reports—yesterday in Subic, in Zambales; even on SCTEX, there was a landslide on the road.)
Two men were killed and two others were injured in a landslide at the Subic Bay Freeport Zone in Subic, Zambales, on Saturday morning amid continuous heavy rains.
Monsoon rains are expected to continue over Luzon on Sunday, the state weather bureau PAGASA said.
In its 4 a.m. public weather forecast, PAGASA said monsoon rains are expected in Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac and Pampanga. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: LPA inside PAR may develop into tropical depression ‘Pilandok’
articles.summary: A low-pressure area (LPA) that entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on Saturday evening, Aug. 29, may develop into a tropical depression within the next few hours, the Philippine…

blocks.text: A low-pressure area (LPA) that entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on Saturday evening, Aug. 29, may develop into a tropical depression within the next few hours, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Sunday, Aug. 30.
PAGASA weather specialist Obet Badrina said the LPA was located 1,340 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of Sunday morning.

“Base po sa pinakahuling datos natin, itong low-pressure area na ito ay posible po maging bagyo within the day at tatawagin po natin itong Bagyong ‘Pilandok’ (Based on our latest data, this low-pressure area may develop into a tropical cyclone within the day and will be called ‘Pilandok’),” Badrina said.
The LPA could also affect the southwest monsoon or “habagat,” which continues to bring rains over parts of Luzon.

“Inaasahan din natin na sa pagkilos nitong low-pressure area na ito, maging bagyo man po, posibleng palakasin ulit nito ang habagat (Meanwhile, as this low-pressure area moves, whether it develops into a tropical cyclone or not, it could possibly strengthen the southwest monsoon),” Badrina said.
He said PAGASA would continue to monitor how the LPA could interact with the habagat.

“Sa ngayon po kailangan pa rin natin ito imonitor kung paano yung magiging dynamics po o makakaapekto itong low-pressure area na maaaring maging bagyo sa habagat (For now, we still need to monitor its dynamics and how this low-pressure area, which may develop into a tropical cyclone, could affect the southwest monsoon),” Badrina said.
The habagat remains the weather system mainly affecting Luzon as of Sunday.
Rainy conditions are expected particularly over Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Central Luzon, Metro Manila, Calabarzon, and Occidental Mindoro.

The rainfall outlook for Sunday showed that Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga could receive 100 to 200 millimeters or rain, considered heavy to intense.

Metro Manila, Ilocos Norte, Abra, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro could receive 50 to 100 millimeters, or moderate to heavy rainfall.
On Monday, Aug. 31, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan.
Fifty to 100 millimeters could prevail over Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro.
By Tuesday, Sept. 1, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Abra, Benguet, and Zambales.
Batanes, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, La Union, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Bataan, and Pampanga could receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rainfall.
Despite the possible strengthening of the habagat, Badrina said rainfall over the western section of Luzon could decrease by Monday or Tuesday.

“Posibleng mabawasan yung mga pag-ulan na mararanasan po natin partikular na sa western section ng Luzon sa araw ng Lunes o araw ng Martes (Rainfall that will be experienced, particularly over the western section of Luzon, could possibly decrease on Monday or Tuesday),” Badrina said.
However, he urged the public to remain cautious as flash floods and landslides remain possible, particularly in western Luzon.
Meanwhile, PAGASA is also monitoring Tropical Depression Saudel, formerly called “Obet.”
Saudel was located 1,105 kilometers west-northwest of extreme Northern Luzon and is not directly affecting the country.
“Sa ngayon ay hindi naman ito direktang nakakaapekto sa ating bansa (For now, it is not directly affecting the country),” Badrina said.
The rest of Luzon and the Visayas may experience cloudy skies, while Mindanao is expected to generally have fair weather, although localized rain showers and thunderstorms remain possible.

articles.title: For Gabriel Federico, hearing impairment never stopped the music
articles.summary: When a severe hearing impairment makes his music path harder, UP Diliman’s Gabriel Federico chooses to adapt rather than walk away

blocks.text: “I suggest, I encourage you, to transfer courses,” Gabriel Federico’s doctor told him during a check-up, as his hearing impairment worsened when he was a college music student.
Gabriel was down and discouraged. He prayed and talked with his mother about what to do next. After several days, he came to a decision.
“I’m sad, but I will still continue,” he said. “The Lord has a plan for me. I will persevere.”
Gabriel didn’t transfer. He kept studying music at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

He got there with an underdeveloped right ear and a left ear that requires a hearing aid. His moderately severe to severe hearing impairment eventually forced him to change the way he listened, practiced, performed, and communicated.

blocks.caption: Gabriel Federico (center) performs with the University of the Philippines Abelardo Rondalla during a concert in Venice, Italy. All photos courtesy of Gabriel Federico

blocks.text: The music-centered academic setting at UP became an early test for Gabriel to adapt to his condition. One of the hardest parts was dictation, he said, which required students to listen to melodies, rhythms, and multiple voices and write them down.
For Gabriel, it meant extra hours most classmates didn’t need. “Every time I listened to an orchestra or a choir, I had to repeat it over and over,” he said.

“I would focus on a specific instrument or voice for each repeat and with my condition, I had to listen to it with maximum volume every time. I also had to make ways to isolate each distinct sound, which meant extra hours dedicated to practice.”

Gabriel also found ways to adapt outside the classroom. During the pandemic, his father bought him a bone-conduction device after his doctor advised him to avoid conventional earbuds because of the risk of infection.
“I think I’m a pioneer of using the bone conductors,” Gabriel said jokingly.
The device lets him experience music through vibration. He remembers listening to Vivaldi’s Four Seasons and realizing how much he could perceive through it.

“When I listened to Four Seasons with the vibration earphones (how Gabriel referred to the bone conductors at times), I heard that there was significant harp support that I wasn’t able to notice before,” he said.

The same discipline also carries into ensemble work. Before every rehearsal, he makes sure he catches every interpretation and cue the director wants implemented for his part. This preparation is essential for Gabriel to get familiar with an ensemble through both the music and the cues around him.
When the director is giving instructions, he doesn’t hesitate to ask for silence.
“Every time the director speaks, I always ask the other performers to be silent so I can hear the instructions better,” he said. If he still can’t catch something, he turns to whoever is beside him.
“I am very reliant to both social cues and music,” Gabriel said. That is why he makes sure to wear his hearing aid at every rehearsal and performance.

But Gabriel’s journey through music is not only a story about working harder because of his hearing impairment. It is also about learning to trust God and recognizing the people who helped him along the way.
Gabriel first encountered music through his grandmother’s piano. Playing it whenever he could gave him joy that other hobbies did not.
“I tried and did a lot of things,” he said. “I took drum lessons and got involved in different sports. Come high school, I realized that playing the piano is the one I like the most.”

blocks.caption: Gabriel Federico poses with his grandmother, whose piano became one of his earliest connections to music

blocks.text: Playing also gave him a way to connect with his grandmother. “Whenever I visited my lola, I made sure to play the piano in her living room,” Gabriel said in Filipino.
“Most of the songs I played were also from her era, which gave her a somewhat happy and nostalgic feeling. She would just sit there, listening. After an hour, she would clap with joy.”

Gabriel doesn’t consider himself someone who was simply gifted. “People would more often than not say that I was given this talent and that I had it since birth,” he said. “I never agreed with that notion. I got to this level of talent because I work hard.”
The insane amount of work he put in had a cost. There was a period in his early college years when he put immense pressure on himself to immediately be great.

“Pressure was building up inside of me,” Gabriel said. “I was practicing immediately right after classes, which was at around 6 pm. At around 8 pm, I would take a quick break and would continue until 11 pm. I would sometimes go beyond midnight just practicing and listening to songs. This was when the anxiety grew and I felt the negative effects it had on my body.”
A friend from the same college, whom Gabriel looked up to as an older brother figure, eventually stepped in.
“You just got here,” his friend told him. “Enjoy it for what it is and don’t worry too much. You don’t have to tire yourself out to succeed.”
Another moment came when Gabriel began questioning his decision to stick to his music course.

“I feel like I don’t belong here,” he told a senior from one of his organizations. “I think they made a mistake by picking me to be part of this program because I am really having a hard time right now.”
His friend reminded him that it wasn’t luck that got him in the program.
“There’s a reason why the panel chose you over the others. We don’t know what it is but what you can do now is to press on and continue working hard. Show them that they were right in picking you.”
The words stayed with Gabriel. “It’s very important to have a community of friends that can align you, keep you grounded, and humble you if needed,” he said.

blocks.caption: Gabriel Federico speaks during a workshop in Chile in 2024, while he was a student at the University of the Philippines College of Music.

blocks.text: For every trial, doubt, and challenge, Gabriel had something or someone to help him through it. His faith was one of those things. This is why when his doctor told him to transfer courses, he made sure to pray for discenment.
“I kept asking God if I was in the right path,” he said.
After several days, he decided to continue. “Jesus will never leave me even in the hard times,” he said. “He will provide strength and necessities for me to pursue this dream.”

By the time he became part of UP’s recent graduating class, Gabriel knew that God made it possible for him to get this far. He finished with an Associate in Arts in Piano Performance in 2024 and earned a Bachelor of Music in Composition this year.
“I realized after graduation that God’s faithfulness means a lot,” he said. “I have been through a lot and have grown a lot. I am so much different now than who I was as a freshman.”

Over the past year, Gabriel has traveled to Europe, South America, and Hawaii to represent the Philippines as part of the UP Abelardo Rondalla in international concerts and workshops. Now, he is working as a musician, composer, arranger, and music educator.
Looking back, Gabriel saw not only the work he had put into his degree but also the people and resources that helped him along the way.
“Jesus provided the friends, family, strength, and wisdom for me to graduate,” he said.
Now in his next chapter of teaching, Gabriel is applying the lessons from his journey.

“I’ve learned how to be more authentic, how to sympathize, how to be deliberate, and how to understand things,” he said. “I seek and encourage quality over quantity when it comes to teaching and learning.”
His experience with hearing impairment has also changed the way he approaches his students.
In high school, Gabriel said he was embarrassed to disclose that he had a PWD (person with disability) card. Eventually, he realized that he shouldn’t hide that part of himself.

“I learned over time that it’s not something that you should be ashamed of,” he said. “It’s something that you should be transparent about. Life will be miserable if someone denies you. I should not deny who I am.”
Gabriel eventually realized that the same understanding should apply to his students.
“I shouldn’t deny who my students are,” the 25-year-old Gabriel said. “I should also be transparent to my students. So that I know how to approach them and how to give them individualized lessons.”
Gabriel once needed people who understood his struggles, encouraged him when he doubted himself, and reminded him that he belonged. Now, he hopes to become that person for his own students.
“I’m not pushing them to pursue music,” he said. “I just want them to love music. To love what they are doing. To enjoy it.”
When asked to summarize his journey in one word, Gabriel did not mention perseverance, music, or hearing impairment. He simply gave one word: “Trust.”
His mother repeatedly reminded him of Proverbs 3:5-6, which has somewhat served as his life verse.
“At all times, I trust in the Lord because I acknowledge that if it’s just me, I will fail,” Gabriel said. “I know the Lord. He is faithful. He knows everything. He wants what’s best for me.”

For Gabriel, trust means continuing even when he does not know exactly what lies ahead. It meant trusting God when his doctor told him to consider leaving music, and trusting the people who reminded him that he belonged. Now, as a teacher, it also means creating the kind of environment for his students that others created for him. – Rappler.com

articles.title: La Mesa Dam overflows as habagat threatens more rain
articles.summary: Excess water is flowing toward Tullahan River as more habagat rain threatens NCR.

blocks.text: Residents wade through floodwaters along Zapote Junction in Las Piñas on Saturday morning, Aug. 28, 2026 as the flooded road remains closed to vehicles.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — La Mesa Dam overflowed early Sunday, August 30, sending excess water toward the Tullahan River as the southwest monsoon continued to bring rain over Metro Manila and large parts of Luzon.
State weather bureau PAGASA recorded the dam's water level at 80.30 meters as of 5 a.m., above its 80.15-meter overflow elevation.
Excess water from the reservoir will flow directly into the Tullahan River, potentially affecting low-lying communities in Quezon City, Caloocan, Valenzuela, Malabon and Navotas, PAGASA said.

In Quezon City, areas identified by PAGASA include Fairview, Forest Hills Subdivision, Quirino Highway, Sta. Quiteria and San Bartolome. In Valenzuela, the advisory identified areas along the North Expressway and La Huerta Subdivision.
PAGASA warned that continued rainfall could further raise the river's water level.
The weather bureau is also monitoring a low-pressure area located 1,340 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of 3 a.m. The southwest monsoon, meanwhile, is affecting Luzon and the Visayas.
More rain, flood risk

Metro Manila may experience moderate to occasionally heavy rain over the next 12 hours, with all rivers and streams in the capital likely to be affected, according to PAGASA's general flood advisory issued at 6 a.m.
Heavy rain had already fallen over the Pasig-Marikina-Laguna de Bay river basin in the 12 hours ending at 5 a.m. Moderate to heavy rain was forecast through 5 p.m.
PAGASA warned that road and street flooding remained possible because of accumulated rainwater, poor or clogged drainage systems and higher tide levels, potentially making some roads impassable.
Waterways being monitored include the upper and lower Marikina River, Pasig River, San Juan River and waterways draining toward Laguna de Bay.
The Tullahan River basin, where heavy rain was also recorded overnight, may receive moderate to occasionally heavy rain through Sunday afternoon.
Flood advisories across Luzon
The flood threat extends beyond Metro Manila.
PAGASA forecast heavy to intense rain over the Ilocos Region, with rivers and tributaries in Pangasinan, Ilocos Sur, La Union and Ilocos Norte likely to be affected.
Moderate to heavy rain may affect the Cordillera Administrative Region and Central Luzon.
In the Cordilleras, waterways in Abra, Ifugao, Benguet, Kalinga, Mountain Province and Apayao remain under watch.
In Central Luzon, PAGASA identified waterways in Bataan and Zambales and all rivers and tributaries in Bulacan as likely to be affected.
CALABARZON may also receive moderate to occasionally heavy rain, with waterways in Laguna, Cavite, Rizal, Batangas and Quezon under monitoring.
Light to moderate rain is forecast over MIMAROPA and Western Visayas, where residents near waterways and low-lying or mountainous areas were also advised to remain alert for possible flash floods.
PAGASA advised residents in low-lying communities and near riverbanks and mountain slopes to take appropriate precautions and follow instructions from local disaster officials.

articles.title: Families balance hope and despair in race to find survivors in Nepal as 41 Australians still missing
articles.summary: The walls of a teaching hospital are filled with pictures of unidentified victims as authorities collect DNA samples and plan burials before morgues fill up

blocks.text: Some of them are young, some old; most of them appear to be men. Some of them could be sleeping, except for the mud that covers their bodies. Some, it seems, would be impossible to recognise even if you knew them well.
Every few hours Nepalese authorities hang pictures of the deceased, who have not been identified, on a wall at the back of a teaching hospital in Kathmandu.
Saluja, a young woman who did not give her last name, stood among a group of more than 100 people watching. Her cousin, 31, was not on the wall that day.
“It’s very hard to identify their faces,” Saluja says.

As she speaks, some in the crowd take videos to send to other relatives; they stand around comparing them, trying to work out whether the person in the photo is their loved one. The bodies have a piece of paper lying on top of them, showing which district they were found in, with a number to contact.
“My cousin is missing,” Saluja says. “He worked in a hydro power plant … Since the flood, we have not been able to contact him.
“It was the first area to get affected, so we really don’t know. But we are hoping for the best.”

While she talked, her other cousin, his older brother, was on the plane flying home from Australia. Since Wednesday, Kathmandu has swelled with international visitors – not tourists but people looking for their loved ones.
The Nepalese government has deployed about 15,000 personnel – from the army to the police – to move up the valley and into the areas decimated by the flood, hoping to find survivors.

blocks.caption: A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding at the confluence of the Trishuli and Tadi rivers in the Nuwakot district, Nepal. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP

blocks.text: While they battle arduous search conditions – areas completely cut off, roads destroyed, bridges washed away and a new lake threatening to burst – loved ones from Australia rush to Nepal to be with their families. They come to chase leads and to wait.

“My older cousin, he’s a doctor in Australia, and his wife is a dentist,” Saluja says. “So they both are coming back. They’re going to try with the search and to be with the family as well. They obviously want to be with the family.”
It’s been four days since the glacier collapsed high in the Himalayas, sending a wall of water, ice and mud down to destroy everything in its path.
The number of people killed has risen to 669, with nearly 3,000 people lost. On the Chinese side, more than 550 people are unaccounted for. Forty-one Australians are still missing.
On Saturday, New South Wales man Michael Keats was confirmed to be one of them. He had reached the Nepal-Tibet border just moments before disaster struck, his family said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Australian's missing in Nepal. Clockwise from left - Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and Family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan. Composite: Supplied by the families

blocks.text: “Confusion around the timing of the floods initially led us to believe our beautiful Michael would be safe in Kathmandu, preparing to fly home,” they said.

“Unfortunately, it was confirmed relatively quickly by the Isha Foundation that Michael and his Kailash travel group had arrived at Gyirong Port on the Nepal-Tibet border just 10 minutes before the tragic floods hit.”
Keats’ family said their thoughts and prayers were with everyone affected by the tragedy.
“[Michael] is gentle and kind, with a unique light that touches everyone lucky enough to know him,” they said.
Sagar Shrestha serves as the director of the Disaster and Crisis Management Department at the Nepal Red Cross Society in Kathmandu. He said the death toll could climb into the thousands.
“But they are still finding survivors,” he says. “Some of them are being found in the jungle; they’ve gone up the mountain and are being helicoptered out.”
He said there were 14 hydropower plants along the river, six of which were under construction. It’s believed people could still be alive in the majority of them.

One of the key issues has become “the dignified management of the dead”, he says, as morgues and hospitals have filled up in some areas. According to local media, officials in the Chitwan district will collect DNA samples from 229 bodies that are starting to decay and are no longer identifiable, before burying them.
“It is now the major concern,” Shrestha says. “And the second thing is that if we are not being able to manage the dead bodies, there could be some kind of health issues.”
after newsletter promotion
Since the crisis started, Sagar Pandey has barely slept. Pandey, the chief executive of the Himalaya Glacier Company, says 47 people from the trekking service are lost, including 15 Australians.

He had Australians in two different locations: five people 1.5km from the border of Tibet and Nepal, who were meant to be coming back that morning after breakfast and another 10 who had left the Syabrubesi valley and were driving towards the border checkpoint.
“I believe they were trapped because all three cars and jeeps are missing,” he says. “There were a total of 14 people: three drivers and then one guide and 10 Australians.”

Pandey has been spending his days going between the hospitals and checking in with the morgues to see if anyone on his tours has shown up. He is contacting family members of loved ones who are overseas and helping those who have just arrived. He has also been grieving his brother, who was guiding one of the treks.
On Wednesday, he chartered a helicopter to the disaster zone – he could see about 800 people standing on the mountain, who have all been rescued now, he says.
“There is a very low chance of survival that someone can still be alive,” he says. “The next process is to find the body if possible.”

There has been one glimmer of hope – on Saturday afternoon the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, announced Australian woman Cara Severino was found safe after consular officials worked out where she was, and reached her via four-wheel drive.

blocks.caption: Australian woman Cara Severino, who had been unaccounted for following the devastating floods along the Nepal-China border, was safely located. Photograph: Office of Senator Penny Wong

blocks.text: In a statement, Severino said she got out safely by teaming up with other survivors and using a tractor to drive out of the national park.

“My heart goes out to all the Nepalese families who are grieving loved ones,” she said. “We passed a guy hiking up to Thulu Safru who lost his whole family when their whole town was destroyed. It’s just so devastating and undeserving.”
“I feel for the families of those still missing; I know how much my family and friends went through.”

On Saturday afternoon, the Australian ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, was waiting at the airport. Six more members of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s crisis response team had just arrived to help.

“There is a lot of damage to infrastructure, damage to power generation capability, damage to phone lines, telegraph poles, so communications is out,” he says. “Even the Nepali forces have lost contact with some of their personnel.

“Given the nature of search, rescue, and recovery operations, there are people in the water, in the mud. They’re obviously in danger should further flooding occur, and we can get heavy rainfall at any time given the monsoon.”

The disaster unfolded over three Nepalese districts – the one closest to Kathmandu has been the easiest to conduct search and rescue operations, because the accessibility is better and the valley is wider. Most Australians were last heard from in the top district, which was hit first by the flood.
No one knows how long it will take to search the area and find everyone, Ernst says, but in the event an Australian is found, the embassy will be told immediately.

“We understand that this is an incredibly difficult situation for [families],” Ernst says. “They should feel confident that the Australian government and the Nepalese government are doing everything we can to find their loved ones.

“They are very welcome to maintain contact with the Department of Foreign Affairs through our contact numbers and our contact centre in Canberra. If they’re here in Kathmandu, they’re welcome to make contact directly with the embassy, including with me.”

articles.title: Dozens of soldiers killed or arrested after an apparent mutiny in Niger's capital, state TV reports
articles.summary: NIAMEY, Niger (AP) — Dozens of soldiers were killed or arrested after a group of young troops attempted a mutiny in Niger's capital in what was seen as a major threat to the country's ruling junta,…

blocks.text: NIAMEY, Niger (AP) — Dozens of soldiers were killed or arrested after a group of young troops attempted a mutiny in Niger's capital in what was seen as a major threat to the country's ruling junta, according to a state television broadcast and analysts.

It was the culmination of nearly 24 hours of unrest that appeared to be staged by young soldiers aggrieved over the worsening militant violence under the country's military junta. Russia's Africa Corps provided aerial and ground support to local forces to resist the rebellion, according to analysts and diplomats.

State broadcaster RTN showed footage of dozens of mostly young soldiers being paraded in public after sustained gunfire and explosions were heard overnight into Saturday at a key military base located within Niamey's main airport and near the presidential palace.
"The fighting lasted a few hours in several places, which allowed (security forces) to gradually control the situation, arrest and incapacitate these moody soldiers," state TV reported.
The whereabouts of military leader Abdourahamane Tchiani were unclear.

Senior Nigerien military officers visited the Africa Corps base at the airport "and expressed gratitude to its servicemen for their assistance in suppressing the rebellion," Russian media quoted Moscow's Ambassador to Niger Viktor Voropayev as saying.

The rebelling soldiers had camped at the military base until late Saturday while the presidential guard secured the presidential palace and was deployed to regain control of the base, analysts and diplomats said.

The loyalist forces have regained the "upper hand at least at the airport (and base)," according to Wassim Nasr, a senior research fellow at the Soufan Center. Some forces were, however, heading to the capital and it remained unclear if they were coming to support the mutiny or the junta, Nasr added.
The Associated Press could not independently confirm whether the Nigerien security forces regained full control of the base.
Unrest started with a hostage situation
Some of the mutinous soldiers came from the southwest of the country, among the regions worst-hit by insecurity, diplomats and analysts said.

The state broadcaster stopped its live transmission for some time on Saturday morning before it resumed. It broadcast a statement from Niger's Defense Minister Gen. Salifou Mody saying a group of soldiers took some officers hostage at the base and shot at "sensitive sites" in a "break with the discipline and military regulations."

The airport is a strategic hub that hosts a Nigerien air force base as well as the headquarters of the joint Niger-Burkina Faso-Mali military force. All three neighbors are now under military rule, following a string of coups in Africa's Sahel region, but are struggling with insecurity.

Niger's junta came to power after a 2023 coup which it said was prompted by the elected government's inability to stem armed violence. Since then, the impoverished West African country of more than 25 million people has severed ties with longtime Western security partners, turning instead to Russia. But the junta has been unable to stem militant violence and rampant killing of security forces, fueling unrest within the military, observers say.

The ruling military council, known as the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, called for unity. "Our Defense and Security Forces are mobilized for the Defense of the Fatherland. Let us remain united, vigilant and supportive," it said in a Facebook post.

Algeria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the country has assured Niger, its southeastern neighbor, of its "full solidarity and firm support, with a view to overcoming this ordeal and promoting a rapid return to stability."
Niger's military junta has struggled to stem violence, fueling unrest
It is the third time this year that the base at the Diori Hamani International Airport has been attacked, after two earlier assaults by jihadi rebels.

The attacks are "becoming commonplace and will continue to fuel unrest and aggravate tensions within the army ranks," said Heni Nsaibia, West Africa senior analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a conflict monitor.

"Deteriorating insecurity drove the coups that swept across the central Sahel, and the latest events show how these same pressures are now fueling unrest within the militaries that seized power," Nsaibia said.
The mutiny adds to pressure on the military authorities, which have been unable to contain deadly jihadi violence.
Before the 2023 coup, Niger had been the West's last reliable partner in the region in battling jihadists linked to al-Qaida and the Islamic State group in the Sahel.

However, the country's security forces, aided by Russia's Africa Corps, have been overstretched on multiple fronts by jihadi groups whose repeated attacks in the last year have resulted in mass casualties within the military.

articles.title: ‘They’re concrete acts of stewardship’: Cayetano defends Laguna Lakeshore project amid row with Lacson
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano has again defended the Laguna Lakeshore project, highlighting the remarkable progress of the Laguna Lake within the jurisdiction of Taguig City in recent…

blocks.text: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano has again defended the Laguna Lakeshore project, highlighting the remarkable progress of the Laguna Lake within the jurisdiction of Taguig City in recent years and its vast untapped potential.
Senator Alan Peter Cayetano, Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson (Facebook)
Cayetano, in a recent Facebook livestream, also called for better stewardship of God’s creation, as he defended his city’s decision to pursue infrastructure projects within the Lakeshore.

“Nung congressman pa ako ng 1998, naging passion ko na po kung paano pagandahin ang Laguna Lake. Nagkaroon lang po siyempre ako ng opportunity sa side ng Taguig dahil nga ito ang aking home city… Napakarami po kasing gamit ng lake (Back when I was a congressman in 1998, improving Laguna Lake became a passion of mine. Naturally, I had the opportunity to focus on the Taguig side since it is my home city... After all, the lake has so many uses),” Cayetano said in two August 27 live streams along the Taguig Lakeshore.

“Ang pagiging sa gobyerno, ang pagiging public servant — hindi po kami ang may-ari ng resources… Kami po ay stewards, tagapamahala lang. Lahat ng tao kahit na wala sa gobyerno, meron po tayong obligasyon maging good stewards (Being in government, being a public servant—we do not own the resources... We are merely stewards, managers. Everyone, even those outside of government, has an obligation to be good stewards),” he said.

Cayetano related the City of Taguig's lakeshore projects as concrete acts of stewardship, designed to protect the lake from erosion, pollution, and illegal settlements while ensuring public access for all.

“Nung ginawa y’ung C6 or road dike, basically, pinoprotect po y’ung lakeshore. And part of its protection is not only na huwag mag-erode, (but para) hindi bahayan ng informal centers kasi kung mabahayan yung dumi, dito mapupunta sa lawa. The other thing is to make it for public use (When you built the C6 or road dike, basically, you were protecting the lakeshore. And part of its protection is not only to prevent erosion, (but to) not house informal centers because if they were houses, the waste would end up in the lake. The other thing is to make it for public use),” the senator explained.

Cayetano also countered allegations of land-grabbing by pointing out that the local government actually reserved the area for public use, reversing the historical pattern of private encroachment along the lakeshore.

“May allegations na may kinakamkam kami. Hindi ko lang alam kung pag sinabing kami, kung kaming mga Cayetano, kung ako, o kami ng ibang leaders… Doon sa bandang gitna, marami na pong private (land) kasi may 1,100 hectares ng lupa na nasa labas ng road dike. Meron po doon na private property, merong gobyerno (There are allegations that we are appropriating land for ourselves. I am just not sure who is meant by ‘we’—whether it refers to us Cayetanos, just me, or us together with other leaders... In the middle section, there is a lot of private land, as there are 1,100 hectares situated outside the road dike. There are both private properties and government-owned lands there),” he said.

“Pero ito lahat po, precisely ni-reserve at ginawan ng paraan ng local government na maging public para hindi kamkamin. So baliktad sa allegation na kinakamkam. Titingnan niyo po y’ung history. Maraming kumakamkam po ng lupa dito. Pero ang history po ng Cayetano ay tumutulong na maging good stewards para sa gobyerno (But all of this was precisely reserved and secured by the local government for public use to prevent it from being seized by private interests. So, the allegation that it is being grabbed is the exact opposite of the truth. If you look at the history—there are many who do grab land here. But the Cayetanos’ track record shows they help act as good stewards for the government),” he emphasized.

On Saturday, August 29, Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson released further information and identified four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig which he said have been issued fraudulent land titles, while four others lack plotted title lots in the Land Registration Authority’s (LRA) digital file.
Lacson said his public disclosure of the details of the initial findings is to dispel insinuations that his earlier exposes on illegal reclamation activities in Taguig City were “fake news.”
“Since Senator Cayetano keeps publicly asking for evidence, I’ll give it to him, in the spirit of public interest,” he said.
In response, Cayetano again, took to Facebook livestream to refute Lacson’s allegations, referring to the former national police chief as a “Marites” and a “Senator-Judge Troll.”
“That senator-judge has been trolling me almost every day. It’s all just gossip, or, as they say, inconclusive, argumentative, and hearsay,” Cayetano said.
“So, if Senator Lacson—our senator-judge-troll—wishes to inspect the developments at the lake, he is most welcome,” he stressed.

articles.title: Canada installs large Lake Ontario sign in latest jab at US
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a billboard on Canada's shoreline with the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."

blocks.text: Watch: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveils 'Lake Ontario' sign
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has hit back at Donald Trump by installing a large sign on Canada's shoreline with the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."
The US president signed an executive order on Thursday seeking to change its name to Lake America and has shared a series of AI-generated videos about the lake that straddles both countries.
"Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario," Ford said.

The war of words was triggered after trade talks collapsed, with the US imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs next month.
Watch: "He's losing it" - Americans react to Lake Ontario name change
Trump said the decree was effective immediately as he signed the order to rename it Lake America.
While he has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks, other countries are not required to follow. Canadian officials have dismissed Trump's move.
On Saturday, Trump also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, with one showing him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with one that says: "Welcome to Lake America."
Another video depicted a flock of Canada geese sporting the US president's hair and holding rifles as they patrolled the shoreline of a newly named Lake America.
Ford said Trump's renaming of the lake was because he "didn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves".

Standing in front of the newly unveiled Lake Ontario sign, Ford added: "Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever."
It echoes Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's previous response to the row, insisting "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever".

blocks.caption: Map of the Great Lakes region of North America showing Lake Ontario highlighted in red. The map labels Ontario and Quebec in Canada and U.S. states including New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin. The other Great Lakes, Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Huron,…

blocks.text: The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.

Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

When Trump entered the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application.
In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".
