articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz expects to be himself at US Open despite 4-month absence
articles.summary: NEW YORK — After sitting out more than four months nursing an injured right wrist that caused him to miss the French Open and Wimbledon, Carlos Alcaraz didn’t decide to return for the US Open…

blocks.text: Carlos Alcaraz of Spain reacts with partner Serena Williams of the United States in their mixed doubles match against Erin Routliffe of New Zealand and Lloyd Glasspool of the United Kingdom during Fan Week at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on August 25, 2026 in the Flushing neighborhood of the Queens borough of New York City. Sarah Stier/Getty Images/AFP

NEW YORK — After sitting out more than four months nursing an injured right wrist that caused him to miss the French Open and Wimbledon, Carlos Alcaraz didn’t decide to return for the US Open to be anything less than his Grand Slam-winning self.
“You’re going to see Carlitos playing the way he always has,” Alcaraz said.

The 23-year-old from Spain is set to play his first competitive singles match Monday since getting sidelined by the wrist injury in mid-April. He insists he has not changed anything about his mechanics and expressed confidence about physically feeling great.
“I need competition,” Alcaraz said Friday. “We, my team and me, believe that I’m ready. It wasn’t an easy decision. I just did whatever it took to be ready.”

Alcaraz is the defending champion and favored to go back-to-back, a year after beating Jannik Sinner and overtaking him for the No. 1 ranking. The field this time does not include Sinner, who withdrew because of a right knee injury.
“We are not going see each other for, like, six months now, seven months,” Alcaraz said. “It’s kind of a weird situation, to be honest.”
Alexander Zverev is the top seed in Sinner’s absence. But all eyes are on Alcaraz, who earlier this year won his seventh Grand Slam title by defeating Novak Djokovic in the Australian Open final.

“Everyone is going to be pretty tapped in to see his first match,” 11th-seeded American Frances Tiafoe said. “If he comes back anywhere near his level, it’s tough. Regardless, even if he’s not at his tip-top (shape), you’ve still got to beat him in five (sets).”

Alcaraz opens against Roman Safiullin as he dives right back into best-of-five-set tennis in his return. He did get a chance to shake some rust off by playing a couple of mixed doubles matches with Serena Williams this week, but he knows not getting a full ramp up to the U.S. Open adds another layer of difficulty.
“It’s really challenging,” Alcaraz said. “Probably in terms of preparation and everything, (it) is not the best time.”
But the energy of playing in New York was enough of a draw that he said, “There is no better tournament than the U.S. Open to be back.”
Can he win it off such a long layoff? He knows Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal have done it but does not want to set any expectations.

“I’m not going to set a limit for myself,” Alcaraz said in Spanish. “I don’t want to focus on a specific result. I want to focus on the process we’ve gone through. Just go out there, enjoy it and feel good.”

Zverev, who’s now four years removed from tearing ligaments in his right ankle, was reluctant to compare two very different injuries. But he expects Alcaraz to be formidable as the tournament goes on.
“Wrist is never easy,” Zverev said. “I expect him to be maybe a bit rusty the first or second match, but once he gets through that, I think he’s going to be a contender, for sure, here.”

After dealing with intrusive thoughts during his time away from the sport, Alcaraz is still playing a mental game to not worry too much about the injury. His goals are to get through the U.S. Open healthy and stay away from the fear that creeps into his head.
“I just have to go 100%,” Alcaraz said. “I’ve got to trust my team. I’ve got to trust my people that tell me that it’s going to be fine.”

articles.title: Ecuador ex-president convicted of corruption
articles.summary: QUITO, Ecuador — An Ecuadoran court on Friday convicted ex-president Lenin Moreno of accepting bribes from a Chinese company that built the country’s biggest hydroelectric dam. The Attorney…

blocks.text: QUITO, Ecuador — An Ecuadoran court on Friday convicted ex-president Lenin Moreno of accepting bribes from a Chinese company that built the country’s biggest hydroelectric dam.

The Attorney General’s office said that Moreno, who governed from 2017 to 2021, was among four people convicted in the case involving the construction of the Coca Codo Sinclair dam by China’s Sinohydro.
Moreno was vice-president under socialist president Rafael Correa at the time of the alleged corruption, between 2007 and 2013.
He succeeded Correa, with the latter’s backing, but later fell out with his mentor by shifting to the right and aligning himself more closely with the United States.
The court in Quito has not yet sentenced him.
Moreno remains free pending his sentencing.
Prosecutors have asked for him to receive a six-and-a-half-year prison term.
The 73-year-old paraplegic, who served as the United Nations special envoy on disability issues, insisted Friday after the ruling that he had never received “a single cent” from Sinohydro.
He blamed the case on “the Correa regime,” saying his former-backer-turned-rival, who has also been convicted of corruption but is exiled in Belgium, “promised to take revenge on me.”
Prosecutors say Sinohydro paid bribes totaling $76 million, around four percent of the cost of the hydroelectric project.
Three other Ecuadoran nationals were convicted alongside Moreno, including two former managers of the power plant.
Around 20 people have been implicated in the case in total, including Moreno’s wife, his daughter, businesspeople, and a former Chinese ambassador to Quito. /das

articles.title: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU membership talks
articles.summary: The Nordic nation shelved earlier plans to join the EU over fishing rights, but geopolitics, including Trump's threat to seize Greenland, has prompted a rethink.

image.caption: Icelanders are voting on whether to restart EU accession talksImage: Leonhard Foeger/REUTERS

blocks.text: Iceland held a national referendum Saturday on whether to restart negotiations to join the European Union.
The Nordic nation has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc’s 28th member.
Iceland's left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.
Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest
What do we know about Iceland's referendum?
As they headed to one of hundreds of polling stations, voters mulled one simple yes or no question: Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?

The question relates to a previous attempt by the Icelandic government to join the EU in 2009, at the height of the global financial crisis that devastated the local economy. The accession plan was later shelved.

Saturday's vote was described as too close to call, with a Gallup poll on Friday suggesting a narrow majority of Icelanders oppose reopening talks. Other recent polls suggest a narrow lead for the yes vote.
Although Iceland has never been an EU member, it is already closely integrated with the bloc.
It is a member of both the European Economic Area (EEA) — which gives access to the EU's frictionless single market — and the Schengen Area free-travel zone.
Of Iceland's roughly 400,000 population, around 265,000 were eligible to weigh in on the referendum.

blocks.caption: Saturday’s referendum is too close to callImage: B. Niehaus/snapshot/IMAGO

blocks.text: What are the deciding factors among voters?
Voters have grown increasingly concerned about geopolitics, including the threat from Russia and US President Donald Trump's threats to seize nearby Greenland from Denmark.
Icelanders, who gained independence from Denmark in 1944, have been asking whether they could be next.
"We can't really trust the US anymore," said Hildur Knutsdottir, a horror fiction writer who plans to vote in favor of EU membership.
Arctic nations sit at the center of a growing contest for the polar north, as the United States, Russia and China jostle for influence over sea routes, natural resources and security.
The left-leaning Icelandic coalition believes EU membership could help counter Trump's ambitions in the North Atlantic.
"The international order that underpinned our security and prosperity for decades is under serious pressure," Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir told Reuters last week.
"In times like these, small nations need to ​think carefully about where they stand and who stands with them," she added.
Is the US driving Iceland to join the European Union?
Fishing, interest rates and national identity
The last attempt to join the EU was shelved in 2015, largely over concerns about joining the bloc's common fisheries policy.

Icelanders have been living off hefty cod and haddock catches for centuries and are loath to open the chilled Arctic waters to Spanish, Dutch and other EU trawlers, which is a requirement from Brussels.
The government has said it could try to negotiate a full opt-out from the policy.
Some economists think Icelanders, who have struggled under high inflation and interest rates, could benefit financially from EU membership and possibly the adoption of the euro.
National identity is another driver of voting, with opponents of EU membership noting how Iceland enjoys all the benefits of European integration without being a full member.

"For a country like ours with our small economy, it's very important to maintain our sovereignty and not to transfer more power than we would have to do to the EU," former Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir said at an ​event in Reykjavik ‌on Thursday.
What happens if Iceland votes to restart EU talks?
A yes vote would trigger a negotiating process with the EU's executive branch, the European Commission.
This would involve discussions on 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.
A foreign ministry memo estimates accession talks could start by the end of the year and take 18 to 24 months.

articles.title: Coco Gauff backs mom post about excessive US Open ticket requests
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Coco Gauff was caught by surprise when she saw her mom take to social media about excessive US Open ticket requests from family and friends. That doesn’t mean she has any issue with…

blocks.text: Coco Gauff of the United States speaks during Media Day ahead of the US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on August 28, 2026 in New York City. Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images/AFP
NEW YORK — Coco Gauff was caught by surprise when she saw her mom take to social media about excessive US Open ticket requests from family and friends.
That doesn’t mean she has any issue with it.
A day after Candi Gauff posted a “blunt but necessary statement” on Instagram saying her daughter’s tickets for the Grand Slam tournament were spoken for, Coco defended the sentiment.

“Honestly, it was needed, and it was directed towards a few family and friends,” Gauff said Friday. “People come out of the woodwork. You haven’t spoken to someone for years. They don’t say, ‘Congrats’ or, ‘Happy birthday’ or nothing. Then they’re like, ‘Oh, I’m in New York, can I have 8 tickets to your match in your box, please?”

Gauff is coming off winning the Cincinnati Open and initially thought her mother’s post — which included a photo of her holding the trophy — was a sweet message about that victory. Instead, Candi Gauff had a point to make.

“Unfortunately, I will not be able to hook you up with a ticket,” she wrote. “Please make arrangements to purchase a ticket. Side note, never ask for more than 2 tickets. Coco is grown now and she has her own friends that she is honoring (with) tickets for the match. Thank you for your continued support.”

Coco Gauff won the U.S. Open in 2023, is ranked fourth in the world and is seeded fourth this year in women’s singles. As the most prominent American at the tournament, she is a fixture at Arthur Ashe Stadium and any of her matches instantly become a hot ticket.
Her parents and others on her team deal with most of the messages, shielding her from another unwelcome distraction.

“We try our best to accommodate everyone, but some of the requests, you would be surprised at how absurd they are,” Gauff said. “I feel like my mom hit a tipping point because it’s been going on since 15, and they really are my safeguards and I am lucky they try to make sure no one is hitting up my phone, so I don’t really get many requests.”
Rather than deal with more of them from distant relatives or friends from elementary school, Gauff said her mom “wanted to post that because she is going to stop responding. At least they know why.”

articles.title: Kai Sotto overcomes comeback jitters in Gilas Pilipinas win
articles.summary: Kai Sotto embraces the pressure and steps up when needed the most as he steers Gilas Pilipinas back on track in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers

blocks.text: TOWERING. Kai Sotto in action for Gilas Pilipinas in the FIBA World Cup 2027 Asian Qualifiers.
FIBA
Kai Sotto embraces the pressure and steps up when needed the most as he steers Gilas Pilipinas back on track in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers
MANILA, Philippines – Kai Sotto erupted in a thunderous roar after his block sealed Gilas Pilipinas’ win over Jordan in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers.
It was the culmination of two years of waiting and pent-up emotions, all released in one defining moment as the 7-foot-3 big man proved to be just what the doctor ordered in his national team return.

“Before the game, I had a lot on my mind. There was a mix of excitement and the realization that it had been such a long time since I last played for the national team,” said Sotto in a mix of Filipino and English.

“I knew I was carrying a lot of pressure, and I’m just really happy that was able to translate into my performance on the court what I had been waiting so long to do — play for the national team again.”

blocks.caption: Kai Sotto overcomes comeback jitters in Gilas Pilipinas win

blocks.text: Sotto finished with team highs of 18 points, 14 rebounds, and 2 blocks as the Philippines escaped with an 82-81 overtime win on Friday, August 28, to get its World Cup bid back on track after losing its last four games in the Asian Qualifiers.

Jordan stayed on the Philippines’ heels until the final second before Sotto swatted away a point-blank layup by Abdullah Olajuwon to secure the victory, much to the delight of a packed crowd at the Mall of Asia Arena.

The block completed the Filipinos’ comeback from 18 points down as they defended their turf even without injured naturalized player Justin Brownlee, with the likes of CJ Perez (16 points), Kevin Quiambao (14 points), and Dwight Ramos (14 points) rising to the occasion.
“I’m really happy that everyone contributed. We had a slow start, but as you saw, we fought our way back. I’m extremely proud of the team,” said Sotto.
Sotto last saw action for the national team in 2024 before an injury in early 2025 sidelined him, but there was little sign of rust as he seamlessly fit back into the squad.
For head coach Tim Cone, that adaptability makes Sotto special.
“He’s really that smart and intelligent. And that makes the people around him better. Everybody’s better when he’s on the floor,” Cone said of Sotto.
“Whether it be passing or screening or rolling, the attention he grabs, he just makes everybody around him better.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Man slain heading home from fiesta disco in San Fernando, Cebu
articles.summary: ​Cebu City, Philippines — A night of fiesta festivities turned grim after a man was found dead lying in a pool of blood along the road in Barangay Magsico, San Fernando, Cebu, early Saturday morning,…

blocks.text: ​Cebu City, Philippines — A night of fiesta festivities turned grim after a man was found dead lying in a pool of blood along the road in Barangay Magsico, San Fernando, Cebu, early Saturday morning, August 29.
Police identified the victim as Juan Baritos Sebial, an adult resident of Barangay Balungag of the same town.

Initial reports from the San Fernando Municipal Police Station revealed that the incident occurred at around 1:10 a.m. Sebial was reportedly heading home from a local disco event held in celebration of the barangay fiesta when he was attacked by an unknown perpetrator.
Authorities received the report at approximately 3:00 a.m., prompting an immediate response from police personnel.
Upon arrival at the scene, responding officers discovered the victim’s lifeless body on the ground.
​Investigator-on-case PCpl. Mario Paul Pino initially processed the immediate area surrounding the body as the primary crime scene.
Subsequent trace analysis, however, led law enforcement to a storefront located more than 100 meters away, where a trail of bloody footprints connected the two locations.

“First tan-aw namo nga ang crime scene kay kung asa ang patay nga lawas, pero as we conduct further investigation kay ang crime scene diay kay naa diay sa tumoy more or less 120 meters approximately,” Pino said.

(When we first checked, we thought that the crime scene was where the body was found, but as we conducted further investigation, we realized that the crime scene was more or less 120 meters further ahead.)
According to Pino, the victim was reportedly lying outside the commercial establishment when an unidentified assailant launched the sudden attack.
“Kung imo ning subayon kung asa iyang lawas ug didto sa tumoy naay mga taak sa footprints nga dunay dugo kung asa posible nakatulog ang suspect sa kahubog.”
(If you trace where the body was found and further ahead, there are bloody footprints where the suspect possibly fell asleep from being drunk.)
Victim was heading home
Authorities surmise the victim was attempting to travel home when the incident occurred and managed to run a short distance before succumbing to the injuries.
“Kani siya, sa atong pagpangutana, posible nga pauli nani siya. Naghigda kuno ni siya sa gawas sa usa ka tindahan nya gidunggab daw ni didto, nya nakadagan pani siya.”
(This is what we got from our questioning: it’s possible he was heading home. Witnesses say he was lying down outside a store where he was stabbed, and he still managed to run away.)
Preliminary coordination with the local barangay captain indicated that the victim had no prior criminal record or documented disputes within the community.
Seeking witnesses in San Fernando killing
​Law enforcement personnel are conducting field operations to ascertain the identity and whereabouts of the perpetrator.

Police leadership has issued an urgent call for public cooperation, appealing to eyewitnesses or individuals with relevant information to come forward while assuring that measures are in place to guarantee witness protection and safety.
“Hinaut nga sa kining mga ingon ani nga kaso kinahanglan jud ang hustisya. Sa mga witnesses dinha, magtinabangay ta ninyo. We’ll do our best to provide security para ma provide pud ang hustisya.”
(We hope that this kind of case finds justice. To the witnesses out there, let’s help each other. We’ll do our best to provide security so that justice can also be served.)
​As of this time, the motive behind the killing remains undetermined.

articles.title: Number of missing in Nepal, China floods soars to nearly 3,000
articles.summary: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan…

blocks.text: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing villages.

The number of missing soared to nearly 3,000 Saturday, according to the latest figures from both countries, with 633 bodies recovered and reports that some of the dead may have been swept downstream as far away as India.

In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list that already included trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
Those who made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonizing wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP.
Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother.
“We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said.
‘Enormous’ trauma
The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous,” and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise.
Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out.
Compounding the search for the missing are fears of further flooding in affected areas.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes to form, and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors.
Nepali police urged all rescuers to “immediately move to a safe location,” saying they had received information that “a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side.”

In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing suspended its rescue operation in the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding before saying the threat had eased.
State news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the area.
‘All swept away’
On the Nepali side of the border, the military located people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than 100 people trapped in the same area.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck.
“The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away,” Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, told AFP.
Nepal reported a death toll of 626 people on Saturday.
There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in Nepal.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, seven people died and 554 remain missing, state news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Pilgrimage route
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.
Sivaranjani Muthunathan was traveling by bus with 56 others toward the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.
“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told AFP on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging toward her.
Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud.
“One by one, we also climbed out through the driver’s side,” then scrambled up a hill, she said. /das

articles.title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows
articles.summary:
Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older people

Taking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce…

blocks.text: Taking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.

Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.
People who have already had a major heart event are also commonly prescribed the drugs, regardless of their age.

What doctors did not know was whether it was safe to prescribe a daily statin to people aged 70 and over who were healthy overall, having never experienced a heart attack, stroke or heart surgery, and whether doing so could prevent these cardiac events.

A co-author of the study, Adjunct Prof Mark Nelson with the Monash University school of public health and preventive medicine, said it was an important piece of missing information, because the biggest risk of major heart-related events “is increasing age”.

“Our society is ageing, and therefore the burden of disease is increasing, making it important to improve our ability to prevent disease in this group,” he said. “So we needed the evidence for this group to see if prescribing statins as a prevention measure works.”

But Nelson said older adults were often overlooked in early statin research because 40 years ago, heart disease was most common in middle-aged populations especially if they smoked, leading public health efforts to focus on preventing premature deaths in that group. Elderly populations may also be sick and on other medications, making trialling drugs risky, he said.

To address the gap, Monash researchers analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of almost 10,000 study participants over the age of 70 who were given either a daily statin or a placebo, in a scientifically-robust type of study known as a randomised control trial. The participants were enrolled with the help of almost 3,400 GPs across Australia.

The researchers excluded people who had a condition that might make taking a statin unsafe, if they were not living independently, or if they already needed the drug because they had suffered a heart attack.
The decade-long study found the medication decreased the risk of a first major cardiovascular event by 30% for those aged over 70.
In real terms, this means one major cardiac event such as a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery could be prevented for every 37 older adults treated with daily statins over almost six years.
Prof James Chong, a cardiologist at Sydney’s Westmead hospital, said if the research “leads to increased statin use globally, the absolute reduction of (heart-related) events can be significant”.
“One of the major changes that may result, in my opinion, is more elderly patients having confidence to take long term statins,” he said.

“However, one thing we have to keep in mind is it was an almost exclusively white population with the mean age around 75 years of age, so the results may not be as generalisable globally without further supporting evidence.”
The findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on Saturday and presented concurrently at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Germany.

Lead researcher on the paper, Adjunct Prof Sophia Zoungas, said: “What we hope to see, now that we have provided such strong evidence, are updated treatment guidelines to help clinicians make use of this new finding.”
Older patients should have a conversation with their GP about whether statins are appropriate to help them stay healthy, the researchers said.

Prof Tom Marwick, a cardiologist at Hobart’s Royal hospital, said there had been a lot of misinformation about statins increasing the risk of dementia, making some older people reluctant to take the drugs.

A benefit of the Monash study was that the findings “really close the book on that, in large numbers,” he said. The study found no statistically significant difference in dementia rates among those who received a statin and those who did not.
Marwick described it as a “well done, really important trial”.
But he said the study also found patients were reluctant to adhere to therapy, with more than 15% of patients in the trial discontinuing their medication.

Marwick said “a slight disappointment” in the findings was that although major heart events were reduced, the disability-free survival was the same among the participants whether they took the statin or the placebo.
In other words, taking the medication didn’t extend life or its quality.
“We can reduce cardiovascular events, but the health burdens of ageing are less amenable,” he said.

articles.title: La Mesa Dam reaches spilling level Saturday afternoon

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The water level of La Mesa Dam reached spilling level on Saturday afternoon due to continuous heavy rains, the Quezon City local government unit announced.
In an advisory, the city government said that as of 1:50 p.m., the water level has reached its overflow level at 80.15 meters.
The excess water from the reservoir may affect low-lying areas along the Tullahan River.
The city government advised residents in the following areas to evacuate when necessary and take precautionary measures due to possible flooding:

items: Fairview
Forest Hills Subdivision
Quirino Highway
Sta. Quiteria
San Bartolome

articles.title: Bodies of 2 missing Aeta children retrieved from Zambales lake
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — The bodies of two Aeta children who went missing after a boat carrying 13 passengers capsized in Mapanuepe Lake near San Marcelino town were recovered Saturday, Aug. 29, three…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — The bodies of two Aeta children who went missing after a boat carrying 13 passengers capsized in Mapanuepe Lake near San Marcelino town were recovered Saturday, Aug. 29, three days after the incident.
The two were identified as Chandnea Serrano dela Cruz, 3, and Anqelito Serrano Liwanag, 8, according to the Philippine Coast Guard.

In a phone interview, Police Maj. Exodus Rodriguez, chief of the San Marcelino police, said a resident traveling toward Barangay Buhawen spotted the body of the 3-year-old girl while passing through the lake.
The resident retrieved the child and brought her to authorities, where her father confirmed her identity, Rodriguez said.
After the girl’s body was recovered, police asked a boatman to accompany them back to the area where she was found, according to Rodriguez.
They then spotted the body of Anqelito nearby and recovered it.
Rodriguez said weather conditions had been unpredictable during the search, with rain and strong winds easing at times before suddenly intensifying.
Despite the conditions, search operations continued for the remaining missing passenger, a 26-year-old pregnant woman.
On Thursday, Aug. 27, the 13 Aeta passengers were aboard a motor banca that capsized near the Sunken Church in Barangay Buhawen while they were returning to their community in Sitio Lumibao.
With the recovery of the two children, eight Aetas have now died in the incident, including five children, while four others survived. /das

articles.title: Roger Federer heads to International Tennis Hall of Fame
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Roger Federer loved to win, of course, and at the peak of his career almost always did. All those victories and trophies he piled up alone would have made Federer remembered forever in…

blocks.text: Swiss former tennis player Roger Federer, Class of 2026 Inductee, waves to fans during the International Tennis Hall of Fame Celebrity Pro Classic in Newport, Rhode Island, on August 28, 2026. (Photo by Joseph Prezioso / AFP)
NEW YORK — Roger Federer loved to win, of course, and at the peak of his career almost always did.

All those victories and trophies he piled up alone would have made Federer remembered forever in tennis, but they were only part of the reason he enjoyed playing. He liked traveling to tournaments, meeting people and making new friends, whether they were on the other side of the net or sitting in the stands.
Only after he finished competing did Federer realize how much that impacted his legacy in the sport.

For the first time, Roger Federer visited the Museum at the International Tennis Hall of Fame, taking in the legends who shaped his journey and reflecting on his own Path to Greatness. In just days, he’ll receive tennis’ ultimate honor. ✨🎾 #InductionCelebration pic.twitter.com/wjAWa8cM5g — International Tennis Hall of Fame (@TennisHalloFame) August 28, 2026

“I think when you retire, I think I said it before, that there was a lot of talk also about maybe my personality and what I brought to the game overall when I wasn’t on court, which I was a little surprised,” Federer said. “I thought it was about, in the moment, forehands and backhands and saving break points and victories and all that stuff.

“But actually it becomes a little bit, not irrelevant eventually, but it’s about what were you remembered for, how did you behave in the locker rooms or in the corridors or maybe with the media, or with the tournament directors, the ball kids.”
Federer will have a chance to reflect back on it all Saturday when he is enshrined in the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island.

The 45-year-old from Switzerland, who will be honored along with broadcaster and former player Mary Carillo, said it would be his first trip to Newport. That seemed surprising, given how many places he’s gone for his tennis.

Sure, there was regular stops such as New York and London and Paris for Grand Slam tournaments, but there were also cities like Cape Town, South Africa, for an exhibition match against Rafael Nadal that drew nearly 52,000 fans; or Mexico City, for one against Alexander Zverev that drew more than 42,000.

Those were near the end of his career, when Federer was forced to limit his schedule for health reasons. He hated having to do so, because he liked going too many places, even ones that didn’t host the biggest events.

“For me, if I look back, that’s kind of what I’m very happy about, that I went through 25 years on tour, and actually felt like I made a lot of friends and a lot of people miss me,” Federer said. “Same with fans. They come up to me and say, ‘What a shame you’re not playing anymore.’
“Then I get a flashback saying it was an amazing time, and I say it every time. I loved it, and it’s a shame I can’t be on the tour anymore. But it was a great, great time and I miss it dearly.”

The fans clearly miss Federer. When he returned to the U.S. Open this week for an exhibition, his first time playing in Flushing Meadows since 2019, the lines of fans waiting to get into Arthur Ashe Stadium resembled a night in the second week of the tournament, not well before it even began.

Federer won five straight U.S. Open titles from 2004-08, during a stretch when he compiled a 247-15 record from 2004-06 and reached a record 10 consecutive Grand Slam finals from 2005-07, winning eight. He went on to win 1,251 matches and 103 tournaments, including 20 Grand Slams.
“He’s the best I’ve ever played against,” Andre Agassi, Federer’s opponent in the 2005 final, said in a video the U.S. Open showed before Federer took the court Tuesday.

The way he won, with far more flair than some stuffy champions of the past but without the temper tantrums of others, earned him accolades that his skills alone couldn’t. He won the ATP Tour’s sportsmanship award every year from 2004-09, and again from 2011-17, and the fan favorite award every year from 2003-21. Those came while earning prize money of nearly $130.6 million.
Federer hits sometimes with his children — he and wife Mirka are parents of two sets of twins — and tries to attend a few events a year to keep him connected to the sport.

“I’m in a very comfortable place today, but I’m still happy to be out there and being in the tennis world from time to time, because it is the glue to everything that surrounds me still today,” Federer said.

“I had the best time, had a lot of friends on tour, from players to people who were organizers, et cetera. So I hope that a lot of the players who retire also feel the same way about the game, because I care dearly.”

articles.title: Rescuers recover mud-caked survivors as Nepal-China flood toll rises
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that killed nearly 600 people and left almost 2,500 missing.

The rescue efforts included a team that rappelled into a severely damaged checkpoint area on the Chinese side of the border between the two countries. Rescuers were on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods Wednesday. Experts warned that the lake, created after a glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow.

Nepal’s army was deployed to help rescue more than 100 people believed trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower plant located in the country’s worst-hit district. Like elsewhere in the disaster zone, their work was complicated by thick layers of mud that covered the site.
The rappelling rescue team descended into the once-bustling border-crossing area from wooded mountain slopes, the state broadcaster China Central Television said.

“As far as I can see, it’s nothing but debris,” rescue official Zou Mingqi told state media. The area where travelers went through border control to enter or leave China has been flattened to a muddy area, according to satellite images.

The floods have killed 579 in Nepal, the country’s disaster-management authority said Friday. Nepali police later put the number of deaths at 553. There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to seven Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders’ efforts to direct the relief response.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Meanwhile, the number of people who were unaccounted for in the country nearly doubled to 1,924 as more local residents were added to the tally. China’s state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak.

In other developments, Nepal on Friday reversed an earlier decision and said it would allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts, apparently under pressure from other countries, especially those whose citizens are unaccounted for, a leading English-language newspaper, The Kathmandu Post, reported.
Authorities warn of flooding from a new lake

Nepali police issued a fresh alert Friday after receiving information that a dam on the Tibet side had burst. Security personnel and rescue and relief workers were told to stay on high alert and move to a safe location if necessary.

It was unclear if the dam bursting was related to flooding concerns over the lake that formed after the initial flash floods. Chinese broadcaster CCTV said the newly formed lake, located more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal, sits at an elevation of 2,950 meters (9,680 feet).

Nepali and Chinese authorities earlier warned of more flooding from the lake, which was already overflowing. Rescue workers heading to the disaster zone were ordered to stop temporarily Friday due to concern the lake would release more water and debris, and people in potentially affected areas were urged to move to safer ground.

Monitoring data from the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources later showed that the lake had dwindled in size. The water level dropped by 10 meters (32 feet) from the high point on Thursday morning, the state broadcaster said.

Some 680 rescuers eventually reached the Gyirong area by foot and via rafts. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area, CCTV footage showed. “Anyone, anyone?” rescuers yelled, according to footage by the broadcaster.
It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit.
Thousands of people have been evacuated while others await rescue

In Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Nepali army rescuers struggled to help more than 100 people believed to be trapped by thick mud in a tunnel that’s part of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project. The army said it had rescued 350 people from the tunnel so far.
Video from the scene showed rescuers helping a man covered in mud out of the tunnel by pulling and pushing.
“It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud,” Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said.
Nepal’s disaster-management authority said 3,253 people had been airlifted by helicopter from the disaster area.

The search-and-rescue efforts have been supported by an outpouring of financial support from neighboring countries, including small, poorer countries like Sri Lanka, said Kanni Wignaraja, the United Nations development agency’s regional director for Asia and the Pacific.
“Sri Lanka has its own huge fiscal problems, but it has just sent $1 million immediately to the Nepal government,” Wignaraja said.
Some felt the ground shake, then saw a ‘black storm’

Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as magnitude 5.2. The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.
Customs officer Karbir Gaire was among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with China, where some 1,500 people had lived.
Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. Wednesday and was working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

“Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us,” he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. “We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.”
Fifteen of Gaire’s colleagues are missing. “It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don’t call it a flood. It was a tsunami.”
Families around the world hope for news of loved ones
Nepal’s tourism board has said that among the missing are more than 500 foreigners.
While the Nepal government shared a public list of people they rescued, there was little information about victims on the Chinese side of the border.

Chinese government officials stuck to their tight media controls. Information about major disasters is typically released with a delay and without personal stories of victims. State media has focused on stories of rescuers working to reach the disaster site or reporting on instructions from top leaders.
About 90 Americans were unaccounted for.
Some of the missing may have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

Indian spiritual guru Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, said in a post on X that 77 people returning from Mount Kailash with groups organized by his Isha Foundation were at the immigration center in Gyirong when the flooding struck.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy, who works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry, said that he spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on that pilgrimage Wednesday morning. It was a highly anticipated trip, something his mother had always wanted to do, he said.
“This was the last we spoke to them,” he said. “They have been unreachable since.” /das

articles.title: Low voter turnout expected in Dasmariñas City special polls due to rain
articles.summary: DASMARIÑAS CITY, Philippines — A low voter turnout is expected in Dasmariñas City’s special election due to the effects of the southwest monsoon, the Commission on Elections (Comelec) said Saturday.…

blocks.text: DASMARIÑAS CITY, Philippines — A low voter turnout is expected in Dasmariñas City’s special election due to the effects of the southwest monsoon, the Commission on Elections (Comelec) said Saturday.
The prediction came as heavy rain poured over the city as residents cast their votes for a new congressional representative to replace former lawmaker Francisco “Kiko” Barzaga.

“Yes, kapag talaga namang ganiyan, siyempre ‘yung iba mas iniingatan nila ‘yung kanilang kalusugan lalo na ‘yung may mga nararamdaman lalo o may mga comorbidities so hindi na lang sila lumalabas sa mga tirahan nila,“ said Comelec Chairperson George Erwin Garcia in a chance interview.

(Yes, in situations like this, people naturally take extra care of their health, especially those who are already feeling unwell or have underlying health conditions, so they simply avoid leaving their homes.)
“Noong nakaraan ang sabi natin 60 to 65 percent. Ngayon kontento na tayo kung kahit maka-50 percent man lang ang bumoto,” said Garcia.
(We previously projected a turnout of 60 to 65 percent. Now, we would be satisfied with a 50 percent voter turnout.)

This, he added, is similar to the turnout of past special elections—like the recent Antipolo City special election, which only saw a turnout of 31 percent, and the plebiscite held in Parañaque City, which had a 17.4 percent voter turnout.
“Pero sana naman dito mas mataas sapagkat napaka importante rin noong posisyon na kanila pong pi-fill up-an,” he said.
(But I hope it’s higher here because the position they are filling is also very important.)
Garcia, however, clarified that voter turnout will not affect the results of the election under the rule of plurality.

“Ibig sabihin, hindi po kinakailangang majority of registered voters ay nakaboto at ang sabi po ng batas din ang ipoproklama ng Comelec ay kung sino lamang ang may pinakamataas na boto na nakuha sa lahat ng kandidato,” said Garcia.

(This means it is not required for a majority of registered voters to have cast their votes; the law dictates that the Comelec shall proclaim the candidate who garnered the most number of votes among all the candidates.)
Dasmariñas City makes up the entire 4th District of Cavite, with 447,387 registered voters across 75 barangays. /gsg

articles.title: Mutya ng Pilipinas marks 58th year, sets Oct. 14 finals
articles.summary: The Mutya ng Pilipinas pageant, the second-longest-running national pageant in the Philippines, is celebrating its 58th anniversary this year. And the organization has released the schedule of the…

blocks.text: The Mutya ng Pilipinas pageant, the second-longest-running national pageant in the Philippines, is celebrating its 58th anniversary this year. And the organization has released the schedule of the events that will mark the occasion.
This year’s edition of the competition was launched in Makati City on Aug. 26, during which the organization released the schedule of activities.
The coronation night will once again take place at the FilOil Eco Oil Center in San Juan City, its preferred venue since its post-pandemic resumption on Oct. 14, 2022.
Applications are ongoing, and the general screening will be on Sept. 30 at the CWC Design Center. The final screening will be held in the same venue on Oct. 1.
The official candidates will be presented at The Bellevue Manila in Alabang, Muntinlupa City, on Oct. 4, while the 2026 Gala event will take place at Fairmont Makati on Oct. 11.
Although the Mutya ng Pilipinas pageant is marking its 58th year this 2026, the coming edition will only be its 55th installment. No competitions were held in four separate years.
What was supposed to be the 25th edition scheduled in 1992 was postponed for the next year because of the deadly eruption of Mt. Pinatubo and other calamities.

The national pageant also had a two-year hiatus in 2020 and 2021 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. It once again had a break in 2023, just a year after its resumption, because many of the 2022 winners crowned in December that year competed in 2024 international contests.
The Mutya ng Pilipinas pageant has been enjoying a placement streak in international competitions, with all delegates sent since 2022 garnering placements in their respective global tilts.
Reigning queen Christina Vanhefflin scored a back-to-back “Power of Beauty” win at the Miss Intercontinental pageant in Egypt in January, where she also finished fifth overall.
She will relinquish her national title to her successor who will be sent to the next edition of the Miss Intercontinental pageant, and try to score the Philippines’ third victory.

Vanhefflin’s fellow 2025 Mutya ng Pilipinas winner Andrea Endicio, who was initially set to compete at the Miss Tourism International pageant before the franchise changed hands, is now heading to the Miss Polo Universe pageant. /ra

articles.title: PasaHero turns the Filipino commute into a whimsical game
articles.summary: The PasaHero project began as Gabriel Del Rosario’s thesis at Ateneo de Manila University, where he wanted to make a game about travelling around the Philippines and delivering packages. He…

blocks.text: The PasaHero project began as Gabriel Del Rosario’s thesis at Ateneo de Manila University, where he wanted to make a game about travelling around the Philippines and delivering packages. He eventually realized that he did not have enough personal experience with the kind of travelling he wanted to portray to make the idea work.

“I initially set out to just make a game about travelling in the Philippines,” Del Rosario said. “It was frustrating working on the initial thesis ideas of travelling/exploring because I simply didn’t have enough lived experiences to make something compelling or educational.”
Then he remembered the familiar phrase: “Papasok kang estudyante, lalabas kang mandirigma.”

blocks.caption: Image via Kwek Kwek Studios

blocks.text: Del Rosario is the founder of Kwek Kwek Studios, the team developing PasaHero. Franz Leonard Atanacio works on game design and takes on other roles when needed, while Johann handles the business side of the studio and also works on design. Arti Vergara leads game design and studio culture, and Riv handles art operations.

The game turns the Filipino commute into a 3D platformer, with the player trying to get to school while dealing with public transportation, traffic, weather and the other problems that come with getting from one place to another.

The choice of platforming comes from Del Rosario’s interest in games such as the classic Super Mario 64. He liked how those games were easy to pick up but still gave players room to improve their movement and discover things for themselves.
“There was a satisfaction in those games that gave the right balance of fun exploration and satisfying movement,” Del Rosario said.

The goal was to give PasaHero the same accessibility while leaving room for players to master its movement and discover its secrets. The difference is the setting. Instead of the fantastical playgrounds common in classic platformers, PasaHero uses an exaggerated version of the Philippines that still needs to feel grounded enough for players to recognize.

“The setting of the game is an exaggerated reflection of commuting locations in the Philippines but it can’t go overboard with its more whimsical or fantasy elements otherwise it would detract the immersion of the player,” Del Rosario said.

“The parking lot in front of Shakey’s Katipunan branch has become a point of discussions and jokes in the Ateneo community. It is because of how difficult it is to navigate when it is filled with cars. People treat it as a maze, but imagine if you can platform over those cars without the owners suing you for property damage.”, added Atanasio about an inspiration for the game.
“A lot of the time the main question I would ask myself is ‘What are commuters already doing?’ and this would serve as my guide on ideas that can work in the game,” Del Rosario said.

Choosing between walking and taking a vehicle, deciding which route to take and managing limited money are all decisions commuters already make. PasaHero turns those decisions into mechanics, with time pressure adding another layer to otherwise routine choices.
Atanacio sees commuting itself as a game.

“If you think about it, commuting itself is a game already,” he said. “You have an objective, multiple means to reach that objective which has their own pros and cons, and limited resources to achieve that objective.”
A train can be faster and cheaper, while a bus might take you directly to your destination. The player has to decide which tradeoff is worth making.
“Do you prefer the faster and cheaper option, or the more convenient option?” Atanacio said. “We can’t have both because the Philippine transportation system sucks.”
That is also why the protagonist is a student on a budget. Del Rosario said the perspective comes from his own experience, since that was the situation he was in for most of his time as a student.

The developers also found that the student perspective makes the game’s scarcity more tangible. There are too few public utility vehicles and too many commuters, forcing players to make decisions about limited resources.
Some playtesters have suggested that the character could simply take Grab or Angkas when things get difficult.
“That would defeat the whole purpose of the game,” Del Rosario said. “This is a game of inconvenience. The pasahero is just a participant that relies on this public transportation system.”
Atanacio also sees the student character as a broadly relatable starting point.
“Everyone has experienced being a student on a budget at least one time in their lives,” he said. “Because of this, it will be relatable to the majority of people playing the game.”
The current playable demo does not yet put much pressure on players to manage their pamasahe, but the team intends for later levels to make budget management more important.
One of the more important ideas behind PasaHero is that commuting is not just about riding a vehicle.

Del Rosario remembers commuting along Commonwealth Avenue at around 5 a.m., when he saw people moving around the highway and jumping onto public utility vehicles. He also remembers an elderly commuter falling while trying to get onto a jeepney. People immediately checked on him before he simply got back up and continued his journey.
“This was the moment that made me heavily dislike how we do commuting and it’s the image that pops in my head when I think about PasaHero,” Del Rosario said.
He remembers the experience as both familiar and frustrating, which is also how he sees the game’s approach to commuting.
“It’s relatable and funny because for commuters it’s familiar and it makes people feel heard but at the same time it’s frustrating that it is relevant and that this is life,” he said.

The team is particularly interested in the experience of the “Supercommuter,” referring to people who travel from outside major urban areas into cities for work or school. Their journeys can involve several vehicles, long queues and difficult walking conditions before they even reach their destination.
“Things like multimodal travel, long queue lines, hostile walking conditions and so on are the many things a Supercommuter faces,” Del Rosario said.

The developers are currently looking at Metro Manila, Metro Cebu and Metro Davao, as well as the rural areas surrounding them. The game is not intended to reproduce any one place exactly, but the vehicles are immediately recognizable: jeepneys, tricycles, habal-habal and other forms of Philippine transportation.
“The goal is to make the setting in PasaHero recognizable as the Philippines but to not be an accurate 1 to 1 representation of any particular place or setting,” Del Rosario said.
The game also exaggerates some of the realities of commuting to make them work as platforming mechanics.
Strong winds can push the player around. Flooding can create new routes using improvised platforms. Traffic becomes an obstacle that has to be watched and avoided.
The team introduces these challenges individually before combining them. A player first learns how to deal with wind, for example, before having to deal with wind and traffic at the same time.
“To make each obstacle in front of the player manageable, it first needs to be introduced and then it can be amped up,” Del Rosario said.

The developers have considered adding more unpredictable elements, including vehicle breakdowns and accidents, but they still need to make sure those systems do not turn the game into something unfair.

“For example, a rainy level where entire roads are flooded would be a nice reference to recent issues regarding Philippine transportation,” Del Rosario said. “However, it also removes the option of riding vehicles as traversing by foot would always be a better option.”
The platforming itself remains one of the team’s biggest challenges. It has to be simple enough for new players while still giving experienced players something to master.
“The platforming took, and is still taking, the longest for me and the team to get right,” Del Rosario said. “It needed to be easy to pick up but fun to master.”
The traffic system has presented another technical problem because the game needs to handle multiple vehicles and pedestrians at once.

Del Rosario points to games such as Until Then and Hari ng Lagim as examples of Filipino developers telling local stories through different genres. He believes the growth of independent development has helped create more space for those ideas.
“I find that there has always been an interest in making games that are Filipino,” he said. “There has always been that interest and passion to make something Filipino.”
PasaHero takes a less traditional route. There is no mythology or historical setting. The Filipino identity comes from something considerably more ordinary.

The game is built around a familiar experience rather than a particular period or tradition. For Del Rosario, that makes it easier for people to relate to even if they come from different backgrounds.

“Even when comparing PasaHero to other platformers, you can see that the setting is ordinary and can’t compare in terms of whimsy or fantasy with others,” he said. “Yet that’s what makes it so relatable and understandable for other people.”

“Our diversity, and culture is varied and mixed in so many wonderful ways that it’s difficult to find the one modern thing that we can all share,” Del Rosario said. “At least with commuting/travelling, it is universal.”
That has also helped the game connect with international players.
When the team exhibited PasaHero at GDS 2026, international visitors were able to understand the game’s basic experience even without knowing the context behind every vehicle or location.
“They grasped what the game was trying to do with the platforming and the setting,” Del Rosario said. “Some of them even relate to the hectic struggle happening to the character.”
The developers found that international players often responded to the mood of the game before understanding all of its cultural references.
“People play the game and see that it’s warm and find it cute then slowly they see the themes of commuting and messy hectic roads to travel,” Del Rosario said.

That approach has helped the team think about how to introduce Filipino experiences to audiences who are unfamiliar with them. Del Rosario said one consultant they met at GDS 2026 gave them a useful principle: when the recognizability of something is low, creators can work with what they are able to evoke and let audiences build an understanding from there.
Getting to school is the game’s central objective because it is the commuting experience Del Rosario knows best.

The current scoring system is based primarily on time. A timer tracks how long a player takes to reach class, rewarding those who can make the journey quickly. The budget system currently plays a smaller role, although it is intended to become more important in later levels.
The developers have also compiled their own commuting experiences on the team’s Discord server and use those alongside research into how other people commute.
The pressure of being late to school also shapes the game’s pacing.
“Calm and slow at the start, chaotic and fast at the end,” Del Rosario said.

For him, the biggest time pressure often comes from getting to the public utility vehicle that will take him toward his destination. Reaching that first major vehicle can determine whether he is already going to be late.
“In this sense, the closer you get to your goal, the more resistance will be met,” he said.

The game will eventually expand beyond its current rural environment into more urban and varied areas. The team also wants to introduce crowds of other passengers, forcing players to navigate around groups of people rather than simply vehicles and environmental obstacles.
That focus on the pedestrian experience has already affected how some playtesters think about commuting.
Del Rosario remembers that some Ateneo playtesters initially questioned why a commuter game had so much platforming.
“Most people hear commuter game and think of the vehicles,” he said. “Yet people should realize that a really large part of it is the pedestrian experience.”
The time between vehicles, dealing with weather and navigating messy traffic are all part of the commute.

One playtester told the team that playing PasaHero made her realize how much walking is actually involved in commuting and how hectic and tiring it can be. Another asked why the protagonist did not simply live near the university.
Another person in the room had the answer: they could not afford it.
For Del Rosario, those conversations are part of what the game is trying to create.
“I want players to enjoy travelling but to also come to terms with how chaotic and messy the public transportation is,” he said.
He hopes Filipino players can laugh at the situations they recognize while also thinking about how much of their lives are spent getting from one place to another.
“The hope is that they also walk away with this bittersweet feeling that this is really how commuting has been for a long time,” Del Rosario said.
The developers also hope the game can connect with people who have never experienced Philippine public transportation.

Del Rosario said he was surprised that some Filipino playtesters were interested in the game specifically because they wanted to learn more about Filipino commuting. The experience at GDS 2026 reinforced the idea that the game’s premise can work beyond its local setting.
“As some of our mentors would say, ‘the experience of travelling is international,’” he said.

That does not mean removing the Filipino details. The vehicles, roads, traffic patterns and other elements remain central to the game’s identity. Instead, the developers are using the broader experience of travelling as a way into those details.
The same principle shapes what Del Rosario wants players to take away from the game.

“I hope that it leads them to reflect on their own commuting experience,” he said. “That it makes them think about how much their own lives are spent in-transit. How much of their lives have been limited by what is accessible for commuting.”

“Reflection and thinking about the times they’ve spent commuting themselves and how it lines up with the game,” he said. “Hopefully, they also laugh and have a good time seeing these times. Like they feel heard.”

Kwek Kwek Studios is already considering what could come next. The team is looking into multiplayer and even international travel for PasaHero. It is also working on another project called Sari Sari Skies, which is built around children racing kites and using Filipino words as power-ups.

“Games may not fix anything directly but it certainly can help make the world feel a lot lighter,” he said. “Use games as your tool to spread fun and to teach. Don’t stop, keep trying and find what it is that you find fun and what you want others to experience!”
