blocks.caption: Protests in Malaysia in 2012 against the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. Meta was alleged in a lawsuit to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya. Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”
The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.
That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

articles.title: Protesters set fire to migrant camp in Ceuta
articles.summary: The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish exclave in North Africa.

image.caption: Police had to intervene when protesters began setting fire to the parts of the campImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRES/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters in Ceuta set fire to a migrant camp and clashed with police on Thursday. The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish enclave in North Africa.
Footage on Spanish television showed a group of demonstrators on a beach, throwing objects into the fire. Police pushed the protesters back while the migrants retreated to a pier.
Earlier on Thursday, a military vehicle was attacked with stones and other objects by about 70 people, a police spokesman in Ceuta told the AFP news agency.
Local protesters tried to stop Red Cross vehicles from reaching the beach to distribute food to migrants. People waving Spanish flags shouted "They should leave" and "Out with the Red Cross."

blocks.caption: Locals in Ceuta accuse the government of mishandling the situationImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: How many migrants are still in Ceuta?
In July, more than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly in the hope of reaching the European mainland.
While the vast majority of them have since returned to Morocco, several thousand remain in Ceuta, living on the streets or on the beach.
Spain's government in Madrid puts the number at below 7,000 while Ceuta officials say it's at least 10,000. Ceuta's population is about 84,000 people.
Growing pressure on Madrid

The Spanish government is under growing pressure over the situation in Ceuta. The conservative opposition is accusing left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to act and abandoning Ceuta's residents.

Madrid has recently moved to speed up efforts to identify the migrants and decide who will be sent back to Morocco. The government also approved extra funding to help unaccompanied minors entitled to special protection.
The crisis comes ahead of general elections next year and has deepened political divisions in Spain. The conservative opposition is calling for a tougher stance on migration.
The mass influx in July had also led to tension within the EU over how to respond to the situation in Ceuta.

articles.title: Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic dead
articles.summary: BELGRADE, Serbia — Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief who was convicted of war crimes for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, died in a hospital on Thursday, according to a…

blocks.text: BELGRADE, Serbia — Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief who was convicted of war crimes for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, died in a hospital on Thursday, according to a United Nations international tribunal.

Mladic, who had suffered several strokes in recent months, was serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity after overseeing the Srebrenica slaughter, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
His conviction for wartime killings as the former Yugoslavia descended into carnage following the fall of communism led the media to dub him the “Butcher of Bosnia.”
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and 2.2 million displaced.
Mladic was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by former Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.
Serbian state officials and Mladic’s family had appealed for his release due to his failing health, but those calls were rejected by the Hague tribunal.
A representative of the Mothers of Srebrenica victims’ association, reacting to Mladic’s death, told AFP that his name would always “symbolize genocide.”
“That will never be erased from his name,” said Sehida Abdurahmanovic, who believes her missing brother was among those killed in Srebrenica.
Srebrenica
In the war’s most infamous atrocity, Serb forces under Mladic’s command executed 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had sought shelter in Srebrenica, which was meant to be a UN-protected enclave.
Their bodies were dumped in mass graves, many of which were dug up and reburied in an attempt to hide the evidence.
The few who escaped told harrowing stories of murder, torture and rape by Bosnian Serb forces.
In November 1995, the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) indicted Mladic, who was dismissed from his post but evaded capture for another 16 years.
At first, he led a life of luxury, pampered by the military in Serbia, where some to this day see him as a hero.
But the pressure mounted on him after Milosevic fell from power in 2000. Mladic was finally arrested in May 2011 and transferred to The Hague.
He was convicted in 2017, with the life sentence upheld on appeal in 2021.
On the streets of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, Hava Suljic told AFP she welcomed the news.
“I’m delighted to know there is one less war criminal walking around in this world,” Suljic, a Bosnian Muslim from Srebrenica, said.
But reactions in the Serb entity of divided Bosnia were in stark contrast.
Former Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik said Mladic’s death had “hit hard” and that the Republika Srpska “will not forget his role,” the Serb statelet’s public broadcaster reported.
Locals who spoke with AFP in the Republika Srpska’s capital, Banja Luka, called Mladic the “greatest.”
“The greatest man has died, the greatest general of the Serbian people,” pensioner Dragan Beric said.
‘Epitome of evil’
Mladic was also found guilty of orchestrating a wider campaign of ethnic cleansing to drive Muslims and Bosnians out of key areas to create a so-called Greater Serbia.
The tribunal said at the time that the crimes committed were “among the most heinous known to humankind.” Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al Hussein described him as “the epitome of evil.”
But many Serbs continued to revere a military commander who portrayed himself as a “simple man” whom fate had chosen to protect his people.
His age has always been a matter of dispute. He claimed to have been born in March 1943, but the tribunal listed his birth year as 1942. Local media widely reported that he had died at age 84.

articles.title: PH may be caught in US rivals’ ‘crosshairs’ – Tinio
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the Philippines in the “crosshairs” of its rivals.

“In the event of a war between the US and China over the Taiwan issue, we can infer that China would target US facilities—both military and commercial—located in the Philippines. Our concern is that the US presence in the country is situated within our strategic and critical economic infrastructure,” Tinio said in a statement released on Thursday.

Tinio’s statement followed his heated exchange with Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro during the House committee on appropriations’ hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of National Defense last Tuesday, Aug. 25.

During the hearing, Tinio raised reports that US soldiers had attempted to enter the Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation Industrial Authority in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental, where the new Philippine Navy dry dock is set to be established.
Teodoro dismissed claims about US interest in the dry dock, saying the presence of foreign troops was for the Balikatan loading exercise.
For Tinio, however, the incident was part of a broader pattern of Washington’s agenda in the country.
He cited the US-led Pax Silica, the US Navy’s use of Subic Bay for repairs and plans for an oil depot in Davao Gulf.

Tinio said the growing US presence in strategic military and economic facilities was particularly concerning because the Philippines lacks the capacity to defend these assets should geopolitical tensions escalate.
“How is the Philippines? The Gulf states are rich countries. They can afford high-tech missile defenses. How are we? What is the capability of the Armed Forces to defend these facilities?” he asked.
Tinio called on the public to remain vigilant against “foreign manipulation and intervention.”
“We must oppose all efforts to sell us out,” he added. /mcm

articles.title: Marcos confers Order of Sikatuna on outgoing Japanese envoy Endo Kazuya
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of Sikatuna, Rank of Datu (Grand Cross), Gold Distinction.
During their meeting, Marcos thanked the Japanese envoy for his contributions to strengthening the Philippines’ relationship with Japan, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said.
The President recognized Endo for promoting bilateral exchanges and deepening cooperation between the Philippines and Japan in areas of defense, security, and development cooperation.

Meanwhile, the award cited the envoy’s support for initiatives aligned with the Philippines’ priorities in infrastructure, education, transportation, maritime domain awareness, and human resource development.

“Endo was likewise recognized for advancing Japan’s longstanding commitment to peace and development in Mindanao, including its support for the peace process, grassroots development and the transition of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao,” the PCO said.

“The citation also highlighted the ambassador’s efforts to mobilize humanitarian and development assistance from the Japanese government during natural disasters and recent regional crises,” it added.
Additionally, Marcos acknowledged Endo’s initiatives that fostered friendship, mutual understanding, and goodwill between the Filipino and Japanese peoples.
The Order of Sikatuna is conferred upon individuals who have rendered exceptional and meritorious service to the Philippines.
The Philippines and Japan are celebrating 70 years of normalized relations this year and 11 years of strengthened strategic partnership since 2015. /gsg

articles.title: Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold in lightning raid on Villena Museum
articles.summary: One of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections has been swiped, almost in its entirety, from Villena Museum. A highly professional group of thieves were in and out in four minutes flat…

image.caption: The Bronze age collection's historical value is incalculable, but even the gold is worth a pretty penny if melted down and therefore lost forever [FILE: Nov 10, 2016]Image: Lanmas/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months.
The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes.
A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items.
What happened in the heist?

"The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation.
The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province.

"They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth."
The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.

Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind.
"All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.

blocks.caption: The collection was discovered more than 60 years ago and is thought to be a little more than 3,000 years oldImage: Museo de Villena

blocks.text: What is the Treasure of Villena?
The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed.
They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE.
The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets.

The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum.

The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million.

According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor.

blocks.caption: The collection includes some of the oldest known iron metalwork, seemingly thanks to the raw materials landing as part of a meteoriteImage: Museo de Villena

blocks.text: Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre
Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year.

Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October, escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period.
Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily.

Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma. Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes.
Louvre heist inspires freight lift ad campaign

articles.title: Ratko Mladic, the man behind Srebrenica massacre, dies at 84
articles.summary: For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and other war crimes. On Thursday, he died in detention at The Hague.

image.caption: Ratko Mladic, seen here in April 1993, was later found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes committed during the Bosnian warImage: Chris Helgren/REUTERS

blocks.text: More than 30 years after the end of the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.

Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later.

At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children.

Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the three-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country half of its total population at the time.
Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead
'Butcher of the Balkans'
In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague.
International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans."
He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian war.

Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy.
"Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying.
Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre
Career in the Yugoslav army

At the beginning of the Croatian war in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentally changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence.

Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic.

blocks.caption: Mladic (left) and Radovan Karadzic, the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs during the war (seen here in August 1993), were both convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former YugoslaviaImage: picture-alliance/ dpa

blocks.text: Flight, arrest and final verdict

At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just 2 years old when his father, a Partisan follower of Yugoslavia's longtime communist leader Josip Broz Titos, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview.

As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class and quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state.
Serbian nationalist
Before the end of the Bosnian war in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years.

Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure.
The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined.

Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian war.
Ratko Mladic life sentence upheld
War criminal who saw himself as a hero

Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. UN officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long overdue, but an important acknowledgment of their suffering.
Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic."

Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls.

While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding, and later survived several strokes while in prison.
Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Marcos sends condolences, offers prayers to Nepal flash floods victims
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border. He also offered…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border.
He also offered prayers for strength of the calamity victims.
“The Philippines extends its deepest condolences to our friends in Nepal and to all those affected by the deadly flashflood yesterday,” Marcos said in his social media post.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to those who lost family, loved ones and friends. Please accept our most heartfelt prayers for strength in this difficult time,” he added.
The Nepal Tourism Board reported that one Filipino traveler was missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal.
According to the tourism board, as of 2:45 p.m. Philippine time, preliminary records showed that 644 travelers had been reported missing in the affected area, including one Filipino.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a briefing earlier that the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration were coordinating with officials in Nepal, as well as with the Filipino community, to determine the extent of the disaster’s impact on Filipinos. /apl

articles.title: Tragedy in Nepal: How do flash floods happen?
articles.summary: When flash floods sweep through the Himalayas, there is often little time to react. Scientists are working to understand the risks and improve early warning systems.

image.caption: Flash floods are a recurring threat in the Himalayas. Climate change contributes to the problemImage: Sunil Pradhan/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The disaster in the border region between China and Nepal was as sudden as it was unexpected: Within just 10 minutes, enormous volumes of water and debris swept 20 kilometers downstream on Wednesday, with devastating consequences for thousands of people in the region.

Flash floods are a frequent occurrence in the Himalayas. "They are more the rule than the exception," says Niels Hovius, head of the Geomorphology Section at the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam. He has worked in the Himalayas and other mountainous regions for many years and is an expert on early warning systems.
What triggered the flash flood?

Scientific data indicate that the disaster began with a glacier collapse in the northern part of the Langtang massif: a large amount of ice broke away and turned into a massive ice avalanche. The Langtang massif is located in central Nepal near the border with China.
Devastating flash floods hit northern Nepal

"This glacier collapse sent huge amounts of ice rapidly downhill," says Hovius. The heat generated by friction melted the ice into water, which then swept up debris and mud. The resulting mudflow moved downhill at speeds "reached by passenger cars on German highways."

Seismological instruments recorded an earthquake measuring 4.4 on the Richter scale at the time of the glacier collapse. However, Hovius says, it was not a "classic" or tectonic earthquake. Instead, the instruments measured the force of the falling glacier.
Why can flash floods in the Himalayas be so devastating?
Flash floods in high mountain regions can be triggered in different ways — by glacier collapses or by so-called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs, or Glacier Lake Outburst Floods).

In such cases, the topography around a glacial lake suddenly changes, for example when a slope collapses into the lake. The large volume of water that suddenly spills over the lake's banks can then turn into torrents rushing downstream. In this particular case, however, it is clear that this was not a GLOF, says Hovius.

Landslides can also cause deadly mudflows without any glaciers or glacial lakes being involved. In the Himalayas, all three types of events are possible, and historical data show that all three occur regularly, Hovius says.
Compared with the Alps, the valleys of the Himalayas are relatively narrow. The water and mud cannot spread out but are instead forced into a confined space, increasing their depth and speed.
Alps warming fast: Europe’s water lifeline is running dry
In addition to the speed of the water and debris, the extent of the devastation caused by a flash flood depends on how far local populations are from the source.
How can people be protected from flash floods?

Nepal faces two major challenges. Many people have settled along rivers in the valleys of the Himalayas — in precisely the areas that are vulnerable to flash floods. Secondly, there are very few early warning systems in the country, which is one of the poorest in Asia.

Even with a timely warning, the particularly devastating flash flood would have given people only a few minutes to reach safety. Hovius describes a flood that occurred in the same region last year. It was smaller, and therefore less severe. At the time, it took the water an hour to reach a settlement — enough time for people to escape if they had received a timely warning.

"There are initiatives in Nepal to establish local acoustic early warning systems," says Hovius. However, these systems are available only on a very limited scale. At most, they cover one percent of areas at risk. The GFZ researcher adds that mobile phones should be used to send people warnings via push notifications. Hovius is researching how the data needed for such a system could be generated.

Checks should also be made on how settlements are planned, Hovius says. At present, the bulk of a community's infrastructure is concentrated along rivers. "People have moved down from the mountains and settled in the valleys over the past few decades. Perhaps it would make sense to move back to higher ground."
Are flash floods in mountainous areas more frequent amid climate change?

"Attributing individual events to climate change is always difficult," Hovius says. But it is clear that glaciers in high mountain regions become less stable as temperatures rise. Larger volumes of water are also accumulating in glacial lakes, making GLOFs more likely.

As for the current flash flood, it is too early to say whether climbing temperatures caused the glacier to collapse. Flash floods have long been a regular occurrence in the Himalayas. "But I think it is likely that we will see more and more of these events," Hovius says, warning that future disasters could be even more serious.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Andre Rankel named Germany's new men's ice hockey coach
articles.summary: Germany's men's ice hockey team has appointed a new head coach following a string of dissappointing tournaments. He's two decades younger than the man he's replacing but he has no previous experience…

image.caption: Former Germany player Andre Rankel spent the past three seasons as assistant coach in BerlinImage: Franz Feiner/HMB Media/IMAGO

blocks.text: The German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) presented former Germany player Andre Rankel as the new coach of the men's national team at a press conference in Munich on Thursday.

Rankel, who spent the past three seasons as an assistant coach with Eisbären Berlin, champions of Germany's top division (the DEL), has never served as a head coach. DEB sport director Christian Künast stressed that he does not see this as a problem.
"Andre is here today because he was the best [of the candidates interviewed for the job]. That's the main point," Künast said.

"I simply don't see Andre as a rookie coach. I've known him for a long time and I have had a lot of conversations with him about how you lead a team. He is ready to take over the national team and that's the most important thing."
Rankel said he was "incredibly proud" to be named Germany coach.

"What I learned as a player and captain over all these years, what constitutes team cohesion and commitment, I now want to pass on as head coach. My goal is to develop a clear idea together with the players and the coaching staff of how we want to play, and to grow step by step based on that.

Although this will be his first job as a head coach, he is highly respected in German hockey having played 17 seasons in the DEL for Berlin. In the capital, he was captain for many years, won seven titles as a player and three more as assistant coach. He also made 46 appearances as a winger for Germany, including at the 2010 Olympic Games in Vancouver.
DEB CEO Frank Lutz said Rankel had been given a four-year contract, a reflection of the fact that the organization is looking to him to help further develop the national team in the longer term.
A generational change for German hockey

The appointment of Rankel, who turned 41 on Thursday, marks a generational change for Germany. Rankel replaces Canadian-born Harold Kreis, 67, who after leading the national team to a silver medal at the 2023 World Championship had a disappointing series of tournaments. Perhaps the most damaging was the 2026 Winter Olympics. The Germany team that entered the tournament was considered the greatest ever and was led by NHL superstar Leon Draisaitl, but it crashed out against Slovakia in the quarterfinals.

While appointing someone with no head coaching experience may seem like a risky move, the DEB have been down this road before. Marco Sturm also had no head coaching experience when he was appointed in 2015. He went on to lead Germany to a silver medal at the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeonchang – their greatest achievement and which marked an upward turn in the national team's fortunes.
With this progress having stalled in recent years, the DEB are betting that Rankel is the man to get Germany's men back on the right track.

Rankel's first tournament behind the bench will be the Deutschland Cup in Düsseldorf, a four-team invitational held annually during the November international break. His first major test will come next May, when Germany host the World Championship in Düsseldorf, Mannheim and Gelsenkirchen.

articles.title: New study shows German football remains male-dominated
articles.summary: The top leagues of German football remain a largely male environment. A new study reveals that only seven clubs have women in upper management levels.

image.caption: Christina Rühl-Hamers is just one of nine women in management positions in German footballImage: Wolf von Dewitz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The nonprofit organization "Fussball kann mehr" (FKM –– Football Can Do More) has released its third report on diversity in professional German football. This time, all 36 teams in the top two divisions took part, and the results reveal a familiar tale of dominance. A revealing 29 of the 36 clubs have an all-male management team.

There was a noticeable increase in women in top management positions in the 2025-26 season though, with four of the 18 new appointments to top management positions being women. The previous season, only one of the 19 open positions at the time were filled by a woman. RB Leipzig's Tatjana Haenni, who became the first female CEO in the Bundesliga in late 2025, is one of them. Nicole Kumpis of Eintracht Braunschweig remains the only female president of a club in the top two flights. Kathleen Krüger's appointment at HSV came after the study's cutoff, boosting the original numbers.
Only nine of the 94 positions at the highest management level are now held by women. The nine women are:

items: Tatjana Haenni, CEO at RB Leipzig
Luise Gottberg, vice president at St. Pauli
Hanna Obersteller vice president at St. Pauli
Petra Saretz, executive board member at Heidenheim
Jennifer Zietz, managing director of women's football at Union Berlin
Katharina Kienemann, executive committee member at Union Berlin
Svenja Schlenker, managing director of HR at Borussia Dortmund
Christina Rühl-Hamers, board member for finance, HR, and legal at Schalke
Anne-Kathrin Laufmann, managing director of sports & sustainability at Werder Bremen

blocks.text: Seen through a comparative lens, this is three more than the previous season. The only number lower than the number of women in management roles is the international diversification on supervisory boards – fewer than 3% of members are not German.

"We would love to report that the spirit of renewal exuded by these top executives is permeating German professional football and that the necessary transformation is in full swing," Katja Kraus, co-chair of the FKM advisory board, said in a press release.

"But progress remains slow; spectacular isolated cases and stagnation at the grassroots level are not mutually exclusive, but rather explain each other. Visible exceptions create an impression of progress that reduces the pressure on what is actually a sluggish structure."

blocks.caption: Katja Kraus believes football's approach to diversity has a lot to learn from the business worldImage: Martin Hoffmann/Imago Images

blocks.text: Women's football has untapped potential

Also addressed in the survey was women's football. The Women's Bundesliga's decision to move away from the DFB and operate independently opens up new doors, especially for women looking to move into management positions. Currently though, men still dominate in the women's game too, with only four of the 14 Women's Bundesliga teams coached by women (Cologne, Union Berlin, Werder Bremen and Hoffenheim).

In the face of structural barriers for women in elite sport, the challenges remain in both men's and women's football. The hope is that in the years ahead, particularly with Euro 2029 being held in Germany, that German clubs will look to implement change when it comes to the diversity of their management.

articles.title: Ex-Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead at 84
articles.summary: The former Bosnian Serb general was convicted of genocide committed during the bloody 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

image.caption: Mladic was dubbed the 'Butcher of Bosnia' for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre [FILE: June 8, 2021]Image: Jerry Lampen/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic, who was serving a life sentence for war crimes committed during Bosnia and Herzegovina's 1992-95 war has died, a United Nations official said.
Serbian state broadcaster RTS reported on Thursday that he died in a prison hospital in the Hague, after suffering several strokes.

A family member of Mladic, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation, confirmed the reports to the Associated Press and said Mladic's son, Darko Mladic, was on the way to the Hague.

The International Criminal Court for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladic of charges including crimes against humanity and genocide in 2017, handing him a life sentence. The verdict was confirmed on appeal in 2021.
30 years on: The Srebrenica genocide explained
Commenting on Mladic's death on Thursday, United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres expressed his support for the war criminal's victims.
"The secretary-general stands in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes for which Mr Mladic was found guilty," spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
'The butcher of Bosnia'
Mladic was held responsible for his role in the 1992 to 1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including July 1995 massacre of some 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica.
The slaughter, the worst single atrocity in Europe since World War II, saw him named the "Butcher of Bosnia."
Under Mladic's command, Bosnian Serb forces besieged Sarajevo and other towns, operated detention camps for non-Serbs and enemy soldiers, and systematically killed prisoners.
Did foreigners pay to shoot civilians during Sarajevo siege?
Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al Hussein described him as "the epitome of evil" after his conviction.
"This is all lies, you are all liars," he shouted when he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017.
On Monday, Serbia's justice minister, Nenad Vujic, asked for Mladic to be transferred to a Belgrade military hospital, warning that his death "could come at any time."
Srebrenica massacre discredited international community
Born in Bosnia in 1942, Mladic was a former Yugoslav army officer who rose to command the Bosnian Serb army during the 1992-95 war.
A hardline nationalist, he portrayed the conflict as a historic struggle against Ottoman rule and celebrated the 1995 capture of Srebrenica.
After the capture of the city, Mladic ordered the evacuation of women, children and the elderly but said all men of fighting age are taken prisoner.
In the following days more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys are systematically butchered by the Bosnian Serb forces and their bodies dumped in mass graves.

blocks.caption: Mladic was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by ex-Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic [August 5, 1993]Image: Str/epa/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In 2022 The Netherlands apologized for the Dutch peacekeepers' failure to prevent the killings.
Mladic himself has never repented.

articles.title: Venus' US Open invitation raises questions about wild cards
articles.summary: Although her current world ranking wouldn't allow it, Venus Williams is set to play singles in the US Open – thanks to a wild card. Who gets these coveted spots—and how?

image.caption: Venus Williams is back at the US OpenImage: Zou Zheng/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Venus Williams hasn't won a singles tennis match since July 2025. The seven-time Grand Slam champion and former women's No. 1 is currently 611th in the WTA rankings and 46 year's old, but she is in the main draw of the 2026 US Open, thanks to a wild card.
"I get a lot of joy out of being different or unexpected or bucking the system,” she told Vogue earlier this year. "I find that thrilling."
Nevertheless, her invitation to play in the women's singles of the US Open raises a fundamental question: How do wild cards work?
The power of the organizers

A wild card allows a player to participate in a tournament even if their current ranking doesn't warrant it. Organizers can use wild cards to promote young players, facilitate comebacks—or bring in big names.
Williams' case is supported by her extraordinary career. She won two of her seven Grand Slam titles at the US Open and her name alone still sells tickets.
'The most effective tool for developing young talent'
In a statement to DW, the German Tennis Federation (DTB) described wild cards as "one of the most effective tools for developing young talent."
It was something that offered youngsters with "experience at the highest international level—experience that cannot be fully replicated through training or competing at lower-tier tournaments."

blocks.caption: Venus and Serena Williams won the women's doubles at Wimbledon in 2008Image: Corinne Dubreuil/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: However, the DTB also noted: "In our view, there is no automatic priority given to either 'big names' or up-and-coming players. The deciding factors are the specific situation and the tournament's objectives."

In addition to sporting criteria, factors such as "a tournament's appeal or marketing potential could also play a role," the DTB explained. However, there must "always be clearly added value for the tournament and the sport."
Mixed reactions from the tennis world
After Venus received a wild card for the Miami Open in March despite being on a losing streak, former world No. 1 Yevgeny Kafelnikov was critical.

"I have incredible respect for Venus Williams' achievements. Multiple Grand Slam singles champion, world No.1, but it's time," he told the Hard Court podcast. He also argued that wild cards would be better used to help younger players in their development.
Andy Roddick, former US Open winner and world No. 1, disagreed.

"You can save all of your 'she shouldn't get a wild card.' If you won five Wimbledons, seven majors, you're part of the most iconic tennis family in history, this is a win for the tournament at Washington DC, the city of Washington DC," Roddick said on his Served podcast ahead of last year's DC Open.

Andy Murray also pushed back against criticism regarding his wild cards back in 2021. After everything he had been through and contributed to the sport, he "shouldn't have to justify why I should get wild cards," said the three-time Grand Slam winner.

Venus' sister, Serena, received a wild card for Wimbledon this year at the age of 44. The 23-time Grand Slam champion had not played a singles match in nearly four years prior to that. She lost in the first round. (Both Venus and Serena have also been granted a wild card to compete in the US Open women's doubles.)
Wawrinka' frown turned upside down

Stanislas Wawrinka, who is retiring after this season had hoped for one final appearance at the US Open – but was initially denied a wild card. It was bitterly disappointing for the now 41-year-old Swiss, who is ranked 127th in the men's rankings but won the tournament in 2016 – one of his three career Grand Slam titles. However, after the slightly higher ranked American, Patrick Kypson, withdrew due to injury, the organizers extended an invitation to a delighted Wawrinka.
"I'm incredibly excited to accept the wild card for the 2026 US Open and look forward to competing in front of the fans in New York once again," he said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Stan Wawrinka had originally been passed over for a wild card for the US OpenImage: Matthieu Mirville/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Tatjana Maria has also experienced just how unpredictable wild card decisions can be. The German won the WTA 500 tournament at London's Queen's Club in 2025, defeating four top-20 players along the way. A year later, the defending champion didn't receive a wild card, with all four invitations going to British players.
"I was pretty sure I'd get a wild card—or at least I hoped so, since I won here last year," Maria said.
She wound up having to go through the qualifying rounds—and won both of her matches to make it into the main draw.
Two bagels and 20 double faults

There was also a bizarre case in Kenya earlier this year. At the International Tennis Federation (ITF) World Tennis Tour W35 tournament in Nairobi, 21-year-old Egyptian player Hajar Abdelkader received a wild card. The World Tennis Tour is a developmental series for the WTA Tour.
Abdelkader lost to Germany's Lorena Schaedel 0–6, 0–6 in a match that lasted just 37 minutes. She won just three points and committed 20 double faults.

The ITF described her performance level as "unacceptable." Tennis Kenya admitted that she shouldn't have been granted a wild card. The ITF announced plans to review its procedures and consider establishing a minimum sporting standard for wild cards.
A better solution?

The US Open itself has found a way to tie wild cards more directly to sporting criteria. In the US Tennis Association's "Wild Card Challenge," players accumulate world ranking points over several weeks; the leader at the end secures a spot in the main draw. Carol Young Suh Lee clinched a main-draw women's singles wild card for this year's tournament, while J.J. Wolf did the same on the men's side.
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: DW users on life in Russia: 'People are mad as hell'
articles.summary: Official polling suggests public sentiment in Russia is deteriorating as economic pressure builds. DW asked its users to share their experiences.

image.caption: Many DW social media users paint a bleak picture of life in RussiaImage: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fuel shortages are disrupting daily routines. Discontent over pay is rising as job prospects weaken. Planning for the future has given way to short-term coping as anxiety spreads in Russia.

Even Russia's major pollsters, including state-run VCIOM and FOM, as well as the independent Levada Center, report a clear decline in public sentiment. The Kremlin, however, insists that conditions remain stable. DW invited its social media users to share their stories. All responses have been anonymized for safety reasons.
'If there is gas at all, there are massive queues of 50 to 100 cars'
A DW subscriber in Moscow's Pechatniki district described a recent attempt to refuel late at night, covering around 40 kilometers (24 miles) in search of stations with supply.

"If there is gas anywhere at all, there's a massive queue of 50 to 100 cars," he said. "We decided that waiting until 3 or 4 a.m. only to head straight to work was a terrible idea, so we went home to sleep. We're on half a tank for now, but by the end of the week we'll either have to hunt for fuel or stand still. Lately, we use the car almost exclusively for trips to the dacha to see our elderly parents."
"Now you have to hunt for gas at night. You don't always get lucky. Often there's no gas at all. If there is, it's a two-to-three-hour wait," said another subscriber.

blocks.caption: Fuel shortage in Russia: Drivers wait in line for gas at a gas station in MoscowImage: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Fuel shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have become a leading public grievance. Data from BenZinMap, a fuel tracking portal, show severe sales restrictions across 66 regions as of August 27, with another 16 reporting localized disruptions or sharp price increases.

Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), told news portal RBC that refining capacity has fallen by nearly a third, a view echoed by independent analysts. Government measures — including export bans, increased imports, and relaxed fuel-quality standards — have failed to close the gap.

The data provided by Russia's state statistics service Rosstat show average retail gasoline prices are up 7.4% this year, outpacing overall inflation of 4.19%. But the averages conceal sharp regional variation. Stations owned by major oil companies have kept price increases relatively modest, drawing long queues. Independent stations are charging significantly more, adding pressure on household budgets.

There are few signs of outright panic, though. Drivers appear to be adapting to intermittent supply. "Gas is tight, but St. Petersburg is still holding up for now," said one user. "There were disruptions with gas, but the situation is better now, though it's not available everywhere," said another.
Putin faces falling popularity as Russian economy slows
'Getting a new job is becoming harder'

Official statistics point to exceptionally low unemployment in Russia, with Rosstat reporting a record-low rate of 2.2%. But the figure is misleading. Recruitment platforms hh.ru and SuperJob report a sharp rise in CVs alongside a decline in job postings, suggesting growing dissatisfaction among workers but limited alternatives.

Wage growth has also slowed. Companies in struggling sectors such as automaking and coal mining are increasingly shifting staff to reduced hours or mandatory leave. Some DW readers also describe a labor market under strain.
"Getting a new job is becoming harder and harder: There are no new openings, and the ones available are either low-paying or involve grueling 12-hour shifts," wrote one subscriber.

"Wage delays make it hard to keep up with loan payments," said another. "I've been working for two-thirds of my salary all summer. It covers food and gym, and that's about it," noted a third. "Layoffs have hit many industries," added a fourth. "The race of inflated salaries is over. And life has gotten monstrously more expensive than before 2022."

This grim sentiment has spread even to prestigious white-collar roles. An IT professional from St. Petersburg described the shift: "There are no sudden economic shocks, just a gradual decline that has been dragging on for the last 10 years. Job prospects are tight, and finding a new role will be extremely difficult."

A 54-year-old Moscow entrepreneur recalled running a service firm for Western clothing brands before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. After major clients pulled out, he was forced to close the business. He later launched a new venture manufacturing apparel in Central Asia and Bangladesh for sale on Russian online marketplaces. Early on, rising consumer incomes drove rapid growth. But as economic pressure mounted, conditions worsened.

blocks.caption: DW users complain about rising prices across RussiaImage: Erik Romanenko/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "At first, sales grew faster than we expected. But this business too got caught in the fallout of current policies, isolation, and economic instability," the businessman explained. "Revenues are collapsing catastrophically. And it's not just us. People are cutting back on almost everything."
'People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars'

The dominant theme in responses received by DW is the absence of a positive vision of the future. Respondents, judging from their comments, are not preparing for a single shock, but for a prolonged period of stagnation or decline.

"In our region, the changes are not yet significant," wrote a woman from Sakhalin, an island in Russia's Far East. "Prices are rising, of course, but overall, it feels like people live just as they did before. Personally, the changes in daily life I feel most are with internet service. It has gotten slower, and the VPN is on almost constantly to bypass censorship. A huge number of people from my personal bubble left Russia, though that has been happening since 2022. We sent our son to another country, too."

When planning becomes difficult, day-to-day coping dominates. "Fuel shortages, drone attacks... Basic trips to Turkey have become unaffordable," said another subscriber. "People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars. There are no hopes for a bright future or a change of power. Everyone lives for today. Drinking has increased significantly — even in Moscow."
Beyond anxiety and apathy, a notable number of responses point to growing social fragmentation, with people withdrawing into narrower circles and avoiding broader discussion.

"People are mad as hell and blame the West for all their troubles. Life has become far poorer, duller, and more dangerous than before the war," noted one subscriber. "People either shut down or cut off any conversation about life and the war immediately. Almost no one is left putting on a brave face or posturing."

"The issue isn't just fuel or the internet — it's the change in people, even quite decent ones," wrote another subscriber, a woman working in healthcare. "There's internal fear, deep irritation — even among those who understand nothing and want to know nothing. But everyone sees the prices. It frightens people. Internal social taboos are vanishing... The intelligentsia suddenly lost its dust, its cultural veneer — especially military-industrial engineers."
Putin admits Ukraine's drones are hurting Russia's economy

articles.title: Days after deadly Nepal flood, families of missing B.C. couples desperate for details

blocks.text: British Columbia
Days after a massive wall of water tore through the Timure region of Nepal, families of two missing Metro Vancouver couples are desperately searching for information about their loved ones.
Federal officials say 32 Canadians still missing
Families of Canadians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood cling to hope

Port Moody couple Dhaval and Megha Shah and Coquitlam couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla are among 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing since the Aug. 26 flash flood struck, killing at least 570 people.
Vikram Khosla said his cousin Shubakshi was in the area for a trek to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others, as a 50th birthday gift to herself.
Nepal-Tibet flash flood death toll climbs as fears of 2nd flood grow
He said the couple had been almost ready to depart for their journey when they spoke with a family member about an hour before the flood struck on Wednesday morning.
No one has heard from anyone in the group since then, he said.
“We are very hopeful that they went up and they are stuck somewhere," he said.
The couple, Singaporean citizens who moved to Canada about four years ago, have two daughters, he said.
Speaking from Mumbai, India, Dhaval's brother Kheval Shah told CBC his brother and sister-in-law were staying at Hotel Kailash, near the border, on Wednesday.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: The family last heard from the two that morning as they were having breakfast, about 15 minutes before the flood struck.
“That hotel is completely submerged, there is no hotel anymore," he said.
“We just want to find out where they were when the water hit.... Ultimately I feel that closure is very important.”
The couple have a 24-year-old daughter, he added.
Canada has said it will send $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground.
CBC News Network speaks to extreme weather researcher about Nepal/Tibet.
But Shah said he wants the Canadian government to push Nepal for more information about the search for the missing.
Khosla, too, shared frustration with the lack of updates.
He said Shubakshi's brother and sister have flown to Kathmandu and are trying to get to the affected area to search for answers.
He wants to see a centralized source of information for the families of missing people to get real time updates.
As of Saturday, about 3,000 people remained missing in the disaster.
No Canadians are among the 121 foreign nationals the Nepal Tourism Board said Friday had been rescued.
With files from Georgie Smyth, Tanya Fletcher and The Canadian Press

articles.title: The great lake divide: Collapse vs. comeback
articles.summary: As some of the world’s biggest lakes are vanishing in real time, others are proving that recovery is still within reach.

image.caption: The Caspian Sea is under enormous pressureImage: Hossein Beris/Middle East Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Some of the world's largest lakes could shrink substantially within this century, with far-reaching consequences for ecosystems and roughly a quarter of the global population living in affected regions.
Although restoration efforts have proved successful in some cases, many inland bodies of water face extreme challenges.
Caspian Sea: A shrinking giant

Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is actually a lake. Bordered by Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, it is the largest inland water body on Earth. But its surface area has been rapidly receding since the 1990s.

This shift is partly due to the use of dams and water-management practices in the Volga River basin. But hotter conditions driven by burning fossil fuels to power societies is also a contributing factor. Rising temperatures increase evaporation rates.

Scientific models project that water levels could fall up to 21 meters (68 feet) by 2100. Even a decline of 10 meters could leave large parts of the shallow northern basin dry, eliminating nearly one-third of the lake's current surface area.

The consequences are already becoming apparent. Ports require increasingly extensive dredging, fish stocks and wetlands are coming under growing pressure and habitats used by the endangered Caspian seal are drying out.
Scientists also warn that exposed lakebeds could release dust and pollutants. Joint conservation efforts among the five coastal states remain politically challenging.

blocks.caption: The water quality in Lake Constance has improved considerably, but evaporation driven by high temperatures poses a threatImage: Markus Keller/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Lake Constance: A pollution turnaround

Like much of Europe, Lake Constance has been impacted by high temperatures this summer. Bordered by Germany, Austria and Switzerland, the 63-kilometer-long (39-mile-long) lake has experienced high evaporation rates that have caused water levels to fall significantly in some places.

In the late 1970s, however, low water levels were not the main concern. At the time, the lake was suffering from severe nutrient pollution and was at risk of ecological collapse. Massive algal blooms and oxygen depletion in deeper waters threatened fish populations and led to swimming bans.

The expansion of wastewater treatment facilities and removal of phosphorus from sewage significantly reduced nutrient concentrations, led to the stabilization of lake trout, which had been at risk of disappearing.
#DailyDrone: Lake Constance
Local communities also benefited. Around 4 million people in the southern German state of Baden-Württemberg rely on Lake Constance for their drinking water.

Yet the ecosystem is far from fully restored. Shoreline development, invasive species and climate change continue to pose major challenges. Restoring more of the lake's natural shoreline could help strengthen its resilience.
Aral Sea: A disaster with glimmers of hope

The Aral Sea in Central Asia has become one of the defining examples of how water extraction can devastate even the world's largest lakes. Only a few decades ago, it was the fourth-largest lake on Earth.

During the Soviet era, vast amounts of water were diverted to irrigate cotton and rice fields, creating an environmental catastrophe whose effects continue today. By 2010, the surface area had shrunk by more than 50,000 square kilometers.

blocks.caption: Where once there was water, vegetation has taken over. Water was already being diverted for agriculture and industry back in the Soviet eraImage: Ekaterina Venkina/DW

blocks.text: Thirty fish species that once supported commercial operations have disappeared, and entire communities along the former shoreline have vanished with them. The Aralkum Desert has emerged where the water once shimmered, covering roughly 62,000 square kilometers.
Today, dust and sandstorms carry salt and toxic residues from the former lakebed across surrounding regions, posing serious risks to human health.

blocks.caption: Land that was previously submerged has been given over to desert shrubs that trap dust and toxins and retain moisture in the soilImage: Ekaterina Venkina/DW

blocks.text: But the North Aral Sea has benefited from the Kok-Aral Dam, which raised water levels. Where a return of the lake is considered unrealistic, saxaul shrubs are being planted to stabilize the sand and contaminated dust. According to the Kazakh government, more than 1.8 million hectares have been planted since 2018.
Muskegon Lake: The big clean up
For decades, Muskegon Lake in the US state of Michigan was polluted by industrial waste and contaminated sediments.

Extensive clean-up efforts by local environmental authorities removed contaminated soil and more than 110,000 tons of historic sawmill waste. As a result, 54 hectares of habitat along the shoreline and in surrounding areas were restored.

blocks.caption: Muskegon is an example of how ecosystems and the economy can benefit from sustainable policies and clean-upsImage: Wirestock/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: In 2025, authorities finally removed Muskegon from the list of severely degraded lakes.

According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the restoration efforts now generate an estimated $28 million (€23 million) in additional recreational value annually and attract roughly 500,000 extra visitors each year.
However, the lake is not entirely free of pollution. Authorities continue to warn against eating certain fish species because contaminant levels remain too high.

blocks.caption: Today the lake is a hotspot for tourists and has become important for recreational timeout in the regionImage: Wirestock/IMAGO

blocks.text: Lake Chad: A region fighting for survival

The vast Sahel forms the transition zone between the Sahara Desert to the north and the African savannas to the south. Stretching across the continent from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, it is home to one of Africa's most distinctive ecosystems: Lake Chad.
Shaped by sand, wind and harsh environmental conditions, the wetland ecosystem is a critical source of water for people and wildlife and supports livelihoods across the region.

blocks.caption: Water levels in the Lake Chad wetlands fluctuate significantly Image: Joris Bolomey/AFP

blocks.text: In the 1960s, during periods of high water, Lake Chad covered up to around 25,000 square kilometers, slightly more than the area of New Jersey. During severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s, it temporarily lost more than 90% of that area.
Since then, the lake has partially recovered. Its size now fluctuates considerably depending on rainfall and the season — ranging from roughly 12,000 to 20,000 square kilometers.

Climate change, irrigation and deforestation continue to put pressure on the lake. According to aid organizations, its decline has contributed to a wider ecological crisis across the region and threatens the food security of millions of people.

blocks.caption: Lake Chad is the lifeline for many millions of people in the region. It has recovered to some degree, but still faces challengesImage: Michael Runkel/robertharding/IMAGO

blocks.text: Some 30 million people depend on the resources of the Lake Chad basin. Hundreds of bird species migrate from Europe and Asia to Africa each winter, and many use Lake Chad as an important stopover site.

Some waterways previously blocked by dams have been reopened. In May, the African Development Bank, the Lake Chad Basin Commission and five neighboring countries launched investment projects worth $10 million. The funding is intended to help preserve the lake both as a habitat and an economic lifeline for the region.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Why social media addiction is so hard to regulate
articles.summary: Meta and other social media platforms face lawsuits alleging they foster addictive use among young people. Now regulators are struggling to rein in their engagement-driven business models.

image.caption: Social media giants like Meta are facing multiple lawsuits over alleged harmsImage: Ismail Kaplan/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Addiction, self-harm, suicide: Social media's engagement-driven strategy is under intense scrutiny for allegedly engineering compulsive use and severe psychological harm, especially in children.
Platforms like Facebook, YouTube and TikTok make huge profits by keeping users hooked via nonstop scrolling, recommendations and constant notifications.
Facebook owner Meta, for example, generated a record $196.2 billion (€168.3 billion) in advertising revenue last year, driven by its ability to keep people glued to their screens.

That business model is now facing major legal and regulatory roadblocks, with social media bans for people younger than 16 spreading globally and a growing wave of lawsuits, mainly in the United States.
In the latest major case, 29 states, including California, Colorado and New Jersey, sued Meta earlier this month, alleging that the social media giant designed its platforms to addict young users.

In a settlement announced on Wednesday, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to 47 states, the District of Columbia and US territories — including a separate $1 billion settlement with Texas. The platform also agreed to implement usage limits and to block teens from using its apps at night.
Social media growth outpaced regulation
Governments around the world have spent the past decade tightening rules, yet policymakers struggle to keep up with the rapidly changing technology.

Several major studies link social media use in teenagers to increased anxiety, depression and body dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, leaked documents from Meta in 2021 indicated that company researchers had identified links between Instagram use and body-image and mental health concerns among some teenage girls.
Meta faces key trial that could reshape Facebook, Instagram

According to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, US teens in 2025 spent about 90 minutes a day glued to TikTok. Tests by groups like Amnesty International in 2023 showed that the platform's algorithm can recommend videos related to depression and self-harm to users who engage with mental health content.

"Companies operating at this scale, with so much influence over people's lives, have to meet basic safety standards," Camille Carlton, senior director of strategy and impact at the Center for Humane Technology, told DW.
"This isn't a radical idea," she said. "This is the same standard we apply to other products such as cars, medications and children's toys."
US move toward tighter child safety
After years of gridlock, bipartisan support in the US is growing for tougher rules to protect children from social media harms, through the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA).
The plans include the strongest safety settings by default for minors and will give parents more tools to control their children's accounts.

blocks.caption: Australia, Indonesia, Brazil and Malaysia have banned social media for childrenImage: Marcus Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The technology is advancing so fast, and the evidence of harm is mounting so fast, that I'm really optimistic that we're going to get major legislation passed in the next session of Congress," social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, author of the bestselling book "The Anxious Generation," told Politico's The Conversation podcast last week.

While KOSA could impose a clear duty of care on tech giants to anticipate foreseeable harm and design features to prevent them, Carlton is pushing lawmakers to place social media products under US consumer-protection and product-liability rules.
Support for alternative models — in theory
In Germany, Cornelia Sindermann, a psychology professor at Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule in Heidelberg, has been studying users' attitudes to alternative social media models.
These include pure subscription plans to avoid ads, which Meta has been testing on Facebook and Instagram in the 27-member EU and the United Kingdom.

Sindermann's 2024 research also found that more than half of adults and two-thirds of adolescents would be willing to pay for a public-service version of, say, Facebook, with much stronger guardrails.

While social media platforms will likely "reinvent aspects of their business models and test additional revenue streams," Sindermann told DW she is "doubtful" that these alternatives will replace the most popular social platforms.
AI investment complicates regulation
Another issue for policymakers is that the same social media platforms used by billions are the ones pouring hundreds of billions into top-tier artificial intelligence (AI) projects.
Some analysts argue that social-media data provides valuable real-world behavioral data for AI development.

As these tech giants grow ever more powerful, their new AI businesses are proving just as difficult to regulate. Experts are increasingly concerned that the same flawed practices that shaped social media are now being built into far more powerful AI products.
So, while social media fights for our attention, AI is now positioned to influence human thought, behavior and relationships in ways that are difficult to imagine, noted Carlton.
"When the incentives driving a product are misaligned with human well-being, we can't expect companies to consistently prioritize the public interest on their own," warned Carlton.

articles.title: CDU's Volkmann: Ukraine aid is not charity
articles.summary: Former German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's grandson Johannes Volkmann spoke to DW about why Germany must continue to support Ukraine.

image.caption: Johannes Volkmann is the grandson of late German Chancellor Helmut KohlImage: Ievgen Shylko/DW

blocks.text: At 29, Johannes Volkmann is one of the youngest members of Germany's parliament — and one of the most dedicated supporters of Ukraine. When he was head of the council of the Lahn-Dill district in the state of Hessen, he launched a municipal partnership with the Ukrainian city of Brovary near the capital Kyiv to deliver supplies to those in need.

As a member of the Bundestag's Committee on Foreign Affairs and the United4Ukraine group, an international network of lawmakers, he continues to advocate for Ukraine. During his latest trip to the country, he spoke with DW about why he thinks aid to Ukraine is so important.
DW: Mr. Volkmann, you were last in Ukraine exactly a year ago. What has changed since then?

Johannes Volkmann: The number of airstrikes — and thus the threat to the civilian population — has increased significantly again. And at the same time, there is a sense that the Ukrainian people still want to stand their ground. I have utmost respect for that. Ukraine is demonstrating that freedom and democracy can defend themselves and fight back. That is a very important message of hope.

German support is particularly important for Ukraine's defense capabilities — Germany is the largest bilateral donor to Ukraine in Europe. At the same time, political forces in Germany oppose this support. The voters of these parties share this view and consider aid to Ukraine a waste of money. What would you say to them?

Everyone needs to understand that Ukraine today is not only defending itself, but also protecting Europe. Russian imperialism is not only a threat to Ukraine's borders, but also to those of our allies in the Baltic states and in Poland. That is why every euro we invest in Ukraine today is a good investment in our own security.

On top of that, Ukraine is able to help us more and more in Europe by sharing its experience on the battlefield with European armies — with regard to modern technologies, drones, the training of soldiers and modern tactics.
When it comes to experience, Ukraine has a tremendous lead in these areas. That is why Ukraine is now effectively a provider of security in Europe and no longer merely in need of security.
Germany pledges €50m to repair Chernobyl nuclear shelter

The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which currently leads the polls, has called for an end to German support for Ukraine. Many in Ukraine are wondering: What will happen if the AfD performs even better in the next German election and becomes part of the government?

I can understand this fear. The Bundestag was elected to serve until 2029. For me personally, as well as for my parliamentary group, the CDU/CSU, it is clear that Ukraine must be supported militarily because it is in our own interest in terms of security. For me, the AfD's position on Ukraine is an important reason why my party has ruled out any cooperation with them.

There is also a humanitarian responsibility: If millions of Ukrainians flee their homeland because Russia's war of aggression succeeds — and, of course, they won't want to live under Russian colonial rule — then that will destabilize our countries. That would place a much greater financial burden on us than supporting Ukrainians today in their defense of their homeland.
Drone warfare: German startup draws on Ukraine's experience
Do you view Russia as a military threat to Europe and Germany? Some are asking: If Russia has struggled so much in Ukraine militarily, what threat can it pose to NATO?

It is important to understand that Russia's hybrid attacks on Europe are not primarily aimed at military conquest but rather at achieving certain political objectives. These include the destruction of EU and NATO cohesion.

So, it is entirely possible that Russia, perhaps with threats involving nuclear weapons, could attempt to occupy specific areas in the Baltic region to test the significance of NATO's Article 5 — the solidarity clause. This is why it is all the more important that we remain vigilant about this issue and develop the capacity to defend ourselves in order to deter Russia from any such aggression. We can only protect peace through our own strength; weakness will be seen as an invitation to attack.
Made in Germany — Rebuilding Ukraine

Germany was one of the countries particularly hesitant and cautious regarding Ukraine's possible accession to NATO. At the 2008 NATO summit in the Romanian capital Bucharest, it was against granting Ukraine a Membership Action Plan (MAP). Many in Ukraine believe that their country's rapid admission into NATO — or at least the granting of an MAP — could have prevented Russia's hybrid war in 2014 and the full-scale invasion in 2022. Was Germany's policy at the time a mistake?

It is clear that the hypothesis put forward by the German government at the time has turned out to have been wrong — the assumption that trade, for example in gas via the Nord Stream pipeline, would create mutual dependencies and thus prevent violence from occurring. The same applies to the assumption that neutrality would protect other countries.

It was a big mistake for Germany to not listen to the insights of our neighbors to the east, who, because of their own experiences with Moscow, historically have a much better understanding of what Russia actually wants.

Apart from accession to NATO, many Ukrainians view membership of the European Union as the best guarantee of security. But German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has ruled out Ukraine's accelerated admission to the bloc. Could Germany be making the same mistake again?

NATO membership and EU membership are two very different matters. The EU is a very comprehensive community based on the rule of law. There are 35 negotiating chapters necessary for accession. To rush through the process despite Ukraine not being ready in certain areas would do neither it nor the EU any favors.

At the same time — as the chancellor has also made clear — the idea is not to hold Ukraine back. It has to be clear that once certain milestones are met, the process of European integration will move forward.

Ukraine is fighting to be a European country. That is why I think it goes without saying that Ukraine, too, can be a full member of the European family with free self-determination. We should do everything in our power to support Ukraine on this path.

One issue many in Ukraine are concerned about is corruption and scandals — including those in President Zelenskyy's inner circle. How dangerous are such cases for the international support for Ukraine?
