articles.title: How Germany supports recovery of Berlin Pride attack victims
articles.summary: After a terrorist attack, public attention tends to focus primarily on the perpetrator. But what about the victims? What support can they expect? And what lies ahead for them?

image.caption: Commemorations for the victims of the Berlin Pride attack started arriving mere hours after the attackImage: IMAGO/Wolfgang Maria Weber

blocks.text: On the evening of July 25, according to German authorities, Abdul Ballout, drove a white van into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate, where thousands were celebrating Berlin Pride. He then got out of the vehicle and began attacking people at random with a large knife. He killed a 65-year-old woman from Poland and injured her daughter, along with 30 other people, some of them seriously.

Many details have emerged about Ballout, his links to extremists, his criminal record and his family. A day after the incident, he was shot dead by police officers while trying to flee during an arrest attempt.

The identities of the victims, and how they are coping after the attack on the event celebrating LGBTQ+ rights, are not publicly known. Still, many are likely to live with its consequences for months, if not years, to come. The only details disclosed by Berlin's governing mayor concern the age and nationality of the woman who was killed. Otherwise, Germany's strict data protection laws protect victims' privacy.

Victims can approach the media themselves at any time if they choose to make their stories public, Roland Weber, the German federal government's commissioner for victims of terrorism and extremist violence, told DW.
Calls for political consequences after Berlin Pride attack
Support for the victims

In Germany, people affected by such attacks are often reluctant to come forward publicly or identify themselves as victims, said Julia Kühne. She should know: Kühne is the spokesperson for the Association for Victims of Terrorism (VoT Germany), which is part of an international federation of terrorism victims.
"The perpetrator needs to disappear from the media, now that he has been caught and killed. Those affected should naturally be brought much more to the forefront," said Kühne.
How are those who were injured in the attack doing today? Weber has visited some of them in hospital.
"What I saw there was distressing. But thanks to modern medicine, and because the doctors are optimistic, there is reason for hope that everyone will recover as fully as possible," he said.

"In some cases, however, that remains uncertain. Only time will tell. Some of the injured have already been discharged from hospital and are now receiving outpatient treatment. Others will begin various forms of therapy and rehabilitation."
How are the victims being supported?

The Federal Commissioner for Victims and Weisser Ring, a victim support organization, arrange trauma treatment, provide immediate financial assistance, and advise victims on long-term care and victims' pensions.
Weisser Ring is a volunteer-run organization that works closely with the police to provide advice and support to victims of crime in Germany.

"In cases of terrorist attacks, there is also a special provision: victims can apply for hardship payments," said Weber. "These are funds made available by the Bundestag. Hardly anyone knows about them, and making people aware of them is part of our job. We provide guidance and help ensure that applications are submitted as quickly as possible."
Germany reviews Berlin Pride attack security failures

Weber is also responsible for supporting the relatives of the Polish woman who was killed and her daughter, who was injured in the attack. Nationality is not a factor in this regard. He assists victims with follow-up costs and compensation whenever an act of terrorism or extremist violence has been committed on German soil.
Number of traumatized victims still unclear

The victims of the attack are not only those who sustained physical injuries. According to VoT Germany's Kühne, even people who witnessed the attack from several hundred meters away may be considered victims.

"There are people who do not develop problems until years later," she told DW. "They may suddenly begin to suffer from sleep disturbances, experience nightmares, develop panic attacks or struggle with social phobia. In some cases, these symptoms do not emerge until years afterward because those affected were initially either still in shock or had returned to their everyday lives and were therefore able, at least to some extent, to suppress what they had experienced."

Kühne also noted that survivors of previous terrorist attacks may be retraumatized by media coverage of the current attack in Berlin and find themselves in need of support once again. She knows this from personal experience: she herself survived the 2016 attack on Berlin's Christmas market, which ultimately claimed 13 lives and left more than 70 injured.
In the shadow of RAF terror: The children left behind
Victim support: Problems in practice

Weisser Ring, which supports victims of crime across Germany, believes adequate compensation schemes and pension entitlements for victims of terrorism are now in place. However, not everything runs smoothly in practice, said Rolf Schmachtenberg, the organization's state chairman in Berlin.

"In cases where people have suffered permanent harm, the assessment procedures are often quite lengthy," he said. "We also continue to encounter administrative bottlenecks, with some authorities still relying on paper files and fax communications. They then have to wait for information from other agencies, which can significantly delay the application process. In my view, the main problem is one of implementation."

Over the past decade, Germany has experienced 13 terrorist attacks motivated by Islamist or political extremist ideologies, leaving 39 people dead and 475 injured. The support provided by the federal government's commissioner for victims has no time limit. Weber continues to assist people affected by attacks dating back to the 1980s.

blocks.caption: Commemoration continues of the nine people killed in 2020 in a racially motivated terrorist attack in the city of HanauImage: Kadir Ilboga/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Victims seek answers

For many victims, coming to terms with the horror and suffering also means finding answers to the question of why the perpetrator acted and why they, in particular, were targeted, said Weber. In some court proceedings, perpetrators have remained silent. In the case of the Berlin Pride attack, however, the perpetrator was killed, meaning there will never be complete clarity about his motives.
In Germany, investigations are discontinued once a suspect has died. No court will ever determine whether Abdul Ballout selected his victims for one particular reason or another.
"As a result, some questions will remain unanswered," said Weber. "The search for answers is something most victims have in common, but it cannot always lead to certainty."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: In Germany, record heat meets climate action fatigue
articles.summary: Climate action does not seem to be a priority for the German government — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why aren't more people taking to the streets in protest?

image.caption: Record low water levels on the Rhine and elsewhere in Germany have highlighted changing climate conditionsImage: Thomas Frey/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: When Lars Werner of the "Last Generation" climate activist group glued himself to the road four years ago to protest for greater climate action, Germany had not yet seen 12,500 heat-related deaths (the 2026 toll, so far), or record temperatures across Western Europe, and fully loaded ships were still navigating the Rhine without difficulty.
"Of course, I could say 'I told you so,' because it was foreseeable and comes as no surprise whatsoever," Werner told DW.
"The fact is, even back then, I was constantly explaining in my presentations that the Rhine would eventually run dry during hot summers and that this would have an incredible impact on the economy."
Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships

This summer, entire villages have been evacuated due to forest fires, farmers are expected to lose about 3 million metric tons of grain and rapeseed to drought, and hospital patients and the elderly in nursing homes are facing an acute threat to their lives in buildings with no air conditioning.
But so far, the federal government has remained astonishingly quiet. Despite the crisis, it has still not convened a "heat summit."

"It is utterly irrational for the federal government to resort to tinkering with regulations — such as lifting the Sunday ban on truck traffic — in the hope of somehow scraping by without implementing a comprehensive climate protection policy for the long or even short term," said Werner.
Fridays for Future finds it difficult to motivate people

The government no longer has to worry about "Last Generation" protesters calling out its inaction by setting up road blockades. The climate activists halted their protests two years ago, worn down by hostility, fines and prison sentences. Now, the task of fiercely criticizing political decision-makers on climate policy falls primarily to the Fridays for Future Germany (FFF) movement.

"The federal government is doing virtually nothing when it comes to effective climate policy. Instead, various 'pseudo-solutions' are being promoted — such as dredging the Rhine to make it deeper or lifting the Sunday driving ban for trucks," FFF spokesperson Linda Kastrup told DW. She deplores what she sees as short-term fixes for the symptoms of the climate crisis, and notes that effectively nothing sustainable is being done.

blocks.caption: In November 2022, activist Lars Werner glued himself to the street in Munich to protest CO2 emissionsImage: Benjamin Rückert

blocks.text: Only a few hundred protesters turned out for a demonstration outside the chancellery in Berlin a week ago. It was a far cry from the protests in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to demand climate action.

A recent study by the Bertelsmann Foundation found that 80% of people in Germany are worried about climate change, and more than 50% want to see more government spending on climate protection. But that doesn't mean they're take to the streets.
Kastrup isn't surprised.

"When Chancellor Friedrich Merz completely dismisses and ignores climate policy — when we see tens of thousands of heat-related deaths in Germany alone yet not a single word is said about it — it inevitably leaves people with the impression in their private lives that climate protection doesn't matter. Naturally, that makes it very difficult to motivate people to take to the streets," she said.
In addition, there has been a rise in hateful speech directed at climate activists on social media.
"Two days ago, I posted a reel and within a very short time, there were 2,000 hateful comments on it," said Kastrup.
Focus has shifted to Ukraine, Gaza

Sebastian Haunss, a political science researcher at the University of Bremen, said it's surprising that the scorching summer of 2026 has not led to climate protests. He finds it remarkable that on the one hand, more and more people in Germany are installing solar power systems, but on the other, they take vacations on environmentally damaging cruise ships.

"A strong counter-position has emerged," he said. "Specifically, political actors like the AfD [the far-right populist Alternative for Germany Party — Editor's note] are pursuing an agenda that opposes climate protection regulations. Such actors — whether at the international or national level — did not exist just a few years ago."

Also, Haunss pointed out that large organizations like Fridays for Future have been replaced by a vast number of local groups, who operate largely out of the public eye. However, he believes a pivotal event could bring people back onto the streets in large numbers at any moment.

"Then there is the competition for attention; the COVID pandemic and the war in Ukraine pushed the climate issue out of the spotlight, and current economic concerns also play a major role," said Haunss, adding that many of those who took to the streets against climate change a few years ago are now focusing on different topics.
"In some cases, their issues have shifted, and other topics — such as the war in Gaza and solidarity with Palestine — have moved to the forefront."
A divided government

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) now wants to amend the constitution, the Basic Law, to make heat protection a joint responsibility of the federal government, the states, and the municipalities.
However, the larger coalition partner, the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), is skeptical of the plan and has cited "legal concerns."

"Within the coalition, I do indeed see us — the SPD — as the bulwark for energy transition to renewables," Nina Scheer, energy policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group, told DW. "All my colleagues in our parliamentary group would like to achieve more in terms of climate protection. But we also have to accept setbacks regarding climate measures in order to maintain unity within the coalition."
For instance, Scheer said, she voted in favor of making air travel cheaper and expanding regional airports, although she personally finds it wrong.
Climate activists try bold new strategies to make an impact

Scheer has long advocated for a faster expansion of renewable energy, and does not see eye to eye with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU), who favors gas over wind and solar power for energy supply.

"Reiche goes around pushing the narrative that while we do want climate protection and remain committed to the goals, renewables are simply too expensive. And to that, one has to say: 'No, that is simply not true,'" said Scheer.

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement and the national Climate Action Act, Germany has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2045. However, recent statements by some politicians have raised doubts as to whether the federal government is pursuing this goal with great determination.
"We cannot halt climate change from Germany alone," Chancellor Friedrich Merz said recently, a statement that Scheer considered disastrous.
"Fundamentally, it is a rejection of greater climate action, even though we ought to be stepping up our efforts," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Afghan allies still waiting for the safety Germany promised
articles.summary: After the Taliban retook power on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring Afghan staff to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

image.caption: Thousands of Afghan local staff and their families have been evacuated to Germany since 2021Image: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: It's hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June 2026, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.
Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."
In August 2026, five years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany.

He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable," he said.
Afghan refugees at risk as deportations surge in Pakistan
New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union and the center-left Social Democrats under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government has remained firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2,500 ($,2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.
Afghan migrants stuck in Pakistan reject German cash offer
Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission program for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry has maintained it is in the right. "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."
According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.
German aid organization continues support

Javad Niazi and his family continue to worry for their future. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport in August 2021, the German nongovernmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning. "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people," she told DW. "And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be four weeks has now become five years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans — with success. They've won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," said Beyer.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was canceled," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

Correction, August 15, 2026: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that Alexander Dobrindt is Germany's foreign minister. He is the German interior minister. DW apologizes for the mistake.
'The world has forgotten Afghanistan'

articles.title: Germany: Evacuated villagers return after Eifel wildfire eases
articles.summary: Most residents evacuated from the village of Gey have returned home after firefighters brought a major wildfire in Germany's Eifel region largely under control. DW has more.
articles.byline: Richard Connor, Roshni Majumdar, Emmy Sasipornkarn, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Firefighters walk through the village of Gey, evacuated amid the wildfire in the Hürtgen ForestImage: Georg Hilgemann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: August 16, 2026
Thanks for reading!
Much of the weekend in Germany was focused on the efforts tocontain the wildfire in Hürtgenwald in the Eifel region.
Germany's largest recorded forest fire in North Rhine-Westphalia was under control on Sunday after a dayslong emergency operation.
Most emergency crews have withdrawn, but helicopters and thermal imaging flights were still monitoring hotspots for any signs of reignition.
Around 2,000 residents evacuated from the Hürtgenwald district of Gey also returned home.
Meanwhile, firefighters just across the border in Belgium continued battling a major wildfire that has destroyed about 3,000 hectares in the High Fens nature reserve.
Separately, about 400 firefighters were tackling a fast-moving wildfire in Saarland, a small state in southwest Germany.

articles.title: Berlin's Russian House: A hub for propaganda and espionage?
articles.summary: The Russian House stands in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it's being used to spread propaganda for Putin's Russia. Now, French authorities have said it is being used by the Kremlin for…

image.caption: The Russian House has been a fixture on Berlin's Friedrichstrasse since 1984Image: Schoening/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it is the subject of fierce disagreements and has long been a bone of contention in Berlin.

The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.
But now, more than 40 years later, French authorities have linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin earlier this week.

In response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that there are two bilateral agreements between Germany and Russia regarding real estate matters that cannot be easily revoked.

"It is, so to speak, an agreement that governs both the Russian House here in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut that we operate in Moscow," Giese said. Any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other.
German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.

Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian."

Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website.
The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda.

blocks.caption: Symbols of friendship remained on display in Berlin's Russian House in October 2023, more than year after the Russian invasion of UkraineImage: Dmyrto Katkov/DW

blocks.text: Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, a Holocaust film was shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis.

In an interview in August 2025, Robin Wagener, a member of the Bundestag for the opposition Green Party, told DW: "It is time we recognized that this is not mutual cultural exchange, but Russian war propaganda in Germany."
Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow

The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes.

Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term.

Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.
It is an open secret that the German government is shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow.
The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia.

A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts.
Berlin detains German-Ukrainian woman for Russian espionage

So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year.
Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible

According the cultural agreement, the contracting parties welcome "direct contacts between social groups and associations, including trade unions, churches, religious communities, artists' associations and political, cultural and other foundations."
However, in recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations."
This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties.
Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible.
This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in August 2026 to reflect news developments.

articles.title: Why women are breaking men's endurance records
articles.summary: Sophie Woods has completed the 2,000-kilometer Via Alpina faster even than the fastest-ever man. DW explains why she is not the only woman breaking men's records in extreme sports.

image.caption: Sophie Woods is not the first woman to break a men's record in endurance sportImage: Zoe Salt

blocks.text: New Zealand runner Sophie Wood, who competes under her maiden name, Sophie Grant, recently accomplished something truly remarkable.

Running for 29 days across the Alps, from Trieste to Monaco, Woods covered around 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) while climbing a total of more than 100,000 meters (328,083 feet) – on an average of three to four hours of sleep per night.
This made her the fastest person ever to complete the Via Alpina. The 42-year-old ultra-runner finished the route more than seven days faster than the fastest man ever to do so.
"It gives me goosebumps thinking about it, to take the overall record is amazing," Woods told DW.
"I was there for the adventure. I didn't really want to be running for longer than a month, that was enough."
The longer the distance, the smaller the gender gap
Woods is not the only woman to have broken a men's record in endurance sports in recent years.
In 2026, Rachel Entrekin won the Cocodona 250, a race covering roughly 400 kilometers in the United States, setting a new overall course record.
A year earlier, Tara Dower ran the Long Trail in Vermont. a distance of about 440 kilometers, in 3 days, 18 hours, and 29 minutes, beating the previous men's record by 2 hours and 40 minutes.

In 2019, Germany's Fiona Kolbinger became the first woman to win the Transcontinental Race. Cycling nearly 4,000 kilometers across Europe, she finished just under eight hours ahead of the second-placed male rider. That same year, Jasmin Paris became the first woman to win the 430-kilometer Spine Race in Great Britain, shattering the previous course record by more than 12 hours.

A comprehensive analysis by RunRepeat and the International Association of Ultrarunners examined over five million results from more than 15,000 ultramarathons. The findings showed that the longer the distance, the closer women came, on average, to matching men's times.

blocks.caption: In 2019, Fiona Kolbinger became the first woman to win the Transcontinental RaceImage: Mateusz Birecki/IMAGO

blocks.text: In the events analyzed, on average, the men were still 11.1% faster. At the 100-mile mark, the gap narrowed to just 0.25%. At distances exceeding 195 miles, the women were on average 0.6% faster.
'We're good at solving problems'
So why are women able to keep pace—or better—when the physical demands increase?

Certain physiological factors may play a role. On average, women possess a higher proportion of fatigue-resistant Type I muscle fibers and rely relatively more on fat as an energy source during endurance activities.
The advantages men typically enjoy—such as greater muscle mass and higher maximal oxygen uptake—may be less decisive in ultra-long events than in shorter races.
"Probably we are better at burning fat, and therefore it makes us able to go longer," Woods said – before pointing to other possible factors.
"I think we're good at putting our egos aside. And I think we're good at solving problems."
Competing in an ultramarathon is about much more than who can run the fastest. There are key decisions to be made about sleep, nutrition and physical pain. That's where her team comes in.
"I just put my life in their hands," she said.
"You kind of control everything you can and then you just throw it into chaos and see what comes out in the wash."
As little as 90 minutes of sleep, 7,000 calories a day

The extreme physical strain was evident in her sleeping patterns – towards the end, she was sleeping as little as 90 minutes a night. When she simply couldn't go any further, she would lie down right next to the trail.
"You just curl up on the side in a little mossy glen and hope that no one thinks you've died," she said.
"The sleep deprivation was one of the hardest parts of the whole thing."
Her alarm would often go off again as early as three in the morning.

blocks.caption: Sophie Woods broke both the women's and men's records on the Via AlpinaImage: Ulrich Wagner/IMAGO

blocks.text: At the same time, maintaining her physical energy was a huge problem, with her team estimating that she was consuming between 6,000 and 7,000 calories a day – through sports drinks, soft drinks, as burritos, falafel wraps, sandwiches, pasta, and McDonald's food. She ate much of this while on the move.
In the Dolomites, heat and pain added to the challenge.
"I bawled my eyes out in the Dolomites," she said.
"I was really hot. I was really sore. I was really swollen. I was shuffling along and I was just like: I don't know if I can do this."
Despite it all, she carried on.
Women long neglected in sports research
Despite setting the record, Woods wonders what she and other women could achieve if their bodies were studied as thoroughly as men's.
"As a woman, you need to be very careful when you read these studies to actually see who they are studying, because often it will be 10 male cyclists," Woods said.
"We have just been left behind in all of the research for decades," she said.
"As women, we are fighting for crumbs in the sporting world. We are fighting for more coverage, we are fighting for more research, we are fighting for more sponsorship."

The fact that several individual men's records have been broken by women doesn't mean that women are inherently better endurance athletes than men. Men still hold many records and are, on average, significantly faster over shorter distances.
However, in an interview with the BBC, sports physiologist Nicholas Tiller described very long endurance events as "the great equaliser."
Woods is simply not interested in who holds the advantage on paper.
"I think the bravest thing to do is to try," she said.
"Try the scary thing. It doesn't matter what happens in the end because at least you've tried."
Life uphill: India's ultramarathon mom
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Hunger stones: The history behind 'if you see me, weep'
articles.summary: Centuries-old hunger stones are emerging as Europe's rivers recede. Among the most famous is the Decin hunger stone in the Elbe River with its cryptic message.

image.caption: The famous Decin hunger stone, with its cryptic inscription, dates back to 1904Image: Ondrej Hajek/CTK/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: As Europe's rivers recede during periods of drought, long-hidden traces of the past have resurfaced.
Alongside Nazi-era shipwrecks, unexploded World War II bombs and prehistoric mammoth remains, some rivers reveal history literally written in stone.
One such inscription, in German, reads: "Wenn du mich siehst, dann weine" — "If you see me, weep."
These words are etched on a hunger stone in the Elbe River near Decin in Czechia, close to the German border.

blocks.caption: The 2026 drought has revealed historical artifacts lying under Europe's rivers, like this century-old shipwreck in CroatiaImage: David Jerkovic/Pixsell/IMAGO

blocks.text: Why 'hunger'?
Hunger stones, or "Hungersteine" in German, are riverbed boulders that usually stay underwater and hidden, but become exposed when river levels drop significantly during prolonged droughts.
Unlike a high-water mark, which records the highest water level, the hunger stone marks the lowest.

For centuries, communities carved dates or inscriptions onto these stones whenever the waters of rivers like the Elbe, Danube or Rhine receded dramatically. Some hunger stones bear lists of years, including 1616, 1746 and 1842.

blocks.caption: The 2026 drought has seen water levels in the Danube river reach new lowsImage: Cristian Cristel/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: In a 2019 study "Extreme Droughts and Human Responses to Them: The Czech Lands in the Pre-Instrumental Period," Czech historian and climatologist Rudolf Brazdil and his colleagues drew on chronicles, administrative records and other documentary sources to examine how drought-affected communities lived long before systematic weather measurements.

For people living along rivers such as the Elbe, low water created a host of problems. Barges carrying timber, grain and other goods struggled to navigate shallow channels, disrupting trade along one of Central Europe's vital transport routes. In severe cases, shipping had to be restricted or halted altogether.
And drought also meant crop failure, rising prices — and hunger.

blocks.caption: Hunger stones like this one didn't just commemorate years of drought; they also attempted to mark low water levelsImage: Arno Burgi/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: More than just drought memorials
While hunger stones were often treated as symbolic reminders of drought, they've proven to be more than that.

A 2020 study published in the journal Climate of the Past found that many of the dates and markings on Elbe hunger stones closely matched documented periods of exceptionally low water. The researchers concluded that many of the inscriptions were intended to record how low the river had fallen, rather than merely commemorate drought years.

The study also documented drought year markings on the Decin stone dating back to at least the 16th century, underscoring that the famous inscription "If you see me, weep" of 1904 represents only one chapter in the hunger stone's much longer history.

blocks.caption: Hunger stones, like this one in Techlovice, often bear years and water level marksImage: Wikipedia

blocks.text: A doomsaying stone?

Yet, its fame lies mainly in its seemingly foreboding message. Even its sighting during the more recent European droughts of 2020 and 2022 inspired media coverage, describing its message as "chilling", "grim" or a "harbinger of hard times."

In his 2019 study "Die Botschaft der Hungersteine" (or "The Message of the Hunger Stones"), Bernd Gross drew on newspaper reports, postcards and local historical records to reconstruct the history of the Decin hunger stone and noted that its inscription may have been inspired by an older one.

Gross cited newspaper reports from the 1890s that described a hunger stone near Techlovice, upstream from Decin, that reportedly bore German inscriptions such as: "We cried — We cry — And you will cry."
The man most often associated with the Decin stone's inscription is F. Mayer, a local innkeeper and boatman and member of the Elbe shipping community.
According to Gross, Mayer had the now-famous phrase carved onto the stone during the drought of 1904, dated July 18, along with his name.

blocks.caption: This 1904 photo featured the 'celebrity' Decin hunger stone, seen by thousands of visitorsImage: Wikipedia/Public Domain

blocks.text: A celebrity of its time

At the time, newspapers referred to it as the Bodenbach or Tetschen hunger stone, after the neighboring towns that today form part of Decin. They reported on the exposed stone and its message, while contemporary accounts described thousands of visitors who went to see it.
Postcards featuring the hunger stone also circulated widely, spreading awareness of the site far beyond the Elbe Valley.

The Reichenberger Zeitung, in circulation from 1860 to 1938, reported on August 28, 1904: "Day after day, groups gather on the rock; everyone wants to set foot on it at least once. However, the markings carved into the sandstone are likely to lose their visibility due to this frequent trampling."
Visitors were reportedly intrigued not only by the inscription but also the earlier dates carved into the rock, recording drought years stretching back centuries.
The stone that nearly disappeared
Ironically, the drought of 1904 that put the Decin stone and its inscription on the map very nearly caused its destruction.

Local river authorities decided to remove rocks and other obstacles from the Elbe to improve navigation, and Gross' study states that there were concerns that the Decin hunger stone could be removed as well.

Following the intervention of the Tetschen Boatmen's Cooperative, which petitioned the imperial authorities, the stone was spared. News reports stated that officials agreed to route planned river works around it in order to preserve what was already regarded as a historic landmark of the Elbe.

blocks.caption: Many hunger stones lying in the Elbe also bear later dates: this one has 1963 and 2003 on itImage: Arno Burgi/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: And while other obstacles were removed from the river, the Decin hunger stone survived.

The stone's story did not end there. When another severe drought exposed it in 1911, Mayer's famous inscription was reportedly carved again, this time more deeply. Later in 1938, a Czech inscription was added alongside the older markings.
Together, these dates and inscriptions chart centuries of the stone's history and its role as a marker of exceptionally low water levels on the Elbe.

articles.title: Can a drug help prevent trauma? Study with mice suggests so
articles.summary: Researchers in Munich and Stockholm blocked the lifelong social cost of early adversity in mice with a single compound. The catch: it only worked when given during the trauma, not after.

image.caption: Researchers studied mother mice and the effects of trauma on the development of their offspringImage: picture-alliance/imageBROKER/J. Tack

blocks.text: Trauma is usually treated as something you carry, manage, work through and sometimes ease. Rarely as something that could be stopped before it takes hold. That is what a group of researchers in Munich and Stockholm set out to test.

They began by making the first days of life hard. Mother mice were given far less nesting and bedding material than normal. That was enough to make mothers erratic, and the first days of life unpredictable. The mice raised in that hardship grew up looking perfectly healthy — with no obvious illness or anything visibly wrong.

Then researchers put them in groups and watched what happened. Repeatedly, these mice ended up at the bottom. Pushed into the lowest ranks of their social hierarchies, first as adolescents, then again as adults. A difficult infancy had left no visible mark — but it had set the position they would occupy for the rest of their lives.
When the researchers gave some of them a drug, the pattern disappeared.
The study, published in June, was led jointly by Mathias Schmidt at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Munich and Juan Pablo Lopez at the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm.
How does childhood trauma affect the brain and body?
Start with cortisol, the body's main stress hormone. When something stressful happens, cortisol floods the system. This is a standard, protective response.

What matters just as much is the off switch. The body needs to register that the danger has passed and wind the response back down. It does this through cortisol receptors — the parts of cells that detect the hormone and signal the system to stand down.

A protein called FKBP51 controls how sensitive those receptors are. Early hardship, the research suggests, causes the body to produce too much of it. That makes the receptors harder to trigger, so the signal to stand down never fully lands, and the stress response stays switched on far longer than it should.
Schmidt's point is that none of this is something a person can feel.
"Your cortisol response is something you don't feel," he said. "You may think you're very stress resilient, but your body is pumping out cortisol, and you don't know."
Can a drug block the effects of a difficult childhood?
The researchers used a compound called SAFit2, which blocks FKBP51. Given to the mothers during the stressful period, it reached the offspring through breast milk.
The treated mice went on to perform identically, within their social groups, to mice that had experienced no adversity at all — the social cost of a hard start erased.

The effect showed up in the brain as well as in behavior. The team screened gene activity across six stress-related regions and found that early adversity had left a broad imprint across them. The drug largely reversed it, most clearly in two: the medial prefrontal cortex and the nucleus accumbens, regions involved in emotional control and reward.
Can childhood trauma be reversed?
Not on this evidence.
In the Munich study, the compound was given during the stressful period itself, not after. What the study demonstrates is prevention, not repair.

Other studies have shown behavioral effects when the drug is used in adult animals, but full reversal of trauma already in place remains unproven. And prevention only works if you can identify who's at risk before the harm is done — a problem this research doesn't address.
Would this drug actually work on humans?
It's too early to say.

The study tested male mice only, so it is not yet known whether the same holds in females. And SAFit2 remains a research compound 3 effective in animals but not yet developed or safety-tested for human use. Still, Schmidt sees a realistic path toward clinical application within the next decade, noting that stress mechanisms are "very, very similar in animals and humans."
War scars and genes: Can the impacts of trauma be inherited?
How is trauma treated now, and why doesn't it always work?

Existing treatments for stress-related disorders, including PTSD and trauma-linked depression, rely heavily on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These drugs target serotonin pathways. They work for many patients, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and a significant portion of patients don't respond at all.

By contrast, targeting FKBP51 would mean treating the pathology at its source. "We would actually not only be treating the symptoms, but also the cause of the disorder by acting directly [on] a stress mechanism," said Schmidt. "These types of drugs are currently not on the market."

Longer-term, Schmidt envisions a more targeted approach: identifying individuals who are genetically vulnerable to stress, whose FKBP51 expression is already elevated, and treating that group specifically after acute traumatic events.

On the other end of the spectrum are people who, through genetics or prior experience, prove remarkably resilient even under extreme conditions, and may not need medication at all. Understanding who does need it, Schmidt said, and reaching them in time, is where the research is heading next.
What are the signs of unresolved trauma?
Schmidt is careful that trauma is highly individual, psychologically and physiologically. The rough guide he offers is duration, not intensity.

A strong stress reaction immediately after a car crash or a violent event is considered normal — the body doing its job. What concerns clinicians is when the response persists well beyond that: still unable to cross a street a month later, still unable to sleep six weeks on. Those are his illustrative examples rather than diagnostic thresholds, but the principle holds. If a stress response isn't fading, it's advisable to speak to a doctor.
That remains practical guidance for now. The drug, if it ever exists, is at least a decade away — and on current evidence, it would need to come before the damage, not after.
Editor: Kaukab Shairani

articles.title: Can we go green without forever chemicals?
articles.summary: As nations globally move to ban forever chemicals, should renewable energy technologies be exempt for the sake of saving the climate?

image.caption: Are forever chemicals soiling the clean energy revolution?Image: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: From solar panels to wind turbines, batteries and hydrogen cells, many renewable energy technologies driving the energy transition share a common ingredient: a class of man-made substances known as "forever chemicals."
The group contains 10,000 synthetic chemicals also known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which persist in the environment and can take thousands of years to degrade.
Widely detected in drinking water, exposure to certain levels of PFAS is linked to increased risk of cancer, suppressed immune function, decreased fertility and developmental delays in children.
These health impacts have inspired bans on well-publicized sources of toxic PFAS such as clothing waterproofing sprays, Teflon non-stick cookware, firefighting foam, packaging and cosmetic products.
While recent bans in France, New Zealand and Denmark target specific PFAS used in consumer products, the European Union wants a broader ban.

blocks.caption: PFAS are becoming ever-present in drinking water globallyImage: ZDF

blocks.text: The thousands of forever chemicals the EU proposes outlawing includes fluoropolymers, which are valued for their resistance to extreme temperatures, corrosion and UV degradation, and are present in numerous green technologies from lithium-ion batteries to solar panels.
In EV batteries, for example, binders created with PTFE fluoropolymers — also found in Teflon products — are used to coat dry electrodes for greater energy efficiency.

The chemicals industry has pushed back against Europe's mooted ban. An alliance of the world's leading chemical companies, the Performance Fluoropolymer Partnership (PFP) says health concerns about "some types of PFAS" are leading to "unwarranted restrictions" on fluoropolymer production and use.

In a statement on its website describing fluoropolymers as "critical in the fight against climate change," the PFP stated that any bans would "hamstring our climate and energy goals by possibly making the transition more expensive or simply impossible."
Are PFAS necessary to fight climate change?

PFP members include the chemicals arm of US multinational conglomerate, 3M — which is being sued more than $2 billion by the Australian government for its firefighting foam that has leached forever chemicals into the environment — and the Chemours Company, which manufacturers Teflon and was established by chemicals powerhouse, DuPont.

The European Environment Agency says these polymers are considered "relatively less problematic" than the building blocks for PFAS known as monomers. This is due to a larger molecular size that "limits their uptake into living cells" and potential toxicity.
PFAS in water: New solutions and recycling in focus

Yet fluoropolymers still degrade over time, raising "additional environmental and human health concerns," according to the agency. Experts say these polymers will inevitably emit PFAS during their life cycle and enter the environment — and living organisms — through weathering and physical stress over long periods.

"I don't think we're going to solve the climate crisis by getting cancer," said Gretchen Salter of US-based Safer States, which lobbies to safeguard the environment from toxic chemicals. "You can't demonstrate that these chemicals aren't going to do harm."

"Since chemical makers cannot escape the fact that these types of PFAS are harming our health, they are trying to claim that they are necessary for the clean energy transition," Salter said, adding that research shows how PFAS themselves fuel climate harm and toxic pollution.

The petrochemical industry accounts for 30% of global industrial energy demand — which is higher than the iron, steel and cement sectors — and generates 18% of the industrial sector's greenhouse gas emissions. Overall, chemicals used to produce everything from pharmaceuticals to fertilizers, plastics, paints, electronics and cleaning products are responsible for around 6% of global emissions.

Salter said PFAS categorized as fluorogases (F-gases) are also being marketed as "climate-friendly" since they are used for clean tech like heat pumps, and in electric car batteries. But PFAS gases, though largely non-flammable, are "now the largest source of PFAS pollution globally," she said.
PFAS: Mothers fight against forever chemicals

This is partly due to their global warming impact, which is potentially thousands of times higher than carbon dioxide. F-gas leaks can happen throughout a heat pump life cycle via worn seals and improper maintenance and end-of-life disposal. F-gases are also present in fridges and air-conditioning units as a synthetic coolant, where they can leak too.
Are there PFAS-free green tech alternatives?

According to UK-based Chem Trust, which advocates for safer alternatives to toxic chemicals, a suite of PFAS-free clean energy technology is already on the market, including for heat pumps that are being rolled out across Europe as part of a transition from gas heating.

Instead of relying on F-gases, propane is just one alternative energy efficient refrigerant for domestic heat pumps, and with the right design has a negligible fire risk, notes a 2025 Chem Trust report.

The group also says several companies are now producing solar cells without fluoropolymers. Equally, polymer paint that protects wind turbine blades and makes them more efficient is available PFAS-free.

"We are seeing more companies in the EU and across the world embrace the challenge of developing PFAS-free green technologies," said Shubhi Sharma, scientific researcher at Chem Trust, in a statement.

blocks.caption: Fluoropolymer boosters claim rechargeable lithium-ion batteries underpinning the energy transition work better with PFASImage: DR/SP/Andia.fr/IMAGO

blocks.text: But plastics and chemical lobby group Plastics Europe released an assessment report of PFAS-free substitutes in May that argued that "in many critical uses" such as transport, electronics and semiconductors, these alternatives are "either not available or simply do not match the necessary criteria to be considered a viable alternative to fluoropolymers."
Salter of Safer States said efforts to exempt so-called critical and low concern PFAS from class-wide bans means "destroying any sort of incentive to switch to safer alternatives."
"As long as the chemicals industry insists that there are no alternatives, there will be no market to develop any," said the campaigner.

Chemours insists its fluoropolymers and F-gases are "made and used with minimal environmental impact," and says it will achieve a 99% PFAS emissions reduction in the manufacture of fluorinated organic compounds by the end of the decade compared to 2018.

Liz Hitchcock, director of the federal policy program at US environment nonprofit, Toxic-Free Future, told DW that the extreme persistence of PFAS in the environment will inevitably lead to human exposure.
"We've heard claims that there are better PFAS, there are safer PFAS, but we haven't seen the proof."

articles.title: In Ohio, Canada-U.S. trade war sparks anger and uncertainty

image.caption: Joe Koch’s construction company has been in operation since the 1980s. He says he feels caught in the middle of the trade war between Canada and the U.S. (James Young/CBC)

blocks.text: The rat-a-tat-tat of a nail gun and high-pitched whine of a buzz saw echo through the two-storey home as Joe Koch’s carpentry crew completes the final touches.

Koch, the vice-president of operations for his decades-old family business, had hoped there would be three or four other new builds going up in this Ohio subdivision about now, but the U.S. trade war with Canada and many other countries has scuttled that plan.

"People are just going to not build that house this year. They're going to wait 'til interest rates lower. They're going to wait 'til the tariffs subside or the political landscape changes," Koch said.

He sees his business challenges as a microcosm of what’s happening across Ohio. President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canadian and other nations' goods have not only raised the prices he pays but costs for consumers more broadly.

items: One of Trump's top deputies has been unsatisfied with trade deal on the table for Canada, sources say
Carney says trade deal became untenable when U.S. 'asked too much and offered too little'

blocks.text: Koch used to buy Canadian shingles. Now he buys from a local company.
"If there's any benefit [to the trade turmoil], it's that you get that much more resourceful," he said.

The uncertainty and instability of the trade war has made financial planning and supply management difficult. Koch believes when it comes to trade, building relationships and making compromises is important.

"When it comes to the real volatile landscape of the globe, you need partners within your backyard that you're able to go to," he said. "I think it may be great to be able to have everything homegrown — but is that the reality of the world? I'm not so sure."
Koch feels caught in the middle of a trade storm but he’s determined to tough it out.

"It's a game of chess," he said. "There's no victory. It's just battle after battle and you win where you can. You try to minimize the damage wherever there is damage. And then you live to fight another day."
"But we're used to it," he said. "We're Youngstown, Ohio."
'It makes me angry'

Youngstown/Warren, which has a population of around 425,000, has faced economic challenges before. It was once known as the heart of U.S. steel country, until the closure of Youngstown Sheet and Tube in September 1977 put 5,000 workers out of work overnight.

While Youngstown diversified its economy in the decades that followed, more than 20,000 jobs are still tied to manufacturing, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That's across numerous sectors, including steel tubes and pipes, plastics and advanced materials.
‘Nonsensical’: We asked Americans what they think about the trade war

Last year, Ohio exported $17.5 billion US in goods to Canada — roughly a third of its total exports. Ohio’s top exports to Canada included $2.7 billion US in engines and turbines, $1.8 billion in auto parts, $1 billion in plastics and $692 million in iron and steel alloys and semi-finished products, according to data from the Embassy of Canada in Washington, D.C.

Conversely, Ohio imported $3.2 billion US in Canadian crude oil, $1.1 billion in vehicle parts, $1 billion in plastics, $915 million in steel and semi-finished products, and $672 million in aluminum and aluminum materials.
Youngstown sits in a wider congressional district known as OH-6 with a population of more than 775,000.
It exports more than $820 million US in goods to Canada every year, including coal and petroleum, iron steel and ferroalloys, resins and synthetic fibres, aluminum products and plastics.
While not all of these imports and exports are caught in the crosshairs of the escalating tariffs, a prolonged trade war could threaten some businesses in those sectors.
What Canadian goods is Trump targeting with his latest 50% tariffs?

At a local ballpark recently, players were hanging out for a post-game beer in the parking lot under the glow of a warm sunset. But there were also heated words about the Trump administration's trade war with Canada.
“It makes me angry. Why is that? Because, first of all, Canada and us have been very good allies forever, and to do something like this makes no sense at all," said Pam Hall. "It's just ridiculous.”
Next to her, Patricia Vandervoort chimed in: “We don't want Canada to hold it against us citizens — it's not us.”
Hall said the administration’s trade war with Canada and other countries is hitting Ohioans in the pocketbook.

“Everything you buy is more expensive, no matter where it comes from, because of these tariffs. Groceries, basic day-to-day items that you need,” she said. “The tariffs have … done a lot to destroy the economy.”
Their friend Cindy Burns fears Canada may permanently take its business elsewhere.

“I'm sure you're going to strengthen trade with other countries to supplement what we're not giving you or trading with you. You'll go elsewhere and maybe it'll be better and you'll never come back,” Burns said.
“It'll affect our factories, because there won't be a demand that there has been. People will lose their jobs. I mean, it's gonna spiral,” said Vandervoort, a Pennsylvania native.
Not far away, Larry Kelly believes the tariff war could flip seats blue in this red state in the November midterms.

Some polling in the Buckeye state has shown Democrats competitive and even ahead in some key races, including for a Senate seat currently held by Republican John Husted, who was appointed by the Republican governor to replace now Vice-President JD Vance.
“I think it's going to have a dramatic effect on the midterms," said Kelly.
His teammate Mike Glinatsis says the trade war hasn’t affected him that much.
“I mean, I can afford to eat,” he said. “I think Canada had … high tariffs on our stuff. And then Trump made it equal. And that's when people started getting all pissy.”
Tariffs 'a mixed bag'
Others in the business community share Glinatsis’s more positive view of the tariff war.

“There's a mixed bag — it hurts some, it helps some. And there's some companies where it hurts on one side, it helps on the other," said Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber.
One of the major steel companies in town is in favour of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel, Coviello said.

“Sometimes in those meetings, I've got a chamber member that is trying to argue against tariffs sitting across the table from a chamber member that's embracing the tariffs, and it is interesting to hear them talk it out.”
Companies and agriculture producers in Ohio are still trying to figure out how the Canadian counter-tariffs, set to begin on Sept. 8, will affect them.
Coviello said data from Youngstown State University’s Export Assistance Network suggests overall, the trade war has been a “net negative.”
Americans 'rethinking who truly has their back'

The trade war has stymied growth potential for some Ohio businesses, such as Shapes Unlimited, which fabricates aluminum gates, fences and other materials. It employs roughly 40 people in the Youngstown/Warren area and has just moved into a new facility with major investments in technology.

"We'd like to further extend our reach into the provinces, but it isn't cost-effective right now,” said CEO Doug Rende, who has been eyeing markets in Ontario and Quebec, given their proximity to northeastern Ohio.
“The issues associated with transportation surcharges, rising fuel costs and obviously the 50 per cent issues associated with tariffs make it untenable.”
Rende’s business has had to work hard to source aluminum amid the tariff war, with levies ranging from 25 to 50 per cent on imported aluminum and an elevated demand for domestic and scrap supply.
“You can't cut off your nose to spite your face until such time as you're finding ways to more aggressively invest in the capacity,” Rende said.
CBC speaks with steel-making company owner Rahim Moloo on the impact of tariffs
The U.S. did once make more of its own raw materials, he said.

“This country abandoned investments in aluminum manufacturing in the 1980s, where there were 30 smelters. Now there's four. So again, [the government's] fire-ready-aim approach is unnecessarily raising costs to the end consumer, making housing costs less [affordable], and certainly negatively impacting by millions of dollars our ability to be more profitable in utilizing this material on an ongoing basis.”
Rende said he’d like to buy Canadian aluminum because of its quality and its proximity to Ohio, which would help significantly shorten the lag time in its supply chain.
Rende’s patience with the trade war is growing thin.

“Regardless of the political affiliations and points of view of your prime minister and our president, the bottom line is it's affecting us as individuals, as consumers, it's affecting us as businesses and business owners, and it's driving up issues that can be easily averted,” he said.
He believes this spat and its knock-on effects will play a role in how Americans vote in November.
“I think the U.S. population is now rethinking who truly has their back — and we'll see.”

articles.title: Eurovision bars countries at war from hosting
articles.summary: A Eurovision victory will no longer guarantee hosting rights if war or a wider security crisis affects the winning country. The change could have particular significance for recent high-flyers…

image.caption: This year’s Eurovision Song Contest was won by Bulgaria’s entrant Dara, who won with her song 'Bangaranga,' meaning the 2027 contest will take place in the country for the first timeImage: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP

blocks.text: Eurovision Song Contest organizers announced rule changes that would prevent countries involved in an armed conflict from hosting the event.
Israel and Ukraine are among the countries the rule could affect, with both having enjoyed recent success in the competition.
What did the Eurovision organizers say?
Eurovision is typically staged by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition as part of a co-production involving members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).

Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," the EBU said.
Canada to join 2027 Eurovision Song Contest
The EBU may commission an independent security assessment if necessary. If the winning broadcaster is deemed unable to stage the contest, another broadcaster will be selected.
Why is the Eurovision changing the rules?
The EBU did not name any particular country as the reason, but Israel finished second at Eurovision in both 2025 and 2026.

Five countries — Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland — boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna, saying they could not participate alongside Israel because of the war in Gaza. Israel is currently involved in the war in Iran.
The new rule formalizes a challenge Eurovision has faced before.

Ukraine hosted the contest in 2017 despite fighting in the east of the country, but after winning Eurovision in 2022 it was unable to stage the following year's event because of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Liverpool instead hosted Eurovision 2023 in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf.
Russia has been excluded from Eurovision since 2022, when the EBU banned it following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
What else is changing about the Eurovision?
Under the new rules, the EBU is raising the minimum age for performers from 16 to 18 to reduce pressure on young artists.
Lead vocals must also be performed live and cannot be supported by pre-recorded voices.
Russia launches Eurovision rival music contest after ban
The EBU said the clarification was intended to protect the integrity of performances and ensure audiences hear the lead singer live.
Eurovision director Martin Green said the contest's rules were reviewed each year to keep the competition fair and transparent.
Next year's contest will be held in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas following Bulgarian pop singer Dara's victory in Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with "Bangaranga."

articles.title: Mozart tribute ends on sour note after mass figurine theft
articles.summary: A playful tribute to Mozart has turned into a whodunit after 210 gold-colored figures disappeared from one of Austria's busiest tourist spots. The mass theft forced organizers to end the outdoor…

image.caption: Some of the figures in the garden before the bulk of them were stolenImage: Barbara Gindl/APA-Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: More than 200 gold-colored Mozart figures have vanished from a public art installation in Salzburg, forcing organizers to end part of the exhibition early.
The theft has disrupted a major public art project marking the 270th anniversary of composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's birth in his home city.
What do we know about the theft of the mini-Mozarts?
The Mozarteum Foundation said 210 of the 320 figures installed in the city's Mirabell Garden had disappeared. The theft forced organizers to end the garden display early.
Organizers had kept some replacements in reserve, but not enough to offset the scale of the theft.
The manufacturer is also on summer holiday, leaving no quick way to replace them.
Several dozen figures remain on display at the Mozarteum and Mozart's birthplace until the end of August.
The figures had been placed in the Mirabell Garden and at several Mozart-related sites around Austria's fourth-largest city.

blocks.caption: German artist Ottmar Hörl said he thought the theft was cheeky, and organizedImage: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The polymer figures show Mozart with his dog Pimperl, a nod to the composer's everyday life in Salzburg.
German conceptual artist Ottmar Hörl, who is behind the display, said he wanted to show Mozart not as a monument but "as a normal human being despite his genius."
Who might have taken the mini-Mozarts?
Hörl is known for installations made up of large numbers of identical figures depicting famous personalities.
"The worst thing for an artist is when his work dissolves," Hörl said.
Hörl said he did not believe tourists had simply walked off with the 50-centimeter (20-inch) figures.
"This is organized theft," he said, suggesting they were probably taken at night after the garden had closed. "I find it a bit cheeky."
Hörl had planned to sell the figures after the exhibition for around €90 each, putting the loss at roughly €20,000.
A previous Hörl display in Bayreuth suffered a similar fate when 100 figures of composer Richard Wagner disappeared.

"That's just the nature of public space," Hörl said. "When you work as an artist in a public space, you mustn't complain about what is happening there. It ranges from destruction to theft. That’s just how it is."

articles.title: EU waste packaging rules: Why small businesses are worried
articles.summary: The EU has introduced new rules targeting packaging waste and "forever chemicals." Although the changes will be phased in slowly, some small sellers have already paused shipments due to the…

image.caption: The EU wants to cut the use of PFAS 'forever chemicals' in food packagingImage: Arnulf Hettrich/IMAGO

blocks.text: What changes from Wednesday?
In a drive to cut waste and improve public health, new European Union rules take effect on Wednesday, banning high levels of PFAS "forever chemicals" in packaging.
Under the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), any new packaging products entering the market will now have to meet tighter standards if designed to come into contact with food.
PFAS have been linked to increased risks of certain cancers and other health conditions.
Although the amount of material people are exposed to from food packaging is usually low, scientists are worried about the long-term effects.
After all, PFAS are highly persistent chemicals and accumulate in the body and the environment.
PFAS are used to make paper and cardboard packaging both grease- and water-resistant and are found in everything from pizza boxes to TV dinners.
Packaging with lower PFAS reduces the risk of these persistent chemicals migrating into food or the natural world when thrown away.
The new rules are in addition to curbs on bisphenol A (BPA) in food-contact materials, which took effect across the EU last month.

blocks.caption: Recycling rates in the EU are rising, but lower than the increase in packaging wasteImage: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Under PPWR, businesses will not be required to recall or destroy packaging or goods that were already on the market before Wednesday.
While consumers won't notice any difference, businesses have fiercely criticized the changes, which also require packaging to meet new sustainability standards.
Are the new packaging rules too complicated?
Many small businesses and online traders believe the additional cost and red tape are too cumbersome.
They complain that they now have to register their packaging in multiple EU states, often with fees.
"Instead of facilitating cross-border trade, the new rules threaten to make it significantly more difficult," warned Händlerbund, the German online retailers' association.
Händlerbund warned its members: "There is no minimum quantity and no exception for small businesses."
EU lawmaker Elisabeth Dieringer of the far-right Freedom Party of Austria has warned that PPWR would mean five-figure costs for medium-sized firms.
"While corporations have their own departments for this [red tape], the Mittelstand [medium-sized firms] has little choice but to 'eat or die,'" she wrote on X on Tuesday.
Several businesses, from sole traders to medium-sized firms, said they had paused deliveries to and within the EU due to the new rules.
"Under these rules, I would need to appoint an authorized representative in every single EU country I send to," wrote the owner of a small online store, Monstaas Workshop, in an Instagram post.
"The cost is around €300 ($346) per country, per year ... these costs are simply not affordable."
From pollution to progress: Tackling PFAS across continents
Swedish embedded electronic devices maker iLabs Electronics said it would halt web shop orders from EU countries.
"The cost and administrative burden [of PPWR] is now out of proportion to our direct sales volume," iLabs wrote on its website.
A petition on change.org had been signed by more than 45,000 people by Wednesday morning, calling on Brussels to "stop destroying EU micro-businesses."
How bad is the EU's packaging waste problem?
According to the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm, EU countries have witnessed a 20% increase in packaging waste over the last decade.
Without PPWR, Brussels says, discarded packaging was set to rise by another 19% by 2030, driven by the boom in online shopping and convenience food.
EU data shows that 178 kilograms (392 pounds) of packaging waste was generated per person across the bloc in 2023. Of this, 35.3 kg was plastic packaging, only 42% of which was recycled.
At 215 kg per capita (in 2023), Germany's waste from packaging is much higher than the EU average.

blocks.caption: Scientists are worried about long-term exposure to 'forever chemicals' in food packagingImage: Tobias Steinmaurer/photosteinmaurer.com/IMAGO

blocks.text: Each EU resident generates the equivalent of roughly half a kilo of packaging waste every day, data from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency, shows.
According to Brussels, the volume of waste has grown faster than recycling rates over the past decade.
Packaging also ⁠accounts ⁠for about 40% of plastic consumption in Europe, an EU official told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday.
What are the EU's long-term waste targets?
Although PFAS is the main focus of this initial phase of PPWR, the EU has set binding targets to cut packaging waste by 5% by 2030 and 15% by 2040.
From 2028, packaging manufacturers will be required to carry standardized labels that clearly show the materials used and how it should be recycled or disposed of.
Some stores, particularly restaurants and cafes, will be required to offer customers reusable packaging as an option, often at no extra charge.
Deposit-and-return schemes for plastic bottles and soda cans, such as those operational in Germany and the Netherlands, will be rolled out across the EU by 2029.
Then from 2030, all packaging placed on the EU market, including single-use plastic bottles, must be designed to be recyclable.
Packaging will also be required to be kept to a minimum to protect the product and fulfill its function.
This measure is meant to reduce the overuse of packaging for marketing purposes.
Meanwhile, single-use plastic packaging for fresh produce will be banned from 2030.
EU states will be able to set their own penalties for non-compliance, with German authorities allowed to impose fines of up to €200,000 ($230,000) for more serious breaches.

articles.title: AI helping create popular mobile sports games
articles.summary: After the World Cup and before the domestic season, many fans still crave more football. Amateur coders are helping to fill this gap.

image.caption: Football mobile games made by amateurs are changing the industryImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO

blocks.text: After the World Cup and before the domestic football season begins, the world's most popular sport tends to enjoy a relatively quiet period. For some though, the need for football remains.

This summer that demand has been met by the creation of a raft of mobile sports games in which players can dive into nostalgia and storytelling. This craze has seemingly been inspired by the viral 82-0 basketball game in which players can draft an all-time NBA starting five by spinning a random wheel for teams and decades.

Inspired by this, Deniz Sancar, a hobbyist coder who works in advertising, created 38-0-0. Sancar told Mobilegamer.biz that despite having no previous coding experience, he built the game overnight with Claude Code, an advanced AI assistant that is designed to help with coding. The game was No. 1 in the UK App Store games charts in June.
Destiny Eleven: From TikTok to France and the world

Another example is Destiny Eleven. Maxence Pigne, a PSG fan and a project manager, was inspired by a game he saw on TikTok that allowed players to play out the career of a professional footballer. After the 2026 World Cup, Pigne released his version, also created with the help of AI assistant Claude, which took the original idea further by offering more variety and choices in the career.
