articles.title: Tennis star Sabalenka supports sport's new sex test policy
articles.summary: The world number one women's tennis player supports the WTA's new sex testing rules. Others are more critical of the policy.

image.caption: Aryna Sabalenka is supportive of tennis' new sex testing rulesImage: Mark Avellino/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I think it's really important to keep the fairness in our tour," said Sabalenka on Monday. "Obviously, biologically, men are way stronger than women, so I feel like it would not be really fair for a woman to compete against a biological man.

"I believe it took them a little while to make this decision and I support it," the Belarussian continued. "If they want to test us all, I'm happy to do that; it's pretty fair, and let's keep it that way."
Fact check: Trans athlete ban — fair or not?
WTA introduces genetic testing

In July 2026, the WTA (Women's Tennis Association) introduced a one-time, mandatory genetic test for all players. As part of the protocol, players will be tested for the SRY gene, a segment of DNA typically found on the Y chromosome. The test can be conducted by a cheek swab or a blood test.
The new policy also includes a document players must sign highlighting disciplinary action is possible if testing is refused.

The previous WTA policy allowed transgender women to compete if their testosterone levels had been lowered to below 2.5 nmol/L continuously for the previous two years. There are no known transgender women currently playing on the WTA Tour.
Sabalenka is currently the best female tennis player in the world, and has been ranked number 1 for 92 consecutive weeks, so her endorsement carries a lot of weight.

On top of that, she competed in the modern edition of Battle of the Sexes in Dubai in 2025 — a match she lost to Nick Kyrgios, a male Australian player. While billed as a way to generate interest in tennis, some were critical of the match-up.

blocks.caption: Imane Khelif was the subject of great debate after her gold medal in ParisImage: Jiang Wenyao/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: World Boxing introduced it in May 2025 after a lengthy and controversial debate around gold medal winner Imane Khelif at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
World Athletics did similarly in September 2025. Then, in the decision likely to have the most far-reaching impacts, the International Olympic Committee updated their guidelines in early 2026.
How has this new policy been received?
Trans athletes have long been politicized.

Riley Gaines, a former swimmer at the US collegiate level, has become a conservative political activist who is known for campaigning against the participation of trans women in women's sports. Recently, Gaines was seen supporting WNBA star Sophie Cunningham, who had said in an ESPN feature that "biological men" should not compete in female sports in order to protect young girls.

Maria Jose Martinez-Patino, whose personal experience with gender verification dramatically impacted sporting policy on the matter in the 1980s, believes new genetic testing for women at elite level is "a setback of several decades."

"It takes me back to the 1950s and 1960s, when women practically had to go through a series of controls, had to undress in front of a panel of doctors," Martinez-Patino told DW in an interview in 2025. "I get the impression that we haven't advanced from a scientific point of view. We've made practically no progress if it's now categorically said that women with X and Y chromosomes are not women."

World Athletics argues that the SRY gene — present in people with a Y chromosome, usually men — "is a reliable indicator for determining biological sex." Martinez-Patino believes, though, that determining someone's sex is not as simple as that.

"It's not black or white. There are more than 60 genetic mutations which I think are not all that complicated to study. Something that I've always said is that it should be done case by case," the Spanish former hurdler said.

articles.title: More cancer-prone? Why younger generations may be at risk
articles.summary: Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or…

image.caption: Lung, gastrointestinal and uterine cancers are becoming more prevalent among younger generations. A new study shows one explanation as to whyImage: CDC/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Susanna was just 28 years old when she was diagnosed with bowel cancer. Andre developed lung cancer when he was only 34. Both of them have turned to social media to talk about their fight against the disease. Neither of them are medical outliers — not anymore.

The German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) has reported a sharp increase in gastrointestinal cancer cases for patients between the ages of 20 and 39. In the US, researchers have observed a similar development, with an even higher disease ratio than in Germany. Younger people are also increasingly being diagnosed with other types of cancers, including those that affect patients' bone marrow or uterus.

Cancer is usually regarded as an age-related disease. According to the German Cancer Aid non-profit, the average age for men and women with cancer is around 69. Cancer cells form when certain sections of the genetic sequence mutate and can no longer be repaired. The older we get, the less reliable our repair system becomes.
Making cancer cell therapy affordable
Gap between chronologal and biological gap increasing

A study by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine, US, has now found a link that could help explain why an increasing number of people under 50 are developing early-onset cancer. The reason, they suggest, is that younger generations are displaying a wider gap between their biological and their chronological ages. In short, they are aging faster.

While the chronological age counts how many years have passed since a person's birth, their biological age describes how much their body has aged, based on the cellular damage accumulated. Individual organs and tissues can age at varying speeds.
In other words, the same person's liver, heart and brain could each have different biological ages, all of which could differ still from the person's actual age.

The recent study has now for the first time established a link between the increasing gap between biological and chronological ages in younger generations on the one hand, and the risk of early-onset cancer on the other, Ron Jachimowicz explains. He's an attending physician and hematologist at the University Hospital Cologne, as well as head of the Max Planck Research Group for Biology of Aging.
"Don't forget, this is a correlative study," Jachomowicz cautions.
Correlation refers to two things appearing in concert, so it looks like they are related. It does not prove causation, which we speak of when one factor causes another.

While results can provide certain indications that seem quite plausible, researchers were already well aware of the fact "that there is an association between biological age and the risk of developing cancer," Jachomowicz says.
Here's what you need to know about breast cancer
DNA, bloodmarkers and telomeres: How to determine one's biological age

It's not easy to determine a person's biological age. Calculating it requires a number of parameters — there is no single, precise test. Instead, epigenetic tests are used to determine chemical alterations of DNA sequences, evaluating certain blood values and measuring the length of so-called telomeres — that is, the repetitive DNA sequence located at the end of chromosomes that function as protective caps.
There are also physiological tests, to monitor various body and organ functions, as well as cognitive evaluations.

Researchers in the study at hand applied a combination of these various measurement techniques to analyze the data of more than 150,000 individuals drawn from the UK Biobank, a British biometric dataset.

They found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a significantly higher gap between their chronological and biological ages than people born between 1950 and 1954. The younger the cohort examined, the wider that gap appeared to grow.
An investigation involving more than 10,000 US individuals revealed an even higher deviation for participants born between 1990 and 1999, compared to a cohort born between 1965 and 1969.

"In Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US, people born in the 1990s face at least fourfold higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those in the 1960s," the authors write in the study.
Prostate cancer: The shift in early detection
Can I improve my biological age?
We used to assume that a healthy lifestyle could make up 75% to 90% of one's biological age. Now we know that's not true, Jachimowicz explains.
"We can influence about 50% of it," he says, "while the other 50% are genetically predetermined."
To help slow the aging process, he recommends "typical lifestyle interventions," such as working out regularly, eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding drugs and alcohol.
And the value of social contacts should not be underestimated, he adds.
It's not easy to say why, on a biological level, younger generations are aging faster than their parents and grandparents. But there are a few hypotheses.
"Younger people are being exposed to earlier and longer obesity," says Tanwei Yuan, an epidemiologist in the Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Aging Research of the DKFZ in Heidelberg.

Other contributing factors are a sedentary lifestyle, and poor sleep quality due to extended periods of time in front of a screen, Yuan adds. She says the current study delivers valuable insights that confirm hypotheses long held by cancer researchers.
She also stresses the value of a healthy lifestyle to help reduce the risk of early-onset cancer.
"If you feel unwell, go to a doctor and ask for the screening," Yuan recommends.
Could microrobots be used to zap cancer cells?

Yuan knows what she's talking about. The 32-year-old researcher says she had felt unwell for quite some time before being diagnosed with intestinal polyps last year. While these can start out benign, if left untreated, polyps can become cancerous. That's why it's important to listen closely to your body and take measures early, she says.
Can my doctor determine my biological age?
In a word: no, says Jachimowicz.
Determining an individual's biological age is the "subject of current scientific research, but in no way a practical routine or part of everyday clinical work."

However, he believes it should be, especially when it comes to initiating early cancer interventions. He believes this current study is particularly valuable because it highlights this path forward for future studies.
"It's still far off in the future," he says, "but it's very exciting."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Binging on cringe: It's as addictive as 'eating junk food'
articles.summary: Flexing achievements? Cringe. Expressing genuine emotions? Cringe. You want to look away, but you can’t. Cringe. It's so addictive, people have built social media careers by monetizing other people's…

image.caption: Five years ago 'cringe' was Youth Word of the Year in Germany. Today, it's just cringeworthyImage: picture alliance/dpa

blocks.text: I feel it. You probably do, too. Someone posts a crying selfie, proposes at a wedding, or confidently sings off-key at karaoke and we cringe.
We cringe when we see something so awkward, embarrassing, or painfully lacking in self-awareness that it makes us recoil.
But we're attracted to it at the same time because — perhaps — we've experienced similar situations ourselves or we know and care about people who have embarrassed themselves and we felt empathy.

And that's why cringe is also known in psychology as secondhand or vicarious embarrassment. We feel it on behalf of other people as well as their feeling it themselves. And sometimes we just enjoy watching other people suffer in a socially awkward situation.
Cringe has an online community: There are cringe compilations, reaction channels on cringe, comedy and other formats built on people's most cringeworthy moments. And people appear to be hooked.

Stefan Hofmann, a clinical psychologist specializing in social anxiety disorder at Marburg University, Germany, says cringe videos are as addictive as junk food: "If you eat junk food, you want more of it [or] even more outrageous stuff," Hofmann said.
Why we can't we look away from cringe moments

Embarrassment is subjective. A bad grade won't embarrass a person who doesn't care about school, but it can trigger real embarrassment in a person for whom academic success is central to their sense of self, their identity.
"If you see a complete stranger misbehaving in public, you might get angry," said Frieder Paulus, a psychologist and neuroscientist at the University of Lübeck, Germany.
"But if your kid is doing the same stuff, you might feel embarrassed, not only for the kid, but also for yourself," said Paulus, "because [you feel] the behavior of the kid reflects [on] you."
Virtual people: Why you can't always trust what you see

Embarrassment belongs to a class of emotions psychologists call 'self-conscious emotions,' alongside shame, pride, and guilt. Within that class, embarrassment functions as a kind of emotional barometer that signals how well you're living up to social norms, and whether you're presenting yourself the way you want to be seen.

For people to feel embarrassment, they need a sense of self, as in some capacity for self-reflection, plus awareness of the social norms and context involved, and to be aware that there is an audience.
Our reactions to embarrassing situations are visible on a brain scan.
"We see failure ... the arousal region [lights] up because something is not okay," said Paulus.
Why cringe is a useful reaction
Matthew Feinberg, a social psychologist at the University of Toronto in Canada, has found that people understand displays of embarrassment as a signal of prosocial behavior.
And that prosocial behavior creates a feeling of trust in the observer — they see that the person who is embarrassed knows they have done something socially awkward or wrong.
The message is: "I did something silly and I want to signal that it wasn't intentional and that I am a good member of society," said Feinberg.

On whether the same logic applies to the person observing someone else's mishap, Feinberg said witnessing embarrassment "triggers a natural response. My mind tells me to respond to that person with sympathy."

Feinberg said vicarious embarrassment may even be a stronger trust signal than being embarrassed yourself: "Possibly … because you're experiencing it even though you didn't do anything. It's an interesting research question that as far as I know hasn't been explored."
Millions followed her — then fake nudes appeared
Exclusion: The cost of too much cringe

Embarrassment is also an expression of our fear that we may be excluded from a group when we do something embarrassing. For a social species such as that of humans and other animals, that can be dangerous.

"Fear of exclusion and fear of negative evaluation by others is painful psychologically as well as physically," said Hofmann. "It is certainly not the same quality of pain [as physical pain], but it's pain nonetheless."

In Hofmann's clinical work, he has tested so-called "social mishap exposures" in which patients embarrass themselves in an intentional and engineered way in an attempt to disprove the beliefs driving their fear or anxiety.

But cringe isn't something we can simply stop feeling. The emotion, researchers suggest, is involuntary and develops from an early age. And that also goes for associated emotions, such as empathy and trust, but also schadenfreude — not all of our addiction to cringe can be explained as an expression of positive emotion.

Hofmann says some people do experience pleasure when they see other people in embarrassing situations. And this distinction between empathy and schadenfreude also matters. If the pull toward cringe content was only about empathy, watching more of it would make us feel worse over time. But people keep watching cringe videos online.

articles.title: What happens next for Infantino and FIFA?
articles.summary: FIFA President Gianni Infantino is under pressure after the failure of his plan to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup. But will he be ousted? And what is needed for that to happen?

image.caption: Gianni Infantino is under pressure to keep his seat as FIFA PresidentImage: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Now that Gianno Infantino has shelved his plans to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup and other FIFA events, UEFA's boycott of FIFA events is over and matches now appear less in danger. Nevertheless, the European governing body says it is now "rebuilding trust" with FIFA — and the story continues to develop rapidly.

As a result, increased focus will be put on women's football when the U20 World Cup starts on September 5 in Poland, and when the U17 World Cup starts in October in Morocco. There are also matches around the world that will decide the qualifiers for next summer's World Cup in Brazil in the same month. Despite there being scant mention in FIFA's subsidiary proposal of the women's game, it will be the first test of life after it.

While a boycott is now off the table, the games will be harder to navigate given the current chaos around the sport's governing body. This is far from ideal for the teams competing, particularly given the tournament's importance.
FIFA revolt: Can Infantino's Trump connection save him?
Football associations have pulled support for Infantino
With UEFA, Europe's football governors, forming a united front, it is assumed that most, if not all, football associations on the continent will withdraw their support in the coming days.

The first nation to publicly drop their support for Gianni Infantino was Finland, last week. Wales followed on Monday, saying in a statement that "failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept," before England followed suit later in the day.

On Tuesday, Jordan FA President Ali bin Hussein accused Infantino of "blackmail", claiming FIFA offered to help solve the kingdom's problems in exchange for his endorsement. This is in stark contrast to some of the other Asian associations, such as Qatar, the UAE and Sri Lanka, who have publicly supported Infantino.

Germany's FA (DFB) is the biggest sports association in the world, but has yet to officially withdraw its support. It is expected to though, especially when considering the recent words of DFB Director Andreas Rettig. The 63-year-old recently told Stern magazine in an interview that Infantino's recent actions have led to "an irreparable loss of trust" and that football needs to "hit the reset button. We need a different culture. Because trust is the hardest currency."

"From my perspective, Mr. Infantino has invested a great deal of time, money, and energy into maintaining his power structure. Clearly, many decisions served primarily to consolidate his own position," added Retting.
FIFA presidential election next year
The election for Infantino's post is on March 18, 2027, at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco.

He will run for re-election as president for a final four-year term, looking to gain 106 votes from FIFA's 211 member states (Uefa has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10) to win. Each state gets a vote and voting is done in a secret ballot, which takes time.

However, it seems as though Infantino is increasingly under pressure. Following the resignation of Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro last week, reports indicate that the FIFA President has called an emergency meeting on Wednesday.

If 19 of the 37 members of the FIFA Council, the organization's main executive body, vote in favor of his resignation then Infantino may well be out of office sooner rather than later. Several members of the council, including Germany's Bernd Neuendorf, have publicly crititcized Infantino for failing to consult them about his latest plans.

There might also be an Extraordinary FIFA Congress if 43 associations formally request it. Given that UEFA has 55 members, it holds the power to request it at any time. For Infantino to be voted out through a vote of no confidence, 106 votes would be required.

Before his venture to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors ended in chaos after widespread condemnation, Infantino looked almost certain to win re-election. The reported revenues from this summer's World Cup were $15 billion (€13 billion), a significantly higher number than expected and one that would have strengthened his position in the organization, given that much of it would be redistibuted among the member organizations.
No clear candidates to succeed Infantino

There has been a lot of speculation about who might succeed Infantino since his position has come under threat in the last week, but it is too soon to really know the legitimacy of any claims. In any case, any potential challengers must declare their candidacy by 18 November.

Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Paris Saint-Germain chairman, had been touted as a potential candidate given his increasingly influential position in world football. However, the Qatari recently ruled himself out, with a representative for the executive reportedly saying via Politico: "Nasser has absolutely no ambition, no intention, no interest in the Fifa role." Qatar is one of the few federations to have publicly backed Infantino in recent days.
The most obvious candidate is the current UEFA President, Alexander Ceferin, but the Slovenian lawyer is reportedly also not interested in the role.

Concacaf (the confederation of North and Central America and the Caribbean) president Victor Montagliani is one of the few candidates who has expressed interest in the role in the past, but it is unclear whether the man who speaks English, French, Italian and Spanish is ready to challenge now.

Outspoken Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness has supporters, and, after an initial failure, reached the UEFA Executive Committee in 2025. But the outspoken style that has won her admirers is thought not to have the broad appeal needed in a FIFA candidate. Some also believe her gender may count against her.

Finally, AFC chief, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who lost out to Infantino in the 2016 election, could be a contender if the AFC breaks ranks from FIFA in the way UEFA have. A member of Bahrain’s ruling House of Khalifa, the 60-year-old called Infantino's actions "totally unacceptable" and may be tempted to go against him again, though human rights questions contributed to his previous defeat.

articles.title: The economic toll of Spain's wildfires
articles.summary: Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent them?

image.caption: In recent years, Spain has slashed investments in measures to prevent wildfiresImage: Cesar Manso/AFP

blocks.text: Charred tree stumps, melted asphalt, burned-out cars and destroyed buildings: The wildfires in southern Europe are leaving a trail of devastation and causing billions of euros in damage.

Spain's economy in particular is at risk of being choked by clouds of ash. According to the EU's Copernicus Earth observation system, around 206,000 hectares of forest in Spain have already gone up in flames this year.

"According to the European Commission, the economic impact of wildfires in Spain in 2022 amounted to approximately €7.1 billion ($8.1 billion), representing around 4.5% of the country's GDP. This figure reflects not only the direct costs of firefighting but also the long-term economic consequences of recovering the affected areas," Emilio Vizuete Luciano, an economist at the University of Barcelona, told DW.

The fires often devastate the local economy and disrupt trade in the affected regions, Luciano says. "Tourism is also severely affected. Given Spain's strong dependence on tourism, the disappearance of this activity in fire-affected regions has particularly significant economic repercussions."
Has Europe lost control of its wildfires?
Wildfires slow economic growth

Climate economist Sarah Meier of Swiss public research university ETH Zurich has taken a closer look at the economic losses caused by wildfires in southern Europe. Her findings show that in regions affected by at least one wildfire, the growth rate fell by between 0.11% and 0.18%.

According to a 2023 study she co-authored, the decline in growth was even greater when several wildfires occurred simultaneously, rising to as much as 4.5% depending on the extent of the fires. "Our calculations are an average for the period from 2011 to 2018," she explains.
And she issues a stark warning: "The costs become particularly high when wildfires reach larger cities, something that has so far been very rare in southern Europe."

The European Environment Agency (EEA) has also calculated the economic losses caused by wildfires in previous years. In 2017, when nearly 990,000 hectares burned across southern Europe, the losses amounted to almost €10 billion.
Europe is burning
According to the European Commission, the EU loses around 500,000 hectares of land to wildfires every year. Spain, Greece and France are among the countries where wildfires are most widespread.

The economic damage goes far beyond losses to tourism. It also includes the loss of biodiversity, declining forestry revenues, soil erosion, destroyed infrastructure and property, as well as the costs of fighting the fires.

A heated debate has erupted in Spain over the cost of fighting wildfires. Since 2009, investment in prevention has actually been declining — even though the number and scale of wildfires have reached alarming levels over the past decade.

According to official figures, spending on wildfire prevention in Spain fell from €364 million in 2009 to €144 million in 2024. Over the same period, annual spending on actually fighting and extinguishing fires remained stable at around €417 million.

For economist Luciano, there is "a certain irony" to this because prevention has been proven to be the best long-term investment. "It is far cheaper than fighting wildfires once they have already broken out."
Spain's high cost of firefighting

The Spanish forestry services company Forescat has estimated that fighting and extinguishing wildfires costs around €19,000 per hectare. Nearly 400,000 hectares of forest went up in flames in Spain in 2025, amounting to costs of around €7.6 billion.

It's still too early to say how much fighting this year's fires will cost Spain; however, Maria Inmaculada Marmol Tardaguila of MATS, a social organization representing public-sector healthcare workers, says things cannot continue this way.

"Continuing to rely on the heroic efforts of firefighting crews to keep our forests safe is both ecological recklessness and fiscal irresponsibility," she notes on the organization's platform, which has also warned of an increase in respiratory illnesses caused by wildfire smoke.

"The solution is not to keep buying more and more firefighting aircraft, but, for example, to remove combustible material such as deadwood from forests before the first spark catches," she points out.
Unless public officials understand this, she warns, Spain will continue to "burn through its budget at the same rate as its forests burn."
This piece was originally published in German.
Spain turns to grazing to curb wildfires

articles.title: Germany: As temperatures rise, so does climate skepticism
articles.summary: Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?

image.caption: The heatwave in Germany is thought to have killed 10,000 people alreadyImage: Jochen Tack/picture alliance

blocks.text: Climate skeptics are no longer a small but noisy minority. They are now "a mass phenomenon," according to researchers at Flensburg University.

In a study published in the scientific journal Global Environmental Change, authors Katharina Gies and Emanuel Deutschmann reported that between 2022 and 2023 there was a big jump in skeptical attitudes to climate change among the majority of the 3,074 people surveyed. Some 59% said they had more doubts about climate change in 2023 than they had had in the previous year.

The researchers wrote that the respondents' individual economic situations could not be considered the primary explanation for the increase in skepticism. Other factors, they said, were much more decisive: A right-leaning political orientation, distrust of state institutions, and dissatisfaction with democracy.

Social psychologist Marlene Altenmüller said the Flensburg publication is important and fascinating, though she has doubts about its alarming tone. Other studies show that "the number of people who have doubts is still very small," she says. Altenmüller, a junior professor at the Leibniz Institute for Psychology in Trier, conducts research into science reception: How people perceive scientific evidence, and what they think about the scientific system and its researchers.

Altenmüller's research indicates that people in Germany do not have fundamental doubts about scientific evidence. Rather, it varies depending on the topic, and the view the group to which people feel they belong has of the topic.
Extreme heat: Can Europe adapt to climate change?
If a group has doubts about climate change, so do its members
Her work, and that of many other researchers, also shows that politically right-leaning people express more skepticism about climate change.

"If right-wing parties were suddenly to discover that we should in fact take action against climate change, my assumption is that the followers of these parties would also believe in climate change and would support political measures," Altenmüller said.

Nor does she believe that climate skeptics have a different personality structure. Instead, climate skepticism is more likely to be down to the fact that "people orientate themselves according to their group and its identity." The credo for most people is that content is secondary, or, as Altenmüller calls it, "Party over policy."

Underlying this is something psychologists call motivated reception. People always see the world through the lens of their own desires, ideas, values, and political ideologies, and anything that cannot be squared with their own ideas and values tends to be disparaged. Altenmüller's research demonstrates that all of us are predisposed to seeing the world through our own filters.
From climate skepticism to conspiracy theories

Both Altenmüller and the Flensburg researchers emphasize that climate change skepticism comes in different guises. One form is the rejection of climate policy measures. The basis for this may be the assumption that it won't be all that bad, or doubt that human activity is the cause. Another is the belief that all the talk about climate change is simply a con, a conspiracy.

This is the focus of research of Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive science at the universities of Bristol and Potsdam. Among other things, he examines the persistence of misinformation and conspiracy theories, and is interested in the parameters that determine whether people reject or accept scientific proofs, especially in connection with vaccines and climate change. "Certain people are more susceptible to conspiracy theories than others," he said.

The COVID-19 pandemic made this very apparent. Lewandowsky argues that for some people, conspiracy theories that apportion blame for a particular situation provide a welcome opportunity to escape from feelings like fear and loss of control. "That offers some brief psychological comfort to people," Lewandowsky says.

However, he goes on to explain that the comfort they derive from assigning blame does not last long. "There's good evidence to suggest that people who do fall into that rabbit hole over time are suffering," he said. "They're less likely to hold their jobs. They lose social contacts. They become mentally challenged."
How climate change forces Indian farmers to stay single
Why climate skepticism is hardly an issue in India

Climate skepticism and conspiracy theories are mostly a Western phenomenon. Researchers observe them the most in the US, Europe, and Australia. In India and other countries of the global south, climate change is already a question of daily survival, and has been for some time. "In India, a lot of people still suffer from [not] getting access to clean drinking water," says Jagadish Thaker, senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, Australia, and an expert in climate change communication.
For years now, he says, people in the global south have been experiencing first-hand the ways that climate change is exacerbating problems through rising temperatures and extreme weather events.

Consequently, measures to reduce emissions and adapt to changing living conditions are not seen as a matter of political ideology. According to Thaker, people in India are trying to counteract their own vulnerability to climate change while still trying to develop economically.
Countering climate skepticism with respect

Heatwaves and other extreme weather events are a direct threat to human life in Germany, as has become apparent during this summer's heatwaves, which are reported to have killed as many as 10,000 people already.
This is why the authors of the Flensburg study are urging people to take climate change skepticism seriously if they are to successfully anchor climate protection measures in society.

Thaker believes the media plays a decisive role. He believes there is still a general lack of information and understanding of the effects of climate change. "The media coverage of extreme weather events, while it's a lot, it is dramatic, and unfortunately doesn't mention climate change."

Altenmüller says it's important to keep emphasizing that there is a scientific consensus that climate change is anthropogenic, or, caused by human activity. Sometimes, she says, it does matter who says it. Research shows that some scientific disciplines are perceived as more biased than others. Consequently, economists have a better chance of their message reaching a wide audience than sociologists.

Taking the values of people who express skepticism into account could also help to communicate a different point of view to them, says Altenmüller. Communication must emphasize not only the restrictions that need to be imposed through political measures, but also the opportunities arising from this.

People who have themselves experienced extreme weather events probably find it easier to shift their perspective. This is why Lewandowsky is hopeful that the this year's heatwaves and wildfires will make a difference. "At some point, people's personal experiences matter," he says.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
articles.summary: In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

image.caption: Exposure and working conditions play a larger role in women's heat risk than biology or geneticsImage: CRISTINA QUICLER/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Observing recent heatwaves in Europe, one pattern has often been remarked on: More women appear to be dying than men. During Europe's then-record summer of 2022, a study found 56% more heat-related deaths among women than men, drawing on mortality data from 35 countries.

Germany, which has just logged its deadliest heat season since 2016, with close to 9,800 heat-related deaths by mid-July, according to the Robert Koch Institute, is seeing the same pattern again this year.
Are hormones making heatwaves more dangerous for women?
Some of the recent coverage has leaned on the hormonal reading that women's bodies simply aren't equipped for heat. They sweat less, carry more body fat, and progesterone nudges core temperature up.

But scientists who study the effect of heat on the human body say that's largely incorrect. "Overall, studies usually show only slightly more vulnerability to heat in women compared to men," saidAlexandra Schneider, an environmental epidemiologist and deputy director of the Institute of Epidemiology at Helmholtz Munich. "It's not really a very strong signal."

The small differences that do exist are real: Women do have a lower sweat rate, less skin area relative to body size, and fat distribution that affects thermoregulation. Hormones play a role too, but unevenly across a lifetime.
Schneider points to one group in particular: Women past menopause, when cardiovascular risk climbs. Older women with existing heart disease, she says, are probably at the highest risk of all.

But even in those cases, she doesn't think biology is the main cause for the extra deaths during a heatwave. "The living conditions, the social environment where women live, makes probably even more of a risk than just the differences in hormone status."
How to survive heat waves in the city
A research gap, not a biological difference

Toby Mündel, a kinesiology professor at Brock University in Canada, who studies extreme human environments, says that the impact is "overstated," when asked whether there's a real biological basis for the claim that women are more likely to die in heatwaves.
The factors that most determine how a person copes with a heatwave, Mündel says, are age, body size, fitness and habitual activity, and not biological sex.

Sweating is one example. Even though women do sweat less, that doesn't make them more vulnerable, because they compensate in another way. "They send blood flow to the skin, vasodilation, much better than males do," Mündel says, meaning their blood vessels widen more efficiently, moving heat to the surface where it can escape.

Pregnancy, which many assume must be dangerous, is another example. "As a woman progresses through pregnancy, she actually becomes better at handling heat," Mündel says. He draws a clear line between physiology and circumstance: There are good reasons not to have pregnant women doing heavy outdoor labor in extreme heat. But their bodies aren't the reason.
Why does the data suggest otherwise?

Partly, Mündel's argument is based on what gets measured. Studies often count hospital and emergency admissions, and women are far more likely than men to seek medical help. "That is not a physiological thing," he says. "Are they actually struggling, or have they just sought help earlier?"
Underneath it all sits a research gap. "We have about a hundred times as much data and evidence on men. We have nearly zero on women," Mündel says. "It's like comparing cats and dogs."

Numbers from Germany point in the same direction. The Robert Koch Institute attributes the higher female death toll to the fact that women make up a larger share of the oldest age groups. Its estimates also break down deaths per 100,000 people, and by that measure, the picture flips.
In every older age band this summer, the male death rate is higher than the female one. In other words, more women are dying in heatwaves only because more very old women are alive.
In scorching Taipei, locals seek ways to survive urban heat
The real risk is exposure for women, not biology
If the gap isn't physiological, where does it come from?
Laurie Parsons, a researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, studies how heat stress moves through the global economy in construction, garment factories, farming, driving, street vending.

Across the board, he says, women spend 30% to 50% more of their working time above heat-stress thresholds than men. In construction, when comparing men and women doing the same job, the figure rises to around 50%.

The reasons, he says, are structural. Women often wear more clothing for the same job. Men are more confident asking for breaks. And where men's work is visibly strenuous, it's recognized as a heat risk and rewarded with rest. But women's work is steadier, less obviously punishing, and gets no such relief.

Parsons compares it to the difference between a plane crash and asbestos exposure: One is a sudden, visible catastrophe, the other a slow, constant harm that's easy to miss. "Male heat stress tends to be this taller risk, where you get relatively visible moments of physical distress that can be managed," he says. "Female heat stress is constantly there, but much less visible, because it doesn't have those same obvious peaks in the working day."

blocks.caption: Long working hours, limited breaks, and repeated exposure to heat - women often face greater burdens under these conditionsImage: Aaron Favila/AP/dpa

blocks.text: Then the shift ends, he says. Men rest, but women cook, clean and care for children.
Heat also cuts into pay. Parsons says workers under heat stress are around 30% less productive in the garment sector, which he says is the easiest to quantify.

In formal jobs, workers make up for it with longer hours during the hottest part of the day, feeding what he calls "a vicious cycle" of worsening health and falling output. The self-employed have no such buffer. For them, heat stress just means less income, which ripples the wider family over time.
For Parsons, the starting premise is flawed. "Heat stress is not an atmospheric condition," he says. "It is a social condition, which happens within particular atmospheric circumstances."
Edited by Ben Knight
